\lim\limits_{\theta \to (\pi/2)^{-}} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \pm\infty \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \lim\limits_{\theta \to (\pi/2)^{+}} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \pm\infty. $$ Let's now verify that this is true: Using techniques discussed in previous lessons, it's straightforward to show that $$ x'(\theta)=-\sin\theta-\cos(2\theta), \qquad y'(\theta)=\cos\theta - \sin2\theta. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\right) \\ & =-\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\right).\end{aligned} $$ We already know that substituting $\theta = \dfrac\pi 2$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ so evaluating this limit by direct substitution won't work. However, we can evaluate this limit using L'Hopital's rule. - Applying L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the left-sided limit, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\right) \\ & =-\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{′}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{′}}\right) \\ & =-\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}\right) \\ & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}\right).\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\ & =1-2 \\ & =-1.\end{aligned} $$ For the limit in the denominator, it can be shown that $$ \lim\limits_{\theta \to (\pi/2)^-} \left(\cos\theta - 2\sin(2\theta)\right) = 0^-, $$ where the notation $0^-$ means that the denominator approaches zero from the negative numbers. Therefore, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}\right) \\ & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{-}} \\ & =\infty .\end{aligned} $$ - Using similar methods, it can be shown that the right-sided limit is $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}\right) \\ & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{+}} \\ & =-\infty .\end{aligned} $$ Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, we conclude that there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ ![](images/ea/ea0a03e575d962bd8d69505e20166dcc60c77cfe933f30762bb81296ccf7a797.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "7b372073-8035-5855-9367-f29c35485805" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6269 :tutorial/title "Using Limits to Find Vertical Tangents"} {:db/id 17592186189381 :tutorial/content "The first property to consider is how to recover the marginal CDFs of $X$ and $Y$ from the joint CDF. Suppose the joint CDF of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by $$ F(x,y)= {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}( 1 - {e}^{- x} ) ( 1 - {e}^{- 2 y} ) , & x \ge 0 , \hspace{0.278em} y \ge 0 \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. } $$ Let's calculate $F_Y(y),$ the marginal CDF of $Y$ using the following property: $$ F_Y(y) = F(\infty,y) = \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} F(x,y) $$ Therefore, for $y \geq 0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =\lim_{x\to \infty }[(1-{e}^{-x})(1-{e}^{-2y})] \\ & =(1-{e}^{-2y})\lim_{x\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}) \\ & =(1-{e}^{-2y})\lim_{x\to \infty }(1-0) \\ & =1-{e}^{-2y}.\end{aligned} $$ So, the full expression for the marginal CDF is as follows: $$ F_Y(y)= {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}1 - {e}^{- 2 y} , & \hspace{1em} y \ge 0 \\ 0 , & \hspace{1em} \text{otherwise}\end{array} \right. } $$ Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "86beb7b1-97a4-556a-840d-19cd1cf55cd3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6304 :tutorial/title "Recovering a Marginal CDF"} {:db/id 17592186189410 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables. It is known that the conditional probability density function $f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, 1)$ is given by $$ f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, 1) = {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}4 {y}^{3} , & \hspace{1em} 0 \le y \le 1 \\ 0 , & \hspace{1em} \text{otherwise}\end{array} \right. } $$ and that $$ \mu_{Y|1}=\dfrac{4}{5}. $$ What is the conditional variance $\textrm{Var}\big[Y \,|\, X=1\big]?$ The conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\ & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned} $$ where $$ \textrm{E}\big[Y^2 \,| \, X=x \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y^2 \, f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x) \: \textrm{d}y. $$ Therefore, we obtain $$ \begin{array}{cc}\text{E} [ {Y}^{2} | X = 1 ] & = {\int }_{- \infty }^{\infty } {y}^{2} {f}_{Y | X} ( y | 1 ) \text{d} y \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} {y}^{2} \cdot 4 {y}^{3} \text{d} y \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} 4 {y}^{5} \text{d} y \\ & = {[ \frac{2 {y}^{6}}{3} ]}_{0}^{1} \\ & = \frac{2}{3} .\end{array} $$ Finally, $$ \begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \text{Var} [ Y \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} X = 1 ] & \displaystyle = \text{E} [ {Y}^{2} \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} X = 1 ] - {\mu }_{Y | 1}^{2} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{2}{3}} - {( {\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} )}^{2} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{2}{3}} - {\displaystyle \frac{16}{25}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{2}{75}} .\end{array} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "51fd1dbf-d36f-5e8c-b62b-ede292dae6da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6490 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:answer/id #uuid "7c6590b5-a0d8-52fa-9846-bb7a27d9a977" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f^{-1}(x) = (\frac{x}{2} - 5)^{2}" :db/id 17592186189903} {:db/id 17592186192389 :question/id #uuid "2393d607-0f73-59f3-9a5f-ebe45050dda9" :question/math-academy-id "e-10106" :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown mean. Find the likelihood function of the sample $0.4,\, -0.3,\, -2.2,\, -0.4.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is $$ L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta). $$ In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta$ and variance $\sigma^2 = 1,$ for which the probability density function is $$ f(x; \theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\theta}{\sigma} \right)^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty). $$ We can calculate the likelihood function as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\ & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\ & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\ & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned} $$ where $$ \displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i $$ and $$ \displaystyle C = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i^2. $$ For our sample, we have that $n=4,$ and $$ \begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\ & =0.4+(-0.3)+(-2.2)+(-0.4) \\ & =-2.5 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\ & =(0.4)^{2}+(-0.3)^{2}+(-2.2)^{2}+(-0.4)^{2} \\ & =5.25\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(5.25-2(-2.5)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\ & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{-2.625\,-\,2.5\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186192391 :question/id #uuid "19e7744e-9d87-5ad1-9648-029e7dc8e565" :question/math-academy-id "e-10113" :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{8}$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1^2),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{8},$ you're given that $$ \sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 11.8, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 25.2. $$ Find the log-likelihood function of the sample. *Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta$ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* $$ f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty). $$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned} $$ In our case, we are given a sample of $n=8$ independent normal (-\infty,\infty). $$ First, let's write down the log-density function: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}\end{aligned} $$ Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\ & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\ & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned} $$ We are told that $$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 11.8, $$ $$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 25.2, $$ and $n=8.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{8}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(25.2-2\theta \cdot 11.8+8{\theta }^{2}) \\ & =-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-12.6+11.8\theta -4{\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186192404 :question/id #uuid "8760afc0-a7fb-5398-a585-c5559c9d1bb2" :question/math-academy-id "e-10458" :question/problem "The function $f(x) = 3\sqrt{x + k} - 2$ has an inverse Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives $$ x = 3\sqrt{y + k} - 2. $$ Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}x & =3\sqrt{y+k}-2 \\ 3\sqrt{y+k} & =x+2 \\ \sqrt{y+k} & =\frac{1}{3}(x+2) \\ {(\sqrt{y+k})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}(x+2))}^{2} \\ y+k & =\frac{1}{9}(x+2)^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9}(x+2)^{2}-k\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the inverse function is $$ f^{-1}(x) = \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned} $$ }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum $({x}_{1},{y}_{1}),\,…,\,({x}_{20},{y}_{20})$ of $n=20$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=2,$ the mean square error of the model is $8,$ and $$ \displaystyle {S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}=24, $$ find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line. *Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.101)=0.025,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $18$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is given by $$ \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})} $$ *" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations: - $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and - $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample. In this case, we have that $$ \widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=3.5+5x. $$ We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as $$ \underbrace{{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}. $$ Note the following: - $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample. - $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom. - $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by $$ \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})} $$ where we have: - $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model: $$ \text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2} $$ where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model. - ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula: $$ {S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} $$ To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows: - **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=3.5+5x,$ our point estimate is $$ {\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=3.5. $$ - **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have $$ \alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025. $$ We are given that $P(T>2.101)=0.025.$ As a result, $$ {t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{18,0.025}=2.101. $$ Now, we can compute the margin of error: $$ {t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.101\cdot \sqrt{8\cdot (\frac{1}{20}+\frac{{2}^{2}}{24})}≈2.8 $$ - **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval: $$ {\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=3.5\pm 2.8 $$"} {:db/id 17592186192980 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f6dfb82b-0623-5a54-9e30-26de68114a6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80.8 ± 19.6" :db/id 17592186189767} {:answer/id #uuid "1ada4df4-b2a8-5cb1-809b-c3a0d78875ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.7 ± 2.9" :db/id 17592186189768} {:answer/id #uuid "1aebf307-0be2-5a98-bd88-a52683674c70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80.8 ± 22.2" :db/id 17592186189769} {:answer/id #uuid "43f6113e-538e-5116-9405-ad39242dffee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80.8 ± 24.0" :db/id 17592186189770} {:answer/id #uuid "72dad82e-a8b2-548c-9beb-74f808fb9bcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80.8 ± 14.3" :db/id 17592186189771}] :answer-field/id #uuid "74938b78-d8bf-5ec0-b4ec-a53676973c06" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186189766}] :question/id #uuid "723bb838-d847-552c-a43f-14e4d26fe642" :question/math-academy-id "q-143261" :question/problem "

:question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned} $$ In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is $$ \begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned} $$ We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned} $$ Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =3!\cdot 4!\cdot 2!=6\cdot 24\cdot 2=288, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3+4+2=9.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-3\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡288.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, $$ a+b+c=-3+9+288=294. $$"} {:db/id 17592186193073 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d142c298-92b6-5eb8-b79c-25b9f7c9fa90" :question/math-academy-id "q-159772" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼Po(\theta )$ with unknown rate parameter $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample $$ {x}_{1}=4,\,{x}_{2}=2,\,{x}_{3}=1,\,{x}_{4}=2. $$ The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by $$ l(\theta )=a\theta +b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡c. $$ Find the value of $a+b+c.$ *Hint: The probability mass function for a Poisson distribution is given by* $$ f(x)=\frac{{\theta }^{x}{e}^{-\theta }}{x!},\,x=0,1,2,… $$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\ & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned} $$ In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is $$ \begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned} $$ We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\ & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned} $$ Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =4!\cdot 2!\cdot 1!\cdot 2!=24\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 2=96, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =4+2+1+2=9.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡96.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, $$ a+b+c=-4+9+96=101. $$"} {:db/id 17592186193232 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid Given that $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $X,$ what is the second principal component of the data?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If $$ {\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>{\lambda }_{3} $$ are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: - the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$ - the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$ - the $3$rd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to the $3$rd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}.$ Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is $$ \begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\ & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\ & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\ & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned} $$ where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that: - $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $3\times 3$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and - $V$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data. So, the second principal component is $$ \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186193369 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices The standard normal curve has *extremely thin* tails! ![](images/5c/5c73c5fd8613e99814ab47a1a41a46a4511991d3c7eeca33eefe5913a907c10c.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ef808e14-51a9-5fb0-8ce6-b1cd4f760d6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10790 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186193806 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be an $n \times m$ observation matrix with standardized data, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Suppose we have the following **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $X{:}$ $$ X = U \Sigma V^T $$ Note that in the SVD, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal, which implies that $U^T U = I$ (the identity matrix). Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of $X$ can be derived as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\ & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\ & =\frac{1}{n-1}(V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T})(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\ & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}\underbrace{({U}^{T}U)}_{I}Σ{V}^{T} \\ & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T}.\end{aligned} $$ The expression $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Now, notice the following: - The matrix $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ is a diagonal $m \times m$ matrix with the eigenvalues of $C$ (in descending order) on the main diagonal. - The matrix $V$ is an $m \times m$ matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of $C.$ To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix $X,$ the columns of the matrix $V$ in the SVD are the **principal components** of the data." :tutorial/id #uuid "fec0f21a-271c-5558-9427-a50d62b4e629" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14786 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186193809 :tutorial/content "To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables $Y = XV.$ The covariance of $Y$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{C}_{Y}=\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y=\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV)={V}^{T}\underbrace{(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)}_{{C}_{X}}V.\end{aligned} $$ Since $V$ contains the eigenvectors of $C_X,$ the matrix $C_Y$ is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $C_X{:}$ $$ C_Y = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\lambda }_{1} & \ldots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \ldots & {\lambda }_{m}\end{array} \right]}. $$ The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like $Y=XV.$ Therefore, the total variance of $Y$ is the same as the total variance of $X{:}$ $$ \textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i. $$ Substituting $\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},$ we conclude that the total variance is *proportional to* the sum of the squared singular values: $$ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.} $$ Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "9ab13b86-9d0f-53e4-b7b1-bee88604c031" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14956 :tutorial/title "Finding the Total Variance"} {:db/id 17592186193816 :tutorial/content "Let's return to our first example, where we wish to conduct a hypothesis test to determine whether a particular coin is unfair. Recall the following: - We defined $p$ as "the probability that the coin lands on heads when tossed randomly." - Since we want to check whether the coin is unfair, we have the following null and alternative hypotheses: $$ \begin{aligned}{H}_{0}:p & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {H}_{1}:p & \ne \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned} $$ - The significance level is $\alpha = 5\%$. Under the conditions specified in the null hypothesis, the random variable $X$ is a binomial random variable given by $$ X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right) $$ The probability mass function of $X$ under the null hypothesis is shown below. ![](images/79/79306d39f30f044beb30aaa7f6356b7a226c0f3958597d2e230601d51474b801.png) Note the following: - When we select a significance level $\alpha$ in a two-tailed test, the convention is to allow $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ at either tail. - So if $\alpha = 5\%$, we have $\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = 2.5\%$ at either tail. Now, suppose we conduct our experiment and get $2$ heads out of $10$ tosses. If the result $X=2$ is statistically significant, it will lie in the critical region in the *left* tail of the probability distribution of $f(x)$. We can compute the probability of getting $$ X\leq 2 $$ heads under the null hypothesis using our knowledge of the binomial distribution: $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle P ( X \le 2 ) & \displaystyle = P ( X = 0 ) + P ( X = 1 ) + P ( X = 2 ) \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = \left( \genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{0} \right) {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{0} {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10 - 0} + \left( \genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{1} \right) {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{1} {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10 - 1} + \left( \genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{2} \right) {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{2} {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10 - 2} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = 1 \cdot {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10} + 10 \cdot {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10} + 45 \cdot {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = 56 \cdot {( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} )}^{10} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = 0.055 \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = 5.5 \mathrm{\% } .\end{array}} $$ This probability is *larger than* $$ \dfrac\alpha2 = 2.5\% $$ This means that our result is *not* statistically significant. In other words, it is "likely enough" that this event could have occurred if the null hypothesis is true. Therefore, we should *not* reject the null hypothesis. Consequently, we conclude that the coin is fair." :tutorial/id #uuid "3e8ee785-4e26-5bbc-87e7-3fcd0ffc5333" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5430 :tutorial/title "Conducting a Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test"} {:db/id 17592186193825 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll use our knowledge of solving radical equations to compute inverses of radical functions. For example, let's consider the following radical function: $$ f(x) = 3\sqrt{x} + 2 $$ To compute the inverse of $f(x),$ we follow the usual four steps: **Step 1:** First, we replace $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$ $$ y = 3\sqrt{x} + 2 $$ **Step 2:** Then, we swap $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ $$ x = 3\sqrt{y} + 2 $$ **Step 3:** Next, we solve for $y\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}x & =3\sqrt{y}+2 \\ 3\sqrt{y} & =x-2 \\ \sqrt{y} & =\frac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}(x-2))}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9}(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned} $$ **Step 4:** Finally, we replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)\mathbin{:}$ $$ f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x - 2)^2 $$ **Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are $$ x \geq 0, \qquad f(x) \geq 2. $$ Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are $$ x \geq 2, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq 0. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "24753060-4992-520a-b948-f4e049858666" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6511 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186193893 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we made use of the following results: $$ \textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] = \sigma^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) $$ Let's now derive these. First, we will show that $$ S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i. $$ We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})\overset{―}{y} \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}) \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\overset{―}{x} \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}n\overset{―}{x} \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}.\end{aligned} $$ Next, we define $k_i$ as $$ k_i = \dfrac{ x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}. $$ The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra: - $$ \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0 $$ - $$ \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1 $$ - $$ \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}} $$ Now, recall that $$ \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x}. $$ We can rewrite our expression for $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\widehat{{\beta }_{0}} & =\overset{―}{y}-{\beta }_{1}\overset{―}{x} \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-\frac{{S}_{xy}}{{S}_{xx}}\overset{―}{x} \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}}{{S}_{xx}}\overset{―}{x} \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}\overset{―}{x} \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}\end{aligned} $$ We're now in a position to compute $\textrm{E}[{\widehat{\beta_0} }]$ and $\textrm{Var}[{\widehat{\beta_0} }].$ - For the mean, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[\widehat{{\beta }_{0}}] & =\frac{1}{n}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i}{y}_{i}]-\overset{―}{x}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}\text{E}[{y}_{i}]-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i}\text{E}[{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i}) \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}[{\beta }_{0}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}+{\beta }_{1}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{x}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}[{\beta }_{0}{\cancel{{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}}}^{0}+{\beta }_{1}{\cancel{{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{x}_{i}}}^{1}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\ & =\frac{{\beta }_{0}}{n}{\sum }_{i}1+\frac{{\beta }_{1}}{n}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\ & =\frac{{\beta }_{0}}{n}\cdot n+\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1}-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\ & ={\beta }_{0}.\end{aligned} $$ - For the variance, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\widehat{{\beta }_{0}}] & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i}{y}_{i}]+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}{\sum }_{i}\text{Var}[{y}_{i}]+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{y}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}n{\sigma }^{2}+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}^{2}{\sigma }^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}n{\sigma }^{2}+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sigma }^{2}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{n}{\sigma }^{2}+{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}{\sigma }^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{S}_{xx}} \\ & ={\sigma }^{2}(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}}).\end{aligned} $$ So finally, we have $$ \widehat{\beta_0} \sim N\left(\beta_0,\sigma^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right). $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e3cbadc-9a0c-5925-af3f-b47ca4a2ff80" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6968 :tutorial/title "Expectation and Variance of Intercept Parameter Estimates"} {:db/id 17592186193894 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the difference between the means of two normal populations with unknown and unequal variances. Suppose we have two populations $X_1$ and $X_2$, $X_1\sim N(\mu_1, \sigma^2_1), \qquad X_2\sim N(\mu_2, \sigma^2_2)$, where $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are the population means, and $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are the population variances. In a previous lesson, we saw that the difference between the sample means follows a standard normal distribution: $$ Z = \dfrac{\overline{X_1} - \overline{X_2}- (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}} \sim N(0,1) $$ where $\overline{X}_1$ and $\overline{X}_2$ are the sample means, and $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the sample sizes. In most practical situations, the population variances $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are unknown and must be replaced with estimates $S_1^2$ and $S_2^2$. In this situation, the random variable $$ \begin{aligned} T &= ((X^(―)_{1} - X^(―)_{2}) - (μ_{1} - μ_{2}))/(\sqrt{\frac{S_{1}^{2}}{n_{1}} + \frac{S_{2}^{2}}{n_{2}}}) \end{aligned} $$ follows a $t$-distribution with $r$ degrees of freedom, where $r$ can be approximated from sample data using the formula $$ r = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2} \right)^2}{\dfrac{s_1^4}{n_1^2(n_1-1)} + \dfrac{s_2^4}{n_2^2(n_2-1)}} $$ rounded *down* to the nearest integer. Following the usual procedure, a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the difference $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is given by $(\overline{x}_1-\overline{x}_2) \pm E$ where - $$ \displaystyle E=t_{r, \alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}} $$ is the margin of error, and - $P(T > t_{r, \alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$. This confidence interval is sometimes called a **Welch's $\boldsymbol t$-interval,** named after its inventor, the British statistician Bernard Lewis Welch. Finally, note that if the underlying populations $X_1$ and $X_2$ are *not* normally distributed, we can still use this procedure to construct a confidence interval *provided that* the sample sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$ are sufficiently large (typically, $$ n_1, n_2 \geq 30 $$ ). Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0fab9cb-0a03-5226-9c9f-534d6c2b4f5e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6986 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186193895 :tutorial/content "Consider two samples of size $n_x = 14$ and $n_y = 18$ from independent normal populations $X$ and $Y$ with unequal population variances, where the unbiased estimates of $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ from these samples are $$ \overline{x}=47 $$ and $$ \overline{y}=40 $$ and unbiased estimates of the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are $s_x^2=7^2$ and $s_y^2=8^2$. We wish to carry out a hypothesis test at the $10\%$ significance level to determine whether there is sufficient evidence that the population mean $\mu_x$ of $X$ is larger than the population mean $\mu_y$ of $Y$. To solve a problem like this, we proceed as follows. We are told that the populations are normally distributed, but we do not know the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$. In cases like this, the random variable $$ \dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{S_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{S_y^2}{n_y}}} $$ follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, where - $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means, - $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means, - $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes, and - $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$ are the sample variances. In our example, the null and alternative hypotheses are the following: - $H_0: \mu_x = \mu_y$ is the null hypothesis - $H_1: \mu_x > \mu_y$ is the alternative (one-tailed) hypothesis We can estimate the number of degrees of freedom $k$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} k &= \min (n_{x} - 1, n_{y} - 1) \\ &= \min (14 - 1, 18 - 1) \\ &= \min (13, 17) \\ &= 13 \end{aligned} $$ Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e. $$ \mu_x - \mu_y = 0 $$ we compute the test statistic: $$ \begin{aligned} t &= (x^(―) - y^(―) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/(\sqrt{\frac{s_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{s_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}}) \\ &= (47 - 40 - (0))/(\sqrt{\frac{7^{2}}{14} + \frac{8^{2}}{18}}) \\ &\approx 2.635 \end{aligned} $$ Next, we determine the critical region corresponding to our significance level. Given a random variable $T$ that has a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, the table below shows the $t$-scores $t_{k,p}$ such that $$ P(T > t_{k,p}) = p $$ for some particular values of $k$ and $p$.
$k \setminus p$ $0.100$ $0.050$ $0.025$ $0.010$ $0.005$
$13$ $\color{blue}\,1.350\,$ $\,1.771\,$ $\,2.160\,$ $\,2.650\,$ $\,3.012\,$
$14$ $\,1.345\,$ $\,1.761\,$ $\,2.145\,$ $\,2.624\,$ $\,2.977\,$
$15$ $\,1.341\,$ $\,1.753\,$ $\,2.131\,$ $\,2.602\,$ $\,2.947\,$
According to the table, the $10\%$ one-tailed critical value for $k = 13$ degrees of freedom is $$ t \approx 1.350 $$ Since the alternative hypothesis is $\mu_x > \mu_y$, we must consider the right tail. So, our critical region is $$ T \geq \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1.350} $$ Finally, notice that our test statistic $(2.635)$ lies in the critical region, as shown below. ![](images/81/813c8270ac07466c74e50fbc9377d83cfad9e773057d40183550d5dbd204868a.png) So, we reject the null hypothesis $H_0$. As a result, we conclude that there is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{sufficient}}$ evidence that, at the $10\%$ level of significance, we have $\mu_x > \mu_y$." :tutorial/id #uuid "ce70000e-5984-5ef9-a054-816a3c979671" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6987 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:answer/id #uuid "215a6301-7567-5d9a-a9c4-00268409f846" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(- ∞, \frac{10}{3})" :db/id 17592186195293} {:answer/id #uuid "9ad483b2-51f0-5254-b431-81ab1082c88f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[- \frac{7}{2}, \frac{7}{2}]" :db/id 17592186195307} {:answer/id #uuid "ad31ec91-fa92-53a3-ad9f-39bbd693f6ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\log_{3} (2 + \frac{1}{ε})" :db/id 17592186196260} {:answer/id #uuid "f3b5d918-7fcc-50f3-aab8-e6821f1b7fda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\log_{3} (2 + \frac{7}{ε})" :db/id 17592186196263} {:answer/id #uuid "c8c98662-1066-5d61-8986-f43a203b3ee6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\log_{3} (2 + \frac{1}{ε})" :db/id 17592186196267} {:answer/id #uuid "2737992f-d9b0-5845-9366-87adbff16adf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\log_{3} (2 + \frac{7}{ε})" :db/id 17592186196268} {:db/id 17592186198015 :question/id #uuid "e8d75369-b381-53d3-b3af-37c6109c15a0" :question/math-academy-id "e-12327" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral $$ \displaystyle \iint\limits_D \dfrac{y-x}{x+y} \: \mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y, $$ where $D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y-x \leq 1, \: 1 \leq x+y \leq 4 \right\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows: $$ \mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} \longrightarrow {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]} $$ This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane. To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula $$ \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v $$ where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$ To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows: **Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables. The inequalities that define the region $D,$ $$ 0 \leq y-x \leq 1, \qquad 1 \leq x+y \leq 4, $$ suggest that we use the change of variables $$ u = y-x \quad \text{and} \quad v = x+y. $$ This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is $$ \mathbf{T}^{-1}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}. $$ **Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ Our domain in the $uv$-plane is $$ \begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =-2.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$ $$ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{2}. $$ Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ **Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral. Performing the change of variables, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y-x}{x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{u}{v}\,du]dv \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}[{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,du]dv \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,dv \\ & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,dv \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\ & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198016 :question/id #uuid "1ad4ddff-b776-50d9-b698-c0172ee9d3ab" :question/math-academy-id "e-12328" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral $$ \displaystyle \iint\limits_D (2x+y)y^2 \:\mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y, $$ where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $\left(\dfrac32,0\right) ,$ $\left(\dfrac52,0\right) ,$ $(1,3),$ and $(0,3).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows: $$ \mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} \longrightarrow {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]} $$ This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane. To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula $$ \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v $$ where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$ To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows: **Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables. The integrand $$ f(x,y) = (2x+y)y^2 $$ suggests that we use the change of variables $$ u=2x+y, \qquad v=y. $$ This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is $$ \mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}. $$ **Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ The vertices of our domain $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},0) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0,0) \\ & =(3,0) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(\frac{5}{2},0) & =(2\cdot \frac{5}{2}+0,0) \\ & =(5,0) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2\cdot 1+3,3) \\ & =(5,3) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(0,3) & =(2\cdot 0+3,3) \\ & =(3,3)\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle: $$ \Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 5, \quad 0 \leq v \leq 3 \big\} $$ ![](images/c2/c296b1ee0451686608ec4b06c29d114ff1918233886d8471d3b2c118851aa25e.png) **Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$ $$ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =\dfrac12 $$ Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ **Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral. Performing the change of variables, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y){y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 8 \\ & =36.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198019 :question/id #uuid "4eaf3262-b6e3-57bc-9662-42ab52626ee9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12340" :question/problem "![](images/65/6515550b9a280f423cdc2a2e89fd83014733c0783fdd4b2b2966e6a4dd37492a.png) Consider the square region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by $$ \Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: : \: 1 \le u \le 3, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \bigg\}, $$ and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by $$ \mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v). $$ Find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $\Delta$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $\Delta$ separately: - Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)).\end{aligned} $$ This line segment makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$ - Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ Substituting $v=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right)).\end{aligned} $$ This line segment makes an angle of $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$ - Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{6}. $$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned} $$ This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. It lies between the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$ - Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=3$ and $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{6}. $$ Substituting $u=3$ into our transformation equations, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}(x,y)=(3\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned} $$ This is an arc of the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. It lies between the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$ Therefore, the image $D$ of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that is enclosed between - two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=3,$ and - two rays with polar equations $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},$ as shown in the diagram \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. $$ We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves: $$ \begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(1)⟩ \\ & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(1)⟩ \\ & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, the fundamental vector product is $$ \begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2v & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle \\ & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨x+y,\hspace{0.222em}x-y,\hspace{0.222em}xyz⟩{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y={v}^{2}\,z=1} \\ & =⟨{u}^{2}+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨{u}^{2}+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩ \\ & =({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\cdot 0+({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\cdot 0+{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\cdot 4uv \\ & =4{u}^{3}{v}^{3}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the surface integral can be written as $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}4{u}^{3}{v}^{3}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198021 :question/id #uuid "2a32501f-d0f2-5e59-b7cc-a6b459269f6a" g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A. $$ We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned} $$ Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ & =⟨\underbrace{-y}_{P},\,\underbrace{x}_{Q},\,\underbrace{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2}_{R}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2x)-(x)\cdot (2y)+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-2xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+2y]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7}{3})\,\text{d}x \\ & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7x}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\ & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198022 :question/id #uuid "0364a11f-e567-517e-acf2-471708dbdc0a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12358" :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral $$ \begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle \\ & =⟨-2,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Next, we $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}1+2u+v,\hspace{0.222em}u+v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ & =(u-v)\cdot (-2)+(1+2u+v)\cdot 3+(u+v)\cdot 1 \\ & =-2u+2v+3+6u+3v+u+v \\ & =5u+6v+3\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}x,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times ={\int }_{0}^{2}[5uv+3{v}^{2}+3v]_{v=0}^{v=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5u+6)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\ & ={[\frac{5}{2}{u}^{2}+6u]}_{0}^{2} \\ & =10+12 \\ & =22.\end{aligned} :question/math-academy-id "e-12383" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=\left\langle z+2y, \: 3y+z, \: x -z\right\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=-3x+2y$ for $0 parameterized as $$ \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: -3u+2v \right\rangle $$ over the domain $$ D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 2, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}. $$ We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves: $$ \begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3u+2v)⟩ \\ & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\ & =(-3u+4v)\cdot (3)+(-3u+5v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-2v)\cdot 1 \\ & =-9u+12v+6u-10v+4u-2v \\ & =u\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the surface integral 0, \: 1 + xyz \rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by $$ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. $$ Notice that only the $z$-component of $\mathbf F = \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1+xyz\rangle$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. ![](images/97/977d93ad65c9f3690def4242f98f4de5e5c89faf02fe47d06f5ed251d8a4a292.png) Let's consider the flux of $\mathbf F$ through these two sides. - Let $S_1$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z = 1$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_1$ is $$ \mathbf n_1 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, 1\rangle. $$ Using the fact that $z = 1$ on $S_1,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ & =1+xy.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_1$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}1+xy\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{D}1+xy\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}1+xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+\frac{1}{2}y\,\text{d}y \\ & ={[y+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned} $$ - Let $S_2$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_2$ is $$ \mathbf n_2 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle. $$ Using the fact that $z = 0$ on $S_2,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ & =-1.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_2$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-1\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\ & =-{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\ & =-\text{Area}(D) \\ & =-(1-0)(1-0) \\ & =-1\end{aligned} $$ Finally, $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\ & =\frac{5}{4}+(-1) \\ & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198034 :question/id #uuid "b81eb0cb-a740-5e86-921c-4baa8c179e55" :question/math-academy-id "e-12387" :question/problem "For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by $$ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A, $$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula? *Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive $\mathbf j$-component.*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by $$ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. $$ Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y = h(x,z),$ it can be parameterized as $$ \mathbf{r}(x,z) = \left\langle x, \: h(x,z),\: z \right\rangle. $$ We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves: $$ \begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨0,\frac{∂h}{∂z},\,1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, the fundamental vector product is $$ \begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & \frac{∂h}{∂x} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{∂h}{∂z} & 1\end{vmatrix}=⟨\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,-1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂z}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ However, notice that the $\mathbf j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction: $$ \mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_x = - \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z = \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right \rangle $$ Therefore, the surface integral can be written as $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,z))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,1,\,-\frac{∂h}{∂z}⟩\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}+Q-R\frac{∂h}{∂z})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$"} }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{x}^{2}yz+\frac{x{z}^{3}}{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dx\,dy \\ & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y(1-0)+x(\frac{1}{3}-0)\,dx\,dy \\ & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x\,dx\,dy\end{aligned} $$ Next, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x\,dx]dy \\ & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}]}_{x=-1}^{x=2}\,dy \\ & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{x}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy{\int }_{1}^{4}dz\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating each =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-0)\cdot (0+1)\cdot 3 \\ & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ \int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{1}^{4} \dfrac{\sin{y}}{x} \: \textrm{d}z \:
