:question/worked-solution "We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration. We wish to find the limits of integration $u_1(x,y),$ $u_2(x,y),$ $v_1(y),$ $v_2(y),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that $$ \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{z}^{2} e^{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y = \int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(y)}^{v_2(y)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} e^{x^2} \, \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y. $$ From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows: $$ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 2, \:\: z \leq x \leq 2 \right\} $$ Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by $$ E = \left\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 2 \right\} $$ as shown below. ![](images/9f/9fe61cd50d31086b47495f0bd0fd71308fc30286d392f4d0064cf743b93272b0.png) Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $z \leq x \leq 2.$ ![](images/6a/6af345af2d33b53c698e8e1d4eff10e3b3116911e14ee1b4581da7eee8528f94.png) To change the order of integration from $\mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type II *plane* region. To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below. ![](images/53/53ec4e56ca38362b10c05d4cc657f9057005d9692e0fcde1f0846e7e80b4f478.png) The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary: - The bottom boundary of the region is $$ z=0. $$ - The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z = z(x,y),$ is $$ x = z \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad z = x. $$ Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is $$ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,y) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq x \right\}, $$ as shown in the diagram below. ![](images/5c/5ce67f398f60237d763d393d62f9e7346270b954acc7efdc7a096a5f3155f4d3.png) Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xy$-plane with the left curve given by $x = 0.$ ![](images/0d/0dbf7a35fe74730db7c2a07fc4bbe881a66412cee53bf0a606c522f5493e58c2.png) Hence, $$ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}. $$ Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{z}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,dz\,dx\,dy \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}\text{d}z]\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}[z]_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1)\cdot [y]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198040 :question/id #uuid "3fccb151-d67f-525b-8804-62589913084a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12407" :question/problem "Use the change of variables $$ u = x+y^2, \qquad v= y+z, \qquad w = 2z $$ to evaluate the triple integral $$ \displaystyle \iiint \limits_R (x+y^2)^{15}z \: \mathrm{d}V, $$ where the region $R$ is given by $$ R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x+y^2 \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y+z \leq 4, \: 0\leq z\leq 2 \big\}. $$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows: $$ \mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v \\ w\end{array} \right]} \longrightarrow {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v , w ) \\ y ( u , v , w ) \\ z ( u , v , w )\end{array} \right]} $$ This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space. To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula $$ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \ \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v,w), y(u,v,w), z(u,v,w)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right| \: \textrm{d}u \textrm{d}v \textrm{d}w $$ where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$ Note that the change of variables $$ u = x+y^2, \qquad v= y+z, \qquad w = 2z $$ gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is $$ \mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y , z ) \\ v ( x , y , z ) \\ w ( x , y , z )\end{array} \right]}. $$ To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps: **Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ Our domain in the $uvw$-space is $$ \begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 4,\,0\le w\le 4\}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$ The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2y & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ & =1\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\ & =2.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$ The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is $$ \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}. $$ Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ **Step 4**: Perform the change of variables: $$ \begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x+{y}^{2})^{15}z\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}{u}^{15}\cdot \frac{w}{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\ & =\frac{1}{4}{∭}_{Δ}{u}^{15}w\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\ & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}{u}^{15}w\,dw\,dv\,du \\ & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{15}\,du\cdot {\int }_{0}^{4}dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{4}w\,dw \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot [\frac{{u}^{16}}{16}]_{u=0}^{u=1}\cdot {[v]}_{v=0}^{v=4}\cdot [\frac{{w}^{2}}{2}]_{w=0}^{w=4} \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{16}-0)\cdot (4-0)\cdot (8-0) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198043 :question/id #uuid "fe87a57b-09fc-5c98-9d4c-e3ba3b95c2a9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12419" :question/problem "![](images/26/263853df5f080da778a34caacea945119099326f0ba27806d851f793416e9f92.png) Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, \, x, \, -z^2 \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as $$ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. $$ Determine the missing expression." :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, - the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = 0$ is oriented upward, and - the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = -\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}$ is oriented downward. Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately. - Consider the upper plane $S_1.$ Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,x,-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ - Consider the lower hemisphere $S_2.$ We compute the partial derivatives of $z = h(x,y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned} $$ If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then $$ P = 0, \qquad Q = x, \qquad R = -z^2 = x^2 + y^2 - 4. $$ As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\ & =-{∬}_{D}(-0\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198044 :question/id #uuid "5fb5ffe1-51cb-5db8-b0a4-effd27cc623f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12420" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle x, \, y, \, 0 \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the parabolic cylinder $z=1-x^2$ and the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as $$ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. $$ Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, - the upper surface $S_1: z=g(x,y)=1-x^2$ is oriented upward, and - the lower surface $S_2: z=h(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ is oriented downward. Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately. - Consider the upper parabolic cylinder $S_1.$ We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned} $$ If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then $$ P = x, \qquad Q = y, \qquad R = 0. $$ As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot (-2x)-y\cdot (0)+0)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$ - Consider the lower paraboloid $S_2.$ We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned} $$ If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then $$ P = x, \qquad Q = y , \qquad R = 0. $$ As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\ & =-{∬}_{D}(-x\cdot (2x)-y\cdot (2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\ & =-{∬}_{D}-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198045 :question/id #uuid "7a42fb45-176b-5550-a206-41a92859987b" :question/math-academy-id "e-12440" :question/problem "![](images/f9/f9b1b286210d694cd3786fe38190216da503bfa3223114f86c8706f810313e33.png) The curve $C_1$ has endpoints $A(5,3)$ and $B(1,3).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $$ \mathbf{F}(x,y)=\sqrt{y^3}\,\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\,\mathbf{j} $$ through $C_1$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1,$ as shown above. *Hint: You're given that $\mathbf F$ is source-free.*" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent: - $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field. - $$ \displaystyle \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0. $$ - The flux $$ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s} $$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero. - Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s. $$ - There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$ First, notice that $$ \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0, $$ which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field. Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular, $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s, $$ where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. ![](images/2a/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png) Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors. To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula $$ \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x. $$ To apply the formula, - the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and - the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$ Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\ & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned} $$ where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned} $$ We evaluate the flux integral as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\ & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5}\right)-\left(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}\right) \\ & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186198046 :question/id #uuid "8d046f27-886d-5342-8868-e2c3ae731fa5" :question/math-academy-id "e-12453" :question/problem "![](images/92/925b2f032f751e4482632c449fff35f544929f3355655c20d6701e640a7b20a3.png) Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle 0,\: 0,\: z\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $4$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by $$ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S. $$ Notice that only the $z$-component of $\mathbf F = \langle 0,\: 0,\: z\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \rangle$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. ![](images/f5/f5a443b0bb234662c8f4a2bc156b458ac09a8db3ce3cc67933f7465a19db2ef9.png) Let's consider the flux of $\mathbf F$ through these two sides. - Let $S_1$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z = 4$ for $x^2 + y^2 \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_1$ is $$ \mathbf n_1 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, 1\rangle. $$ Using the fact that $z = 4$ on $S_1,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ & =⟨0,\,0,\,4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ & =4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_1$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\ & =4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned} $$ Applying a change of variables $(x,y) \to (r,\theta), \textrm d A = r\,\textrm d r\,\textrm d \theta,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =4{∬}_{D}r\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta \\ & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta \\ & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r \\ & =4\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =8\pi \left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned} $$ - Let $S_2$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z = 0$ for $x^2 + y^2 \leq 1.$ Therefore, for every point on $S_2,$ we have $$ F(x,y,0) = \langle 0,\: 0,\: 0 \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \rangle = \langle 0,\: 0,\: 0\rangle. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\ & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\ & =\frac{8\pi }{3}+0 \\ & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198048 :question/id #uuid "81b0b6e1-41c3-5329-806e-162b8b27b045" :question/math-academy-id "e-12466" :question/problem "The lamina $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \le x \le y ,\, 0 \le y \le 1 \big\}$ has the mass density function $\lambda(x,y) = x^2y.$ Find the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "The moment of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ about the $y$-axis is given by $$ M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A. $$ In our case, $D$ is represented as a type II plane region and $\lambda(x,y) = x^2y .$ Therefore, the moment is $$ \begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\cdot {x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{0}^{y}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot {[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{{y}^{4}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{y}^{5}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\ & ={[\frac{{y}^{6}}{24}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\ & =\frac{1}{24}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198049 :question/id #uuid "9294903c-1b4c-58b6-a878-7f2220ec763d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12470" :question/problem "A thin plate $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y) = 2x$ is enclosed between the curve $y=1-x^2$ and the $x$-axis for $0 \leq x \leq 1.$ Find the moment of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "The moment of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis is given by $$ M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A. $$ In our case, $D$ is a type I plane region, as shown below. ![](images/06/067543543031a1d8cb4ceb9a7901ad7db77629243adc6658d4a9eab3e98fe09f.png) So, we have $$ D = \big\{(x,y) \:: \: 0 \le x \le 1, \: 0 \le y \le 1-x^2 \big\} $$ and $\lambda(x,y) = 2x.$ Therefore, the moment is $$ \begin{array}{cc}{M}_{x} & = \underset{D}{\iint } y \cdot 2 x \text{d} A \\ & = \underset{D}{\iint } 2 x y \text{d} A \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{1 - {x}^{2}} 2 x y \text{d} y \text{d} x \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} 2 x [ {\int }_{0}^{1 - {x}^{2}} y \text{d} y ] \text{d} x \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} 2 x \cdot {[ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} ]}_{y = 0}^{y = 1 - {x}^{2}} \text{d} x \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} x {( 1 - {x}^{2} )}^{2} \text{d} x \\ & = {\int }_{0}^{1} x - 2 {x}^{3} + {x}^{5} \text{d} x \\ & = {[ \frac{1}{2} {x}^{2} - \frac{1}{2} {x}^{4} + \frac{1}{6} {x}^{6} ]}_{x = 0}^{x = 1} \\ & = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{6} \\ & = \frac{1}{6} .\end{array} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198050 :question/id #uuid "cb13bd5e-ec8a-5e5c-a45f-d710ced8c3ad" :question/math-academy-id "e-12473" :question/problem "The thin rod below has the mass density function $\lambda (x) = (x+4)\,\textrm{kg/m}.$ Find the moment of the rod about the origin. ![](images/7f/7f88ca365b75320795e9d38170a8586399d759696638a4bd78c73ca6c6f44b1a.png)" :question/worked-solution "The moment about the origin $O$ of a rod with mass density function $\lambda(x)$ for $a \leq x \leq b$ is given by $$ M_O = \int_a^b x\, \lambda(x) \: \textrm{d}x. $$ In our case, we have $$ \lambda (x) = x+4, \qquad a=0, \qquad b=3. $$ We calculate the moment of the rod about the origin as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot (x+4)\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}+4x\,\text{d}x \\ & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+2{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\ & =(\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}+2\cdot {3}^{2})-0 \\ & =27.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the required moment is $27\,\textrm{kg}\cdot \textrm{m}.$"} {:db/id 17592186198051 :question/id #uuid "4ebe8c87-95ba-58e2-b5d4-1bb19f231dc1" :question/math-academy-id "e-12474" :question/problem "![](images/46/461c4cb760541ea435620803689e193d13c9cb4706a59b031d37da6ffd49ab9f.png) The thin rod above has the mass density function $\lambda (x) = x^3.$ Given that the rod's mass is $4$ units, what is the $x$-coordinate of its center of mass?" :question/worked-solution "The center of mass of a rod placed along the $x$-axis over the interval $a \leq x \leq b$ whose mass density function is $\lambda(x)$ is given by $$ \overline{x} = \dfrac{M_O}{m}, $$ where - $$ \displaystyle m = \int_a^b \lambda (x) \: \textrm{d}x $$ is the mass of the rod, - $$ \displaystyle M_O = \int_a^b \, x\lambda (x) \: \textrm{d}x $$ is the moment of the rod about the origin $O.$ In our case, we have $$ \lambda (x) = x^3, \qquad a=0, \qquad b=2. $$ So, the moment of the rod about the origin is $$ \begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(32-0) \\ & =\frac{32}{5}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \overline{x}= \dfrac{M_O}{m} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{32}{5}\right)}{4} = \dfrac{8}{5}. $$ Note that this result makes intuitive sense. Since $\lambda$ is an increasing function of $x,$ we would expect the center of mass to be located closer to the right endpoint and further from the left endpoint."} {:db/id 17592186198057 :question/id #uuid "985e1b18-0023-55ba-b4e4-69a109d8de58" :question/math-academy-id "e-12485" :question/problem "![](images/04/0405639a97f249bbcc4dc18a7eae5b4df24aefb4b4680b569365b3d841c15e6b.png) A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the $y$-axis and the lines $x=\dfrac{y}2$ and $x=y-2$, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is $\lambda(x,y) =\dfrac y8.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=2.$" :question/worked-solution "The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by $$ I_l = \iint\limits_D \lambda (x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A, $$ where $\lambda(x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$ First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation $$ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 2x \leq y \leq x+2 \right\}, $$ as shown below. ![](images/69/69dcf02cc1883f2b04f81bd6dd486bbe24fedbb813db5778ae3b33ed1fb42e90.png) The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=2$ is given by $$ r(x,y) = |x - 2|. $$ Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=2$ is $$ \begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{2x}^{x+2}\left(\frac{y}{8}\right)|x-2{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{2x}^{x+2}\left(\frac{y}{8}\right)(x-2)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(x-2)^{2}{\int }_{2x}^{x+2}\frac{y}{8}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(x-2)^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}]}_{2x}^{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x-2)^{2}((x+2)^{2}-(2x)^{2})\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}-4x+4)(4+4x-3{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(16-24{x}^{2}+16{x}^{3}-3{x}^{4})\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{1}{16}{[16x-8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{4}-\frac{3{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{16}(32-64+64-\frac{96}{5})-0 \\ & =\frac{1}{16}\left(\frac{64}{5}\right) \\ & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198058 :question/id #uuid "eab955a5-019b-5219-b5d5-32e3818be4b9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12486" :question/problem "![](images/67/67d511da69c49e77822011936522f2b236ccc0fa0e0fcd09ce26b428cc8f738a.png) A plate with mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $y=x$ and $y=4x-x^2$, as shown above. Given that the region has an area of $\dfrac92$ square units, find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=3.$" :question/worked-solution "The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by $$ I_l = \iint\limits_D \lambda (x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A, $$ where $\lambda(x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$ First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation $$ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: x \leq y \leq 4x-x^2 \right\}, $$ as shown below. ![](images/62/6291950b5483f3c102df7249674412c7c11646409cb1b43df604de6bd5ace86f.png) The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=3$ is given by $$ r(x,y) = |x - 3|. $$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by $$ \lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{M}{\mathcal{A}} = \dfrac{2M}{9}. $$ Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=3$ is $$ \begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{x}^{4x-{x}^{2}}|x-3{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{x}^{4x-{x}^{2}}(x-3)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}(x-3)^{2}[y]_{y=x}^{y=4x-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}-6x+9)(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}-{x}^{4}+9{x}^{3}-27{x}^{2}+27x\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{2M}{9}{[-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+\frac{9{x}^{4}}{4}-9{x}^{3}+\frac{27{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\ & =\frac{2M}{{3}^{2}}(-\frac{{3}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{3}^{6}}{4}-{3}^{5}+\frac{{3}^{5}}{2}) \\ & =2\cdot {3}^{3}M(-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{3}{4}-1+\frac{1}{2}) \\ & =\frac{27M}{10}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198059 :question/id #uuid "88848c23-66fe-5937-958c-28d73b593d99" :question/math-academy-id "e-12487" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 1 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ we have the following definitions: - The radius of gyration $R_x$ about the $x$-axis is given by $R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},$ where $I_x$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis. - The radius of gyration $R_y$ about the $y$-axis is given by $R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},$ where $I_y$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis. - The radius of gyration $R_0$ about the origin is given by $R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},$ where $I_0$ is the moment of inertia about the origin. The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as $$ I_y = \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm{d}A, $$ where $\lambda(x,y)$ is the mass density function. The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $\mathcal{A} = 3\cdot 1 = 3.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by $$ \lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{M}{\mathcal{A}} = \dfrac{M}{3}. $$ Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is $$ \begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}9\,\text{d}y \\ & =3M{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\ & =3M[y]_{1}^{2} \\ & =3M(2-1) \\ & =3M.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, $$ R_y^2 =\dfrac{3M}{M} = 3\quad \Rightarrow\quad R_y = \sqrt{3}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186198060 :question/id #uuid "0f7dbe9f-b448-5e76-9932-68e1ff99904e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12488" :question/problem "![](images/8e/8ec9b8832f3286032413c4016e88a58a593dfd1b32164e219dc1c2e56e3b0b97.png) A plate with mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant enclosed between the curve $y=\sqrt x$ and the line $x=1,$ as shown above. The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $x$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=-1.$" :question/worked-solution "The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by $$ I_l = \iint\limits_D \lambda (x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A, $$ where $\lambda(x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$ First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation $$ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt x \right\}, $$ as shown below. ![](images/7f/7faaecf39250dbdd1b92d789f6c217afe883c27533b563dae82ed82d228d9b4d.png) Also, the distance between a point and the line $x=-1$ is given by $$ r(x,y) = |x-(-1)| = |x+1|. $$ Next, the mass density can be written as $\lambda(x,y) = k |y| = ky,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find the value of $k$ by integrating the mass density function over the plate. $$ \begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}ky\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =k{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{k}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-0)\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{k}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{k}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =\frac{k}{4}\end{aligned} $$ Hence, $$ \lambda(x,y) = k y = 4M y. $$ Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=-1$ is $$ \begin{aligned}{I}_{l} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}4My\,|x+1{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}4My(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}(x+1)^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}(x+1)^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ & =2M{\int }_{0}^{1}(x+1)^{2}(x-0)\,\text{d}x \\ & =2M{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\ & =2M{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =2M(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}) \\ & =2M\cdot \frac{17}{12} \\ & =\frac{17M}{6}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198063 :question/id #uuid "5245b67a-8beb-512d-b3c8-2d38db797703" :question/math-academy-id "e-12507" :question/problem "A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ bounded by the lines $y = x,$ $x = 1,$ and the $x$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda(x,y) = 3Mx.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ we have the following definitions: - The radius of gyration $R_x$ about the $x$-axis is given by $R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},$ where $I_x$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis. - The radius of gyration $R_y$ about the $y$-axis is given by $R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},$ where $I_y$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis. - The radius of gyration $R_0$ about the origin is given by $R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},$ where $I_0$ is the moment of inertia about the origin. The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as $$ I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2 + y^2) \lambda(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A, $$ where $\lambda(x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation $$ D = \left\{(x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq x \right\}. $$ Hence, the moment of inertia about the origin is $$ \begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 3Mx\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ & =3M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{4}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ & =3M{[\frac{4}{15}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =3M\cdot \frac{4}{15} \\ & =\frac{4M}{5}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the radius of gyration about the origin is $$ \begin{aligned}{R}_{0} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}} \\ & =\sqrt{\frac{4M}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\ & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}} \\ & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198079 :question/id #uuid "39ffb646-57fa-5d6d-a81f-286948f66d83" :question/math-academy-id "e-12596" :question/problem "![](images/ee/eec7d2b67f0b76bb8ec6874cf63f8cb09005f451d684924118983ea1aa39269c.png) The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y=\ln \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$ that is closest to the origin (as shown above) satisfies the equation $$ 2x + \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAA^2}}=0. $$ What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(0,0)$ and a general point $P(x, y)\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-0)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\ & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned} $$ We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\ln \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right).$ Substituting this into the above gives $$ \begin{aligned}S & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ & ={x}^{2}+{(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{x}\right))}^{2} \\ & ={x}^{2}+{\ln }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\end{aligned} $$ To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following: $$ \begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right) & =0 \\ 2x-\frac{2}{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) & =0 \\ 2x-\frac{2}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x) & =0 \\ 2x+\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} & =0\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the missing expression is $\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}.$"} {:db/id 17592186198143 :question/id #uuid "6cecfc9e-e891-506d-9d5d-ed3c8e6c35cd" :question/math-academy-id "e-13074" :question/problem "Which of the following are null sequences for $n\geq 1$? 1. $a_n = \dfrac{n}{n^2 + 1}$ 2. $b_n = \sqrt{n+1}$ 3. $c_n =\left(\dfrac89\right)^n$" :question/worked-solution "A *null sequence* is a sequence that converges to zero: - Sequence I is a null sequence. By dividing the numerator and denominator by $n^2$, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}{a}_{n} & =\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}\left(\frac{n}{{n}^{2}+1}\right) \\ & =\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}\left(\frac{\left(\frac{n}{{n}^{2}}\right)}{(\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}\right) \\ & =\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}\left(\frac{\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)}{(1+\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}\right) \\ & =\frac{0}{1+0} \\ & =0\hspace{1em}{\color{darkgreen}{✓}}\end{aligned} $$ - Sequence II is *not* a null sequence since $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}{b}_{n} & =\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}\sqrt{n+1} \\ & =\mathrm{\infty } \\ & \ne 0.\hspace{1em}{\color{red}{\times }}\end{aligned} $$ - Sequence III is null. Notice that this is a geometric sequence with the common ratio $r =\dfrac{8}{9}$. Since $\mid r \mid < 1$, the sequence converges to zero: $$ \begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}{c}_{n} & =\lim_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}{\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)}^{n} \\ & =0\hspace{1em}{\color{darkgreen}{✓}}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186198191 :question/id #uuid "49a0934e-130d-56cd-a47f-de3ca0785ae3" :question/math-academy-id "e-13279" :question/problem "Using the formal definition of a limit, prove that $$ \displaystyle \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} \right)= -1. $$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $$ \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} \right)= -1 $$ means that $$ \forall \varepsilon > 0, \: \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \: n \geq N \: \Rightarrow \: \left| \dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} -(-1) \right| \lt \varepsilon $$ In other words, we need to show that for any real $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there exists a natural number $N$ such that, for every natural number $$ n \geq N $$ we have $$ \left| \dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} -(-1) \right| \lt \varepsilon $$ Before we start the proof, we would like to figure out how $N$ may depend on $\varepsilon$. First, we simplifying $\mid a_n - L \mid$, we have $$ \begin{aligned}|{a}_{n}-L| & =|\frac{1-{4}^{n}}{{4}^{n}-10}-(-1)| \\ & =|\frac{1-{4}^{n}}{{4}^{n}-10}+1| \\ & =|\frac{1-{4}^{n}}{{4}^{n}-10}+\frac{{4}^{n}-10}{{4}^{n}-10}| \\ & =|\frac{1-{4}^{n}+{4}^{n}-10}{{4}^{n}-10}| \\ & =|-\frac{9}{{4}^{n}-10}| \\ & =|\frac{9}{{4}^{n}-10}|.\end{aligned} $$ Notice that $$ \dfrac{9}{4^n-10} \gt 0 $$ for any natural $$ n \geq 2 $$ With that in mind, we have $$ \mid a_n - L \mid = \left| \dfrac{9}{4^n-10} \right| = \dfrac{9}{4^n-10} $$ Now, we solve the inequality $\mid a_n - L \mid < \varepsilon$ for $$ n\geq 2{:} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{9}{{4}^{n}-10} & <ε \\ 9 & <ε({4}^{n}-10) \\ \frac{9}{ε} & <{4}^{n}-10 \\ 10+\frac{9}{ε} & <{4}^{n} \\ {log}_{4}(10+\frac{9}{ε}) & {log}_{4}(10+\frac{9}{ε}).\end{aligned} $$ As a result, if we want $$ \left| \dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} - (-1) \right| \lt \varepsilon $$ it's sufficient to take all values of $n$ that are larger than $$ \log_4\left(10+\dfrac{9}{\varepsilon}\right) $$ We can now continue the proof: > Suppose $\varepsilon > 0$. Let's choose some natural number $N > \log_4\left(10+\dfrac{9}{\varepsilon}\right)$. Notice that, since $$ \dfrac{9}{\varepsilon} > 0 $$ then $$ \log_4\left(10+\dfrac{9}{\varepsilon}\right) > \log_4(10)\approx 1.66 $$ and therefore $$ N \geq 2 $$ With that in mind, we'll find the upper bound for the absolute value of the sequence's $n$th term: > Then, for any natural number $n \geq N$, we have > $$ \begin{aligned}|\frac{1-{4}^{n}}{{4}^{n}-10}-(-1)| & =\frac{9}{{4}^{n}-10} \\ & <\frac{9}{{4}^{{log}_{4}(10+9/ε)}-10} \\ & =\frac{9}{(10+\frac{9}{ε}-10)} \\ & =ε.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we make the conclusion: > Therefore, according to the definition, > $$ \displaystyle \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} \right)= -1 $$ The full proof is given below: > Suppose $\varepsilon > 0$. Let's choose some natural number $N > \log_4\left(10+\dfrac{9}{\varepsilon}\right)$. > Then, for any natural number $n \geq N$, we have > $$ \displaystyle \mid \frac{1 - 4^{n}}{4^{n} - 10} - (-1) \mid \mid < (9)/(4^{\log_{4} (10 + 9/ε)} - 10); = (9)/((10 + \frac{9}{ε} - 10)); = ε. $$ > Therefore, according to the definition, $$ \displaystyle \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{1-4^n}{4^n-10} = -1. $$"} {:db/id 17592186198235 :question/id #uuid "9d477733-7178-5b88-926f-a457faaf344a" :question/math-academy-id "e-7285" :question/problem "Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, given by $$ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq 4x+2y \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq y-x \leq 3 \big\}. $$ By performing the change of variables $u = 4x+2y$ and $v=y - x,$ write the following integral in terms of $u$ and $v.$ $$ \displaystyle \iint\limits_D \sin \left(3(x+y)\right) \: \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y $$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows: $$ \mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} \longrightarrow {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]} $$ This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane. To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula $$ \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm d x \, \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \mathrm d u \, \mathrm d v $$ where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$ Note that the change of variables $$ u = 4x + 2y, \qquad v = y - x $$ gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is $$ \mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}. $$ To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows: **Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ Our domain in the $uv$-plane is $$ \begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 3\}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ -1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =6.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$ The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is $$ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{6}. $$ Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ **Step 4**: Perform the change of variables. In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations $$ u = 4x+2y, \qquad v = y-x $$ for $x$ and $y$, which gives $$ x = \dfrac{u-2v}6, \qquad y =\dfrac{u+4v}6. $$ Performing the change of variables, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(x+y))\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\frac{u-2v}{6}+\frac{u+4v}{6}))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\left(\frac{2u+2v}{6}\right))|\frac{1}{6}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\sin \,(u+v)\,du\,dv.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198238 :question/id #uuid "8199670b-efe4-537b-8f8a-228d567a0944" :question/math-academy-id "e-8182" :question/problem "Consider a thin plate $D$ that has the mass density function $\lambda (x,y) = x+y$ and is enclosed between the curve $y=x$ and the $x$-axis for $0 \leq x \leq 1.$ Given that the mass of the plate is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ units and its center of mass is located at $( \overline{x}, \overline{y} ),$ what is the value of $\overline{y}?$" :question/worked-solution "The center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda(x,y)$ is given by $$ (\overline{x},\overline{y}) = \left( \dfrac{M_y}{m}, \dfrac{M_x}{m} \right), $$ where - $$ \displaystyle m = \iint \limits_D \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A $$ is the mass of the lamina, - $$ \displaystyle M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A $$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and - $$ \displaystyle M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A $$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis. Notice that $D$ is a type I plane region: ![](images/b8/b872242423692a20a9d50658c99d9e8cee7c9b2737fb96592bc2bc35b4f72c32.png) So, we have $$ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \:0 \le x \le 1, \: 0 \le y \le x \big\} $$ and $\lambda(x,y) = x+y.$ Since we require the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass, we need to compute the moment about the $x$-axis: $$ \begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}y\cdot (x+y)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}xy+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}xy+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{5}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\frac{5}{6}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\ & =\frac{5}{6}(\frac{1}{4}-0) \\ & =\frac{5}{24}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have $$ \overline{y} = \dfrac{M_x}{m} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{24}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{5}{12}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186198239 :question/id #uuid "37d7f2ae-90b0-5e6f-83c2-7cb21ed4f089" :question/math-academy-id "e-8183" :question/problem "Consider the thin plate $D$ enclosed between the curve $x=\sqrt{1-y^2}$ and the $y$-axis for $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$ Find the $x$-coordinate of its centroid." :question/worked-solution "The centroid of a lamina $D$ with area $A_D$ is given by $(x_c, y_c),$ where $$ \displaystyle x_c = \dfrac{1}{A_D} \iint\limits_D x \, \: \textrm{d}A, \qquad \displaystyle y_c = \dfrac{1}{A_D} \iint\limits_D y \, \: \textrm{d}A. $$ Notice that $D$ is a type II plane region: ![](images/a7/a7992c54f85f85cab3d9f923b8daca62c410393b364d30bcfbf5cff5efc93bbd.png) So, we have $$ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \le x \le \sqrt{1-y^2}, \: -1 \le y \le 1 \big\} $$ and $$ A_D = \dfrac12 \cdot \pi\cdot 1^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}. $$ Therefore, the $x$-coordinate of the centroid is $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{c} & =\frac{1}{{A}_{D}}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\ & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-1}^{1}1-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\ & =\frac{1}{\pi }{[y-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\ & =\frac{1}{\pi }[(1-\frac{1}{3})-(-1+\frac{1}{3})] \\ & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{4}{3} \\ & =\frac{4}{3\pi }.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186198241 :question/id #uuid "9235c493-f092-5f14-b989-be3b4548a90d" :question/math-academy-id "e-8691" :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the maximum value of the sum of cosines of the angle measures of a triangle, given that all three angles are acute." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles. We wish to maximize the function $$ f(x,y,z) = \cos{x}+\cos{y}+\cos{z}, $$ subject to the constraint $$ x+y+z=\pi. $$ Since the angles are acute, we also have the constraints $0 \lt x,y,z \lt \dfrac\pi 2.$ Let $g(x,y,z) = x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: $$ \nabla f(x,y,z) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y,z), \qquad g(x,y,z) = \pi $$ We start by solving the first equation: $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,-\operatorname{sin}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following system of equations: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡y &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right. $$ From the first and second equations above, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned} $$ Since the sine function is one-to-one on the interval $\left( 0, \dfrac \pi 2\right),$ we can conclude that $x = y.$ Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y =x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi \\ x+x+x & =\pi \\ 3x & =\pi \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $$ \displaystyle \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right), $$ and the maximum value is $$ \begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ It's easy to show that this point is indeed the maximum and not the minimum. To do that, we can compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, $$ \begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{12}\right) \\ & ≈1.47 \\ & 5}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462859} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e8c7c96-b1cc-5dde-a9a0-abbbbc82ee3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186462213} {:answer/id #uuid "026c8874-89cb-59ed-b68e-4121b69a008f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186462214}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186462214} :answer-field/id #uuid "908ef17b-a642-5b4a-a3a3-f8a1c602221f" :answer-field/key "$B={q\in Q\,:\,|2q|>5}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462860} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ae0ddd9-724e-56a2-bcab-8344c45a63ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186462215} {:answer/id #uuid "dee8c65a-8131-573c-a2b7-3b5c4032f90f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186462216}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186462216} :answer-field/id #uuid "0b6d889c-fee7-5bfa-bcf5-7ab3278080c2" :answer-field/key "$C={x\in R\,:\,|2x|>5}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462861}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "16d5f3be-e7a0-5c29-a089-f858318b66bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-181722" :question/problem "Which of the following sets are infinite? Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements. We start by solving the following inequality for $x\in R:$ $$ \begin{aligned}|2x|>5 \\ 2|x|>5 \\ |x|>\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned} $$ which gives $$ x<-\frac{5}{2}\,\text{or}\,x>\frac{5}{2} $$ and can be expressed as $$ \displaystyle x\in I=(-\infty ,-\frac{5}{2})\cup (\frac{5}{2},\infty ). $$ With that in mind, let's examine our sets: - The set $A$ is infinite. If $n\in Z,$ the solutions to the inequality $|2n|>5$ are all the integers that lie in the interval $I.$ Therefore, $$ A={…,-4,-3}\cup {3,4,…}. $$ - The set $B$ is infinite. If $q\in Q,$ the solutions to $|2q|>5$ are all the rational numbers that lie in the interval $I.$ Since any real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers, it follows that $B$ is infinite. - The set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B⊂C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite. Therefore, the correct answer is "$A,B,$ and $C.$""} {:db/id 17592186198945 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bb983ed1-12b9-5d18-ae27-ed126eb1224b" :answer/type "q-37701" :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the maximum value of the product of sines of angle measures of a triangle." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles of the triangle. We wish to maximize the function $$ f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z, $$ subject to the constraint $$ x+y+z=\pi . $$ Note that we also have the constraints $0\pi $ or $y>\pi ,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, we can conclude that $x=y.$ Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi \\ x+x+x & =\pi \\ 3x & =\pi \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $$ \displaystyle (\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}), $$ and the maximum value is $$ \begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}.\end{aligned} $$ **Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, $$ \begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 1 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \\ & *The set of rational numbers is countably infinite, i.e.,* > $\mid \mathbb{Q} \mid = \aleph_0$. Let's describe how we can "count" all the elements of the set $\mathbb{Q}^+$, the set of all positive rationals. We'll then use this to construct a bijection from $\mathbb N$ to $\mathbb Q$. First, we write down the elements of $\mathbb Q^+$ in an infinite array that extends forever to the right and bottom, as shown below. ![](images/f0/f0ec1463b9b71ed6050c1d58b0911b3ca42b425dbdd36d83bc51f0679fef4fac.png) We skip any equivalent fraction representations if the corresponding number appears somewhere in the previous rows. For example, notice that $$ \dfrac{2}{2}=\dfrac11 = 1 $$ so we can skip this in the second row of the table. Now, we can traverse the array in the manner shown below. ![](images/d9/d9b12de7f732fdec24d234a26be3888c37a220e2c12052215fa9609640040999.png) By assigning each natural number $n$ to the $n$-th distinct fraction encountered in this path, we define a bijection $f: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q^+$ between $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Q}^+$. $$ \begin{aligned} f(1) &= \frac{1}{1} = 1 \\ f(2) &= \frac{2}{1} = 2 \\ f(3) &= \frac{1}{2} \\ f(4) &= \frac{1}{3} \\ &= ⋮ \end{aligned} $$ Finally, we can use this to construct a bijection $g: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} g(1) &= 0 \\ g(2) &= f(1) = 1 \\ g(3) &= -f(1) =-1 \\ g(4) &= f(2) = 2 \\ g(5) &= -f(2) =-2 \\ g(6) &= f(3) = \frac{1}{2} \\ &= ⋮ \end{aligned} $$ Or, more compactly: $$ g(n) = {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}0 , \hspace{1em} & n = 1 \\ f ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} n ) , \hspace{1em} & n \text{ even} \\ - f ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} ( n - 1 ) ) , \hspace{1em} & n > 1 \text{ and odd}\end{array} \right. } $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "63c24e1a-1539-5298-8b15-9545c8f17a70" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8234 :tutorial/title "The Cardinality of the Rational Numbers"} {:db/id 17592186199596 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we saw how to define the limit of a null sequence (i.e., a sequence whose limit equals zero) and how to construct a formal proof that a given sequence is null. In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include sequences that converge a finite (not necessarily zero) limit. If such a limit exists, it's usually denoted as $L$. Consider the following sequence: $$ a_n = \dfrac{n+1}{n}, \qquad n \geq 1 $$ It's easy to see that the limit of this sequence is $$ {\color{red}{L}}={\color{red}{1}}{:} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} \lim_{n \to \infty}a_{n} &= \lim_{n \to \infty}\left(\frac{n + 1}{n}\right) \\ &= \lim_{n \to \infty}(\frac{n}{n} + \frac{1}{n}) \\ &= \lim_{n \to \infty}(1 + \frac{1}{n}) \\ &= 1 + 0 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned} $$ This means that for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a natural number $N(\varepsilon)$ such that the distance between $a_n$ and $$ {\color{red}{L}} = {\color{red}{1}} $$ is *smaller than* $\varepsilon$ for all $$ n\geq N $$ In other words, $$ \forall n\geq N,\qquad \mid a_n - {\color{red}{1}} \mid < \varepsilon $$ Let's draw a few sketches to illustrate this idea. - If we select $\varepsilon = 0.5$, then $\mid a_n-{\color{red}{1}} \mid < \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq 3$. ![](images/be/bee8ffa92b56e2e8dedc214322481b13a3ab8cd4b73d84a5c1300d10dbd43d4f.png) - If $\varepsilon = 0.3$, then $\mid a_n-{\color{red}{1}} \mid < \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq 4$. ![](images/d2/d27e06c19457ab1c89386cde995c043c6d6d55169ec8fdc32509690bf1880767.png) - If $\varepsilon = 0.1$, then $\mid a_n-{\color{red}{1}} \mid < \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq 11$. ![](images/56/564c5ddf12f0171c5d55da0d669f9f7bff2726707c72e473fa9e8eb6704bd937.png) The key idea is this: By making $\varepsilon$ smaller and smaller, we can *always* find an index $N$ where the distance between $a_n$ and $\color{red}L$ is smaller than $\varepsilon$ for all $$ n\geq N $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "01b59a18-c546-5f7f-9fd3-34c58eb29400" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8387 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "844a3f2a-b514-5b75-bfe6-43868ebe9db0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "H(t) = 3\sin (\frac{π}{2}t) + 5" :db/id 17592186199705} {:answer/id #uuid "994e32e5-02d5-5afe-8934-e19a9e9fc3d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "H(t) =-6\sin (\frac{3π}{2}t) + 2" :db/id 17592186199707} {:db/id 17592186203752 :question/id #uuid "f69fbd84-8d87-5e68-af93-345cdf64fd6c" :question/math-academy-id "e-15126" :question/problem "Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{30}$ be a random sample of size $n = 30$ conducted without replacement from a population of $N=100$ individuals where $25\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Find the probability that the proportion of individuals in the sample having the characteristic is between $35\%$ and $50\%$. Express your answer in terms of $\Phi(z)$, the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution." :question/worked-solution "Given a population of $N$ individuals in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as $$ \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right) $$ where - $n$ is the sample size, - $np > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and - $n(1-p) > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic). The factor $$ \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} $$ is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where - $n\gt 5\%\cdot N$ (i.e., the sample comprises more than $5\%$ of the population), and - The sample is conducted without replacement. If a sample is conducted from a finite population *with replacement*, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required. In our case, we have $$ n = 30, \qquad p = 0.25, \qquad N = 100 $$ Now, since $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle n & \displaystyle > 5 \mathrm{\% } \cdot 100 = 5 \\ \displaystyle n p & \displaystyle = 30 ( 0.25 ) = 7.5 > 5 \\ \displaystyle n ( 1 - p ) & \displaystyle = 30 ( 0.75 ) = 22.5 > 5\end{array}} $$ we can apply the above approximation. The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as $$ \widehat{p} \mid ∼N(p, (p(1 - p))/(n) \cdot \frac{N - n}{N - 1}); ∼N(0.25, (0.25(1 - 0.25))/(30) \cdot \frac{70}{99}); ∼N(0.25, \frac{7}{1584}) $$ The probability we wish to find is $$ P\left(0.35 \lt \widehat{\,p} \lt 0.5\right) $$ So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring: $$ \begin{aligned} P(0.35 < \widehat{p} < 0.5) &= P(\frac{0.35 - 0.25}{\sqrt{\frac{7}{1584}}} < Z < \frac{0.5 - 0.25}{\sqrt{\frac{7}{1584}}}) \\ &\approx P(1.50 < Z < 3.76) \\ &= P(Z < 3.76) - P(Z < 1.50) \\ &= Φ(3.76) - Φ(1.50) \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ P\left(0.35 \lt \widehat{\,p} \lt 0.5\right) \approx \Phi(3.76) - \Phi(1.50) $$"} {:db/id 17592186203753 :question/id #uuid "85d17e0c-373c-5ae7-b5a6-36e401ef4d0f" :question/math-academy-id "e-15127" :question/problem "Of the $182$ members of a gym, $80\%$ work out for more than $100$ minutes each visit. Find the probability that the number of gym members in the sample who work out for more than $100$ minutes each visit is at least $24$. *Hint: The table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

$\, -0.8 \,$$\, 0.1977 \,$$\, 0.1949 \,$$\, 0.1922 \,$$\, 0.1894 \,$
$\, -0.7 \,$$\, 0.2266 \,$$\, 0.2236 \,$$\, 0.2206 \,$$\, 0.2177 \,$
" :question/worked-solution "Given a population of $N$ individuals in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as $$ \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\cdot \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} \right) $$ where - $n$ is the sample size, - $np > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and - $n(1-p) > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic). The factor $$ \dfrac{N-n}{N-1} $$ is the finite population correction factor for the variance. This is used in cases of finite samples where - $n\gt 5\%\cdot N$ (i.e., the sample comprises more than $5\%$ of the population), and - the sample is conducted without replacement. If a sample is conducted from a finite population *with replacement*, then the sample data are independent, and a finite population correction factor is not required. In our case, we have $$ n = 32, \qquad p = 0.8, \qquad N = 182 $$ Now, since $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle n & \displaystyle > 5 \mathrm{\% } \cdot 182 = 9.1 \\ \displaystyle n p & \displaystyle = 32 ( 0.8 ) = 25.6 > 5 \\ \displaystyle n ( 1 - p ) & \displaystyle = 32 ( 0.2 ) = 6.4 > 5\end{array}} $$ we can apply the above approximation. The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as $$ \widehat{p} \mid ∼N(p, (p(1 - p))/(n) \cdot \frac{N - n}{N - 1}); ∼N(0.8, (0.8(1 - 0.8))/(32) \cdot \frac{150}{181}); ∼N(0.8, \frac{3}{724}) $$ The probability we wish to find is $$ P\left(\widehat{\,p} \geq \dfrac{24}{32}\right) = P\left(\widehat{\,p} \geq 0.75 \right) $$ So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring: $$ \begin{aligned} P(\widehat{p} \ge 0.75) &= P(Z \ge \frac{0.75 - 0.8}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{724}}}) \\ &= P(Z \ge - 0.78) \\ &= 1 - P(Z < - 0.78) \\ &= 1 - Φ(-0.78) \end{aligned} $$ From the table, we have $$ Φ(-0.78) = 0.2177 $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} P(\widehat{p} \ge 0.75) &= 1 - Φ(-0.78) \\ &= 1 - 0.2177 \\ &= 0.7823 \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186203802 :question/id #uuid "97316423-10b5-5049-912f-7854c26a96c9" :question/math-academy-id "e-16382" :question/problem "The student council coordinator wants to estimate the difference in the proportion of eighth and ninth-grade students who vote in student elections. He conducts two simple random samples of students in his school. The summary statistics of the two samples are given in the table below.
Eighth Grade Ninth Grade
Students $62$ $70$
Students who vote in student elections $48$ $35$
Which of the following statements is true? 1. The end-points of the $98\%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population proportions are approximately $0.274 \pm 0.129$. 2. All values contained within the $98\%$ confidence interval are negative. 3. The confidence interval data suggests that $p_1 > p_2$. *Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z > 2.326) = 0.01$, where $Z \sim N(0,1)$. Assume that $p_1$ and $p_2$ correspond to the eighth and ninth-grade students, respectively.*" :question/worked-solution "Let us call $n_1, n_2$ the sample sizes of eighth and ninth-grade students, and $\widehat{\,p}_1, \widehat{\,p}_2$ the proportion of students who vote in student elections in the two samples. Since $n_1=62$, $n_2=70$, $$ \widehat{\,p}_1=\dfrac{48}{62}=\dfrac{24}{31} $$ and $$ \widehat{\,p}_2=\dfrac{35}{70} = \dfrac{1}{2} $$ we have that - $n_1 \widehat{\,p}_1 = 48> 5$, - $n_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1) = 62 - 48 = 14> 5$, - $n_2 \widehat{\,p}_2 = 35> 5$, - $n_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2) = 70- 35 = 35> 5$. As a result, we may use a normal approximation: $$ \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{\mid}} \sim N(0,1) $$ where - $\!\widehat{\,p}_1, \widehat{\,p}_2$ are the sample proportions, - $p_1, p_2$ are the population proportions, - $n_1, n_2$ are the sample sizes. Then, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population difference of proportions $p_1-p_2$ can be written as $$ \widehat{\,p}_1-\widehat{\,p}_2 \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}} $$ where $$ P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2} $$ and $Z \sim N(0,1)$. We are interested in finding a $98\%$ confidence interval. So, we have $$ \alpha=1-0.98=0.02 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.01 $$ We are given that that $$ P(Z > 2.326) = 0.01 $$ As a result, $$ z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.01} = 2.326 $$ Therefore, a $98\%$ confidence interval for the difference of the population proportions $p_1-p_2$ is the following: $$ (\frac{24}{31} - \frac{1}{2}) ± 2.326 \cdot \sqrt{(\frac{48}{62}(1 - \frac{48}{62}))/(62) + (\frac{35}{70}(1 - \frac{35}{70}))/(70)} $$ which simplifies as $0.274 ± 0.186$. Let's now examine our statements. - Statement I is false. The end-points of our confidence interval are $0.274 \pm 0.186$. - Statement II is false. All values within the confidence interval are positive: $(0.274 - 0.186, \, 0.274 + 0.186) = (0.088, \, 0.460)$ - Statement III is true. Since all values within the confidence interval are positive, this suggests that the proportion of eighth-grade students who vote in student elections is greater than that of ninth-graders. In other words, $p_1 > p_2$. Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186203857 :question/id #uuid "ca1002c8-c615-5f7b-8876-82cf87c8864f" :question/math-academy-id "e-17349" :question/problem "Consider the \frac{1}{2}} & {\displaystyle \frac{3}{2}} \\ - 4 & 10\end{array} \right]}?$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of a function $f: \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with respect to a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is $$ \nabla_X f(X) = {\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}{\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{11}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{12}}} & \cdots & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{1 n}}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{21}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{22}}} & \cdots & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{2 n}}} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{m 1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{m 2}}} & \cdots & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{m n}}}\end{array} \right]}. $$ In our case, writing out the function $f(X)$ where $X = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{x}_{11} & {x}_{12} \\ {x}_{21} & {x}_{22}\end{array} \right]} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$, we get $$ f(X) = (\det(X))^2 = (x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21})^2. $$ So, the gradient is $$ \begin{aligned}\,\,\,{∇}_{X}f(X) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{11}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{12}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{21}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{22}}\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{11}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2} & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{12}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2} \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{21}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2} & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{22}}({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot {x}_{22} & 2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot (-{x}_{21}) \\ 2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot (-{x}_{12}) & 2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\cdot {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix} \\ & =2({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix} \\ & =2\det (X)\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating at $X = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} & {\displaystyle \frac{3}{2}} \\ - 4 & 10\end{array} \right]},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =2(-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10-(-4)\cdot \frac{3}{2})\begin{bmatrix}10 & 4 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ & Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and $$ \frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} $$ Now, since $$ {∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)=y, $$ we have that $$ \frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}. $$ Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as $$ {y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i}, $$ }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\ & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\ & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\ & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned} $$ The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so $$ {∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}. $$ Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at Assume that $n$ is an integer."} {:db/id 17592186205135 :tutorial/content "Let's now prove that the $k$th sample moment is an unbiased estimator of the $k$th theoretical moment. Suppose we have an I.I.D. random sample of size $n{:}$ $X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3, \quad \ldots,\quad X_n$ The $k$th theoretical moment, denoted $\mu_k$, is defined as $$ \mu_k = \textrm{E}[X_i^k] = \sum_{x\in S} x^k \cdot p(x) $$ and the $k$th sample moment is $$ M_k = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k $$ Recall that $M_k$ is an unbiased estimate of $\mu_k$ if $$ \textrm E[M_k] = \mu_k $$ We can show this is true using the properties of expectation: $$ \begin{aligned} E[M_{k}] &= E[\frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i}^{k}] \\ &= \frac{1}{n} \cdot E[∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i}^{k}] \\ &= \frac{1}{n} \cdot (E[X_{1}^{k}] + E[X_{2}^{k}] + ⋯ + E[X_{n}^{k}]) \\ &= \frac{1}{n} \cdot \underbrace{(μ_{k} + μ_{k} + ⋯ + μ_{k})}_{n\text{ times}} \\ &= \frac{1}{n} \cdot nμ_{k} \\ &= μ_{k} \end{aligned} $$ as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "50c68280-940b-52c4-a445-28e2cc7920f6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10742 :tutorial/title "Sample Moments as Unbiased Estimators of Population Moments"} {:db/id 17592186205148 :tutorial/content "We wish to prove that $$ \begin{array}{c}{S}_{x x} = \sum _{i}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n} {( \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i} )}^{2} .\end{array} $$ We start with the definition of $S_{xx}{:}$ $$ \begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {S}_{x x} & \displaystyle = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} ( {x}_{i} - \overline{x} {)}^{2}\end{array} $$ First, we expand the binomial: $$ \begin{array}{r}\displaystyle \sum _{i = 1}^{n} ( {x}_{i}^{2} - 2 {x}_{i} \cdot \overline{x} + {\overline{x}}^{2} )\end{array} $$ Distributing the summation, we have $$ \begin{array}{r}\displaystyle \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - \sum _{i = 1}^{n} 2 {x}_{i} \cdot \overline{x} + \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {\overline{x}}^{2} .\end{array} $$ Now, since $2, \overline x,$ and $\overline{x}^2$ are constants, we can write this as $$ \begin{array}{r}\displaystyle \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - 2 \overline{x} \cdot \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i} + {\overline{x}}^{2} \cdot \sum _{i = 1}^{n} 1 .\end{array} $$ Next, we use the following results: $$ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = n\overline x, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n 1 = n $$ This gives $$ \begin{array}{cc}{S}_{x x} & = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - 2 \overset{–}{x} \cdot n \overset{–}{x} + {\overset{–}{x}}^{2} \cdot n \\ & = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - 2 n {\overset{–}{x}}^{2} + n {\overset{–}{x}}^{2} \\ & = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - n {\overset{–}{x}}^{2} \\ & = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - n \cdot {( \frac{1}{n} \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i} )}^{2} \\ & = \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - n \cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{2}} \cdot {( \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i} )}^{2} \\ & = \sum _{i}^{n} {x}_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n} {( \sum _{i = 1}^{n} {x}_{i} )}^{2}\end{array} $$ as required. The proofs for $S_{yy}$ and $S_{xy}$ are similar." :tutorial/id #uuid "7dab2448-da48-5100-9373-89c074ae5326" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10852 :tutorial/title "Proving the Shortcut Formulas"} {:db/id 17592186205152 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a sample of size $n$, where the observations are divided into $K$ groups. We want to determine whether the population mean varies by group. In other words, we want to test the following null and alternative hypotheses: - $H_0{:}\: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_K$ - $H_1{:}$ There is at least one population mean that differs from the others, where $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_K$ are the population means of each group. We've already introduced the $F$-ratio test statistic for this problem: $$ W = \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}} $$ Now, we will discuss the distribution of $W$. Let's assume that the data points are independent and follow a normal distribution with equal mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2{:}$ $$ X_{jk} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad j=1, 2, \ldots, n_k, \quad k=1, 2, \ldots, K $$ where $n_k$ is the size of the $k$th group. Also, recall that $$ \textrm{SST} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X})^2, \qquad \text{SSW} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2, \qquad \text{SSB} = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k (\overline{X}_k - \overline{X})^2 $$ Given a sample of $n$ independent normal random variables with variance $\sigma^2$, for the sample variance $S^2$, we have $$ \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim\chi^2(n-1) $$ We can use this result to find the distribution of $\text{SST}/\sigma^2$. Since $$ \textrm{SST} = (n-1)S^2 $$ it follows that $$ \dfrac{\textrm{SST}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2(n-1) $$ We can also apply this result to *each* group mean: $$ \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n_k-1), \quad k = 1, \ldots, K $$ Moreover, the above sums are independent. Since each group variance contributes $(n_k - 1)$ degrees of freedom, we have $$ \dfrac{\text{SSW}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n - K) $$ It can be shown that $\text{SSB}$ and $\text{SSW}$ are independent. Therefore, since $$ \text{SST} = \text{SSB} + \text{SSW} $$ we have that $\text{SSB}/\sigma^2$ follows a chi-squared distribution with $$ n-1 - (n-K) = K-1 $$ degrees of freedom. Notice that our test statistic $W$ is the ratio of two independent chi-squared random variables divided by their respective degrees of freedom: $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{\text{SSB}}{ {\sigma }^{2}}} )}{( {\displaystyle \frac{\text{SSW}}{ {\sigma }^{2}}} )}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{n - K}{K - 1}} & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{\text{SSB}}{\cancel{ {\sigma }^{2}}}} )}{( {\displaystyle \frac{\text{SSW}}{\cancel{ {\sigma }^{2}}}} )}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{n - K}{K - 1}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{\text{SSB}}{K - 1}} )}{( {\displaystyle \frac{\text{SSW}}{n - K}} )}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = W\end{array}} $$ Therefore, $W$ follows a Fisher's $F$-distribution with $\nu_1=K-1$ and $\nu_2=n-K$ degrees of freedom. $$ W\sim F(K-1, n-K) $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "90ff1333-26a6-594a-9739-5ec8c5020d89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10872 :tutorial/title "The Distribution of the F-Ratio"} {:db/id 17592186205195 :tutorial/content "When working with scalar-valued functions defined on matrices, it's often helpful to compute gradients using component-wise differentiation and the chain rule. This approach breaks down the computation into simpler intermediate steps and allows us to clearly see the dependencies. Consider a *scalar* function $L(\mathbf A),$ defined as $$ L(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)^T \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right) $$ where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Suppose we want to compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$, which is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$. The entry in the $i$th row and $j$th column of the gradient matrix is given by $$ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}. $$ To simplify the differentiation, we define $\mathbf y \in\mathbb R^{2\times 1}$ as $$ \mathbf{y} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{array} \right]} =\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}. $$ Then, we can write $L$ in terms of $\mathbf y$ as $$ L = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y}. $$ To compute $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}$, we apply the multivariable chain rule: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^2 \frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} \cdot \frac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}} $$ Note that the summation is from $k=1$ to $k=2$ because $\mathbf y$ has two components, and we're differentiating with respect to each of them. Now, let's analyze the two factors of the product that appear in this summation. - We know that $$ \begin{aligned}{∇}_{y}L & ={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2y \\ & =y.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} = y_k. $$ - Writing $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$ in component form $$ y_i = \sum_{j=1}^3 a_{ij} x_j - b_i, $$ we have $$ \frac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}} = {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}{x}_{j} , & i = k , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. } $$ Only the $k$th row of $\mathbf{A}$ affects $y_k$. Putting our two results together gives $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\ & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\ & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j},\end{aligned} $$ because all terms vanish except the one where $k=i$. Therefore, we conclude that $$ \nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T. $$ In the next example, we will use this formula to compute the gradient for specific vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid
