$$ \displaystyle \left| \dfrac{3}{5}x - \dfrac{11}{6} \right| = \dfrac{7}{3} $$" :question/worked-solution "To solve this equation, we consider both possible cases for the absolute value. - If $$ \displaystyle \left|\dfrac{3}{5}x - \dfrac{11}{6}\right| = \dfrac{3}{5}x - \dfrac{11}{6}, $$ then $$ \begin{aligned}|\frac{3}{5}x-\frac{11}{6}| & =\frac{7}{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}x-\frac{11}{6} & =\frac{7}{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}x & =\frac{7}{3}+\frac{11}{6} \\ \frac{3}{5}x & =\frac{14}{6}+\frac{11}{6} \\ \frac{3}{5}x & =\frac{25}{6} \\ x & =\frac{25}{6}\cdot \frac{5}{3} \\ x & =\frac{125}{18}.\end{aligned} $$ - If $$ \displaystyle \left|\dfrac{3}{5}x - \dfrac{11}{6}\right| = -\left(\dfrac{3}{5}x - \dfrac{11}{6}\right), $$ then $$ \begin{aligned}|\frac{3}{5}x-\frac{11}{6}| & =\frac{7}{3} \\ -(\frac{3}{5}x-\frac{11}{6}) & =\frac{7}{3} \\ -\frac{3}{5}x+\frac{11}{6} & =\frac{7}{3} \\ -\frac{3}{5}x & =\frac{7}{3}-\frac{11}{6} \\ -\frac{3}{5}x & =\frac{14}{6}-\frac{11}{6} \\ -\frac{3}{5}x & =\frac{3}{6} \\ x & =\frac{3}{6}\cdot \left(-\frac{5}{3}\right) \\ x & =-\frac{15}{18} \\ x & =-\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the sum of the solutions is $$ \dfrac{125}{18} + \left(-\dfrac{5}{6}\right) = \dfrac{125}{18} - \dfrac{15}{18} = \dfrac{110}{18} = \dfrac{55}{9} $$"} {:db/id 17592186208393 :question/id #uuid "774df04b-0a98-5433-bd4b-69377177d4a4" :question/math-academy-id "e-20003" :question/problem "What is the sum of the solutions to the equation given below? $\left| s - \dfrac{7}{6} \right| - 11 = -5$" :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the absolute value by adding $11$ to both sides: $$ \begin{aligned} \mid s - \frac{7}{6} \mid - 11 &= -5 \\ \mid s - \frac{7}{6} \mid &= 6 \end{aligned} $$ Next, we consider both possible cases for the absolute value. - If $$ \displaystyle \left| s - \dfrac{7}{6} \right| = s - \dfrac{7}{6}, $$ then $$ \begin{aligned}|s-\frac{7}{6}| & =6 \\ s-\frac{7}{6} & =6 \\ s & =\frac{7}{6}+6 \\ s & =\frac{7}{6}+\frac{36}{6} \\ s & =\frac{43}{6}.\end{aligned} $$ - If $$ \displaystyle \left| s - \dfrac{7}{6} \right| = -\!\left(s - \dfrac{7}{6} \right), $$ then $$ \begin{aligned}|s-\frac{7}{6}| & =6 \\ -\hspace{-0.167em}(s-\frac{7}{6}) & =6 \\ -s+\frac{7}{6} & =6 \\ -s & =6-\frac{7}{6} \\ -s & =\frac{36}{6}-\frac{7}{6} \\ -s & =\frac{29}{6} \\ s & =-\frac{29}{6}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the sum of the solutions is $$ \dfrac{43}{6} + \left(-\dfrac{29}{6}\right) = \dfrac{14}{6} = \dfrac{7}{3} $$"} {:db/id 17592186208519 :question/id #uuid "b44810fa-c705-557f-ba46-22d9be760912" :question/math-academy-id "e-20821" :question/problem "In the system of equations below, $r$ and $s$ are constants: $$ \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}{\displaystyle \frac{5}{6}} x - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{8}} y = 3 \\ r x - 9 y = s\end{array} \right. } $$ If the system has an infinite number of solutions $(x, y)$, what is the value of $r$?" :question/worked-solution "A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. This occurs when both equations have the same slope and the same $y$-intercept. In other words, the two equations represent the same line if one equation is a constant multiple of the other. We start by eliminating fractions from the first equation to make comparison easier. We multiply both sides of the first equation by $24$ (the least common multiple of $6$ and $8$): $$ \begin{aligned} 24(\frac{5}{6}x - \frac{1}{8}y) &= 24(3) \\ 20x - 3y &= 72 \end{aligned} $$ So the system becomes $$ {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}20 x - 3 y = 72 \\ r x - 9 y = s\end{array} \right. } $$ Now, if one equation is a constant multiple of the other, all coefficients and constants are proportional. That means $$ \frac{r}{20} = \frac{(-9)}{(-3)} = \frac{s}{72} $$ To find the value of $r$, we focus on the proportion $$ \frac{r}{20}= \frac{(-9)}{(-3)} = 3 $$ Therefore, multiplying both sides by $20$, we find that the value of $r$ is $$ r = 3 \cdot 20 = 60 $$"} {:db/id 17592186208520 :question/id #uuid "62f09140-f9b7-5d48-b357-d8fe981e2c5f" :question/math-academy-id "e-20822" :question/problem "$$ \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}- {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} x + {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} y = {\displaystyle \frac{7}{10}} \\ a x + b y = {\displaystyle \frac{7}{10}}\end{array} \right. } $$ In the given system of equations, $a$ and $b$ are constants. The system has infinitely many solutions. What is the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}$?" :question/worked-solution "A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. This occurs when both equations have the same slope and the same $y$-intercept. In other words, the two equations represent the same line if one equation is a constant multiple of the other. We start by eliminating fractions from both equations to make the comparison easier. We multiply both sides of the first equation by $10$ (the least common multiple of $5$, $2$, and $10$): $$ \begin{aligned} 10(-\frac{3}{5}x + \frac{1}{2}y) &= 10\left(\frac{7}{10}\right) \\ - 6x + 5y &= 7 \end{aligned} $$ We also multiply both sides of the second equation by $10{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned} 10(ax + by) &= 10\left(\frac{7}{10}\right) \\ 10ax + 10by &= 7 \end{aligned} $$ So, the system becomes $$ {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}- 6 x + 5 y = 7 \\ 10 a x + 10 b y = 7\end{array} \right. } $$ Now, if one equation is a constant multiple of the other, all coefficients and constants are proportional. That means $$ \dfrac{10a}{-6} = \dfrac{10b}{5} = \dfrac{7}{7} $$ To find the value of $$ \dfrac{a}{b} $$ we focus on the proportion $$ \dfrac{10a}{-6} = \dfrac{10b}{5} $$ It gives $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 10 a \cdot 5 & \displaystyle = 10 b \cdot ( - 6 ) \\ \displaystyle 50 a & \displaystyle = - 60 b \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{a}{b}} & \displaystyle = - {\displaystyle \frac{60}{50}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{a}{b}} & \displaystyle = \bbox[4pt,border:1px solid lightgray]{- {\displaystyle \frac{6}{5}}} .\end{array}} $$"} {:db/id 17592186208930 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0288d1c8-90da-55c4-98e8-5a5eabefe8cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 22\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186539481} {:answer/id #uuid "86d96929-a573-5ba1-a568-15337e2bcf56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -29\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186539703} {:answer/id #uuid "cc83261d-2254-5227-8497-098b5fbcaed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-7 \\ -29\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186539828} {:answer/id #uuid "e136544d-ec3c-563b-b13e-653feae14454" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 & 22\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186539864} {:answer/id #uuid "ff114911-6bea-5d83-a4a0-4820ac877a2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}25 \\ -11\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186539914}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539828} :answer-field/id #uuid "6839df18-40b0-55d8-b0ee-244e7c3bdebb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186205341}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8b2d453b-0edb-52e1-a8ad-599845d2374a" :question/math-academy-id "q-269515" :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $$ \displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}? $$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients. Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and $$ {∇}_{x}L={\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot {\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T}. $$ Now, since $$ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A, $$ we have that $$ \begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot {\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T} \\ & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating at $$ \displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}, $$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot y \\ & ={A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\ & ={\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\left(\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\right) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\right) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7 \\ :question/math-academy-id "q-275334" :question/problem "A game randomly selects an integer $n$ from $1$ to $301,$ with each value equally likely. Then, a player is asked to guess an integer uniformly and randomly from $1$ to $n.$ What is the expected value of the player’s guess?" :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, an integer $n$ is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $301,$ and then a number is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $n.$ We are asked to find the expected value of the number selected in the second step. - Let $Y$ be the first random number, an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $301.$ - Let $X$ be the player’s guess, an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$ We are asked to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Since the distribution of $X$ depends on $Y,$ we apply the tower property: $$ \text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\text{E}[X∣Y]] $$ Given $Y=n,$ the number $X$ is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $n.$ So, we have that $$ \text{E}[X∣Y=n]=\frac{n+1}{2}. $$ Therefore, we have that $$ \text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\frac{1+Y}{2}]. $$ Now, we apply the linearity of expectation: $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \text{E}[1+Y] \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+\text{E}[Y])\end{aligned} $$ Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,…,301\},$ we use the formula for the mean of the first $n$ integers: $$ \text{E}[Y]=\frac{1+301}{2}=151. $$ Substituting, we finally get $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+\text{E}[Y]) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+151) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 152 \\ & =76.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186208946 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "125.75" :db/id 17592186531080}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186531080} :answer-field/id #uuid "43b17d3b-03b0-5905-9862-543ee5a6fde9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186205427}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d8f9a785-f3a0-5c7d-87e9-2dbe1e634d2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-275335" :question/problem "A video game randomly selects a level difficulty $d$ from $1$ to $500,$ with each value equally likely. Once the difficulty is chosen, a treasure chest is placed in one of $d$ zones within the level, numbered from $1$ to $d,$ with each zone equally likely to receive the chest. What is the expected number of the zone where the chest appears? The expected number of the zone where the chest appears is {{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, a level difficulty is selected uniformly from the integers $1$ through $500,$ and then a treasure chest is placed uniformly in one of the zones numbered $1$ through $d,$ where $d$ is the selected difficulty. - Let $Y$ be the difficulty level of the chosen level. Since the difficulty is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $500,$ we have $Y∼U\{1,2,…,500\}.$ - Let $X$ be the number of the zone where the chest is placed, which is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$ We are asked to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Since $X$ depends on $Y,$ we apply the tower property: $$ \text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\text{E}[X∣Y]] $$ Given $Y=d,$ the zone is selected uniformly from $1$ to $d.$ So, we have that $$ \text{E}[X∣Y=d]=\frac{d+1}{2}. $$ Therefore, we have that $$ \text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\frac{Y+1}{2}]. $$ Now, we apply the linearity of expectation: $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \text{E}[Y+1] \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\text{E}[Y]+1)\end{aligned} $$ Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,…,500\},$ we compute $$ \text{E}[Y]=\frac{1+500}{2}=250.5. $$ Substituting, we find $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (250.5+1) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 251.5 \\ & =125.75.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186209052 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "7f6c519a-66af-50cf-9a33-2e7e289f3ce0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186206016}] :question/id #uuid "7eacb426-8e9d-5821-abc7-1009533613dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-285566" :question/problem "The function $g$ is defined by $$ \displaystyle g(x) = 2(\frac{1}{3} - x)^{2} + \frac{5}{3}. $$ What is the value of $g\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)$?$g\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) =$ {{field-1}}"} {:db/id 17592186209877 :tutorial/content "Now, let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $f: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}$. Suppose we want to compute the gradient $$ \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})). $$ To do this, we need to apply the chain rule. The chain rule for total derivatives tells us that $$ \underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{1 \times n} = \underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{1 \times q} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}. $$ Now, recall that the gradient of a scalar function is the transpose of the total derivative: $$ \underbrace{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f}_{n \times 1} = \left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T $$ To derive the chain rule in terms of gradients, we apply the identity $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, which gives $$ \begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T} \\ & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\ & =\underbrace{{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}}_{n\times q}\cdot \underbrace{{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T}}_{q\times 1}.\end{aligned} $$ So, the gradient chain rule is $$ \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = \left( \frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} f. $$ Note that the order matters; when expressed in the gradient form, the derivatives are applied *from right to left!*" :tutorial/id #uuid "eb90df7d-906c-5d50-a61a-40222511f26e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12301 :tutorial/title "Computing Gradients With the Chain Rule"} {:answer/id #uuid "0253345d-8a41-5446-803c-ad22cdeb35c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(y - $x + 1 = 0$ - $x - \dfrac{4}{3} = 0$ - $x - 6 = 0$ So, according to the zero product rule, they are also the solutions of the product $$ (x + 1)\left(x - \dfrac{4}{3}\right)(x - 6) = 0 $$ To eliminate fractions, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned} 3(x + 1)(x - \frac{4}{3})(x - 6) &= 3 \cdot 0 \\ (3x - 4)(x + 1)(x - 6) &= 0 \end{aligned} $$ Now, we expand the left-hand side: $$ \begin{aligned} (3x - 4)(x + 1)(x - 6) &= (3x - 4)((x + 1)(x - 6)) \\ &= (3x - 4)(x^{2} - 6x + x - 6) \\ &= (3x - 4)(x^{2} - 5x - 6) \\ &= 3x(x^{2} - 5x - 6) - 4(x^{2} - 5x - 6) \\ &= 3x^{3} - 15x^{2} - 18x - 4x^{2} + 20x + 24 \\ &= 3x^{3} - 19x^{2} + 2x + 24 \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, a cubic equation that has the required solutions is $$ 3x^3 - 19x^2 + 2x + 24 = 0 $$"} {:db/id 17592186212818 :question/id #uuid "5f08e3b7-59ef-5268-a3a9-9dc3e681863b" :question/math-academy-id "e-18977" :question/problem "Convert $33\,\dfrac{\textrm{yd}^2}{\textrm{min}}$ into square feet per second." :question/worked-solution "We're given the rate in $$ \dfrac{\textrm{yd}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ and want to convert it into $$ \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ To do this, we must apply two conversion factors: one for the area units (from $\textrm{yd}^2$ to $\textrm{ft}^2$) and one for the time units (from $\textrm{min}$ to $\textrm{s}$): $$ \dfrac{\textrm{yd}^2}{\textrm{min}} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ One of the conversion factors should change $\textrm{yd}^2$ to $\textrm{ft}^2$. $$ \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{yd}^2}}{\textrm{min}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{yd}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ The other conversion factor should change $\textrm{min}$ to $\textrm{s}$. $$ \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{yd}^2}}{\cancel{\textrm{min}}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{yd}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{min}}}{\textrm{s}} = \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ So, the complete conversion formula is $$ \dfrac{\textrm{yd}^2}{\textrm{min}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{yd}^2} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{min}}{\textrm{s}} = \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them. - We are given the quantity $33\,\dfrac{\textrm{yd}^2}{\textrm{min}}$. - There are $3$ feet per yard. We can write this as follows: $3\,\dfrac{\textrm{ft}}{\textrm{yd}}$ To determine the number of square feet in one square yard, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{(3\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{yd}})}^{2} & ={3}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{{\text{ft}}^{2}}{{\text{yd}}^{2}} \\ & =9\hspace{0.167em}\frac{{\text{ft}}^{2}}{{\text{yd}}^{2}}\end{aligned} $$ - There are $60$ seconds per minute, or $\dfrac{1}{60}$ minutes per second. We can write this as follows: $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{60}\,\dfrac{\textrm{min}}{\textrm{s}} $$ Now, applying our conversion formula, we have $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 33 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{yd}}^{2}}{\text{min}}} & \displaystyle = 33 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{yd}}^{2}}{\text{min}}} \cdot 9 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}{ {\text{yd}}^{2}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{60}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{min}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = ( 33 \cdot 9 \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{60}} ) {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{ {\text{yd}}^{2}}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}{\cancel{ {\text{yd}}^{2}}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{297}{60}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = 4.95 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}{\text{s}}} .\end{array}} $$ Therefore, $$ 33\,\dfrac{\textrm{yd}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ is equivalent to $$ 4.95\,\dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$"} {:db/id 17592186212819 :question/id #uuid "ad8ca4df-81ef-5c68-87b1-57c34cfe0f8b" :question/math-academy-id "e-18978" :question/problem "A park maintenance robot is clearing leaves at a rate of $132{,}000\,\dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{h}}$. Round your answer to the nearest integer. *Hint: $1\,\textrm{m} \approx 3.28\,\textrm{ft}$*" :question/worked-solution "We're given the rate in $$ \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{h}} $$ and we want to convert it to $$ \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ We'll need to multiply by two conversion factors to change both the area unit ($\textrm{ft}^2$ to $\textrm{m}^2$) and the time unit ($\textrm{h}$ to $\textrm{min}$): $$ \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{h}}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ One of the conversion factors should change $\textrm{ft}^2$ to $\textrm{m}^2$. $$ \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{ft}^2}}{\textrm{h}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{ft}^2}} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ The other conversion factor should change $\textrm{h}$ to $\textrm{min}$. $$ \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{ft}^2}}{\cancel{\textrm{h}}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{ft}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{h}}}{\textrm{min}} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ So, our conversion formula is $$ \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{h}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{ft}^2} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{h}}{\textrm{min}} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$ Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them. - The robot's clearing rate is given as $132{,}000 \, \dfrac{\textrm{ft}^2}{\textrm{h}}$. - We are given that there are $3.28$ feet per meter. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are $\dfrac{1}{3.28}$ meters per foot. We can write this as follows: $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{3.28} \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{ft}} $$ To determine the number of square meters in one square foot, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{3.28}\frac{\text{m}}{\text{ft}})}^{2} & =\frac{{1}^{2}}{{3.28}^{2}}\frac{{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{ft}}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{10.7584}\frac{{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{ft}}^{2}}\end{aligned} $$ - There are $60$ minutes per hour, or $\dfrac{1}{60}$ hours per minute. We can write this as follows: $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{60} \dfrac{\textrm{h}}{\textrm{min}} $$ Now, applying our conversion formula, we have $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 132 , 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}{\text{h}}} & \displaystyle \approx 132 , 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}{\text{h}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{10.7584}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{60}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{h}}{\text{min}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = ( 132 , 000 \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{10.7584}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{60}} ) \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}}{\cancel{\text{h}}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\cancel{ {\text{ft}}^{2}}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{\text{h}}}{\text{min}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{132 , 000}{10.7584 \cdot 60}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\text{min}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{132 , 000}{645.504}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\text{min}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle \approx 204 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\text{min}}} ,\end{array}} $$ rounded to the nearest integer. Therefore, the park maintenance robot is clearing leaves at a rate of approximately $$ 204\,\dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{min}} $$"} {:db/id 17592186212820 :question/id #uuid "33cc9ad9-0ba8-5f65-adb6-41b05eccfc3c" :question/math-academy-id "e-18987" :question/problem "Factor the expression $y^2-\dfrac{1}{10}$." :question/worked-solution "Notice that $$ 10 = \big(\sqrt{10}\big)^2 $$ First, we write the expression as a difference of squares: $$ \begin{aligned}y^{2} - \frac{1}{10} &= y^{2} - (1)/((\sqrt{10})^{2}) \\ &= y^{2} - \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\right)^{2}\end{aligned} $$ Then, we factor the expression using the difference of squares formula: $$ y^{2} - \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\right)^{2} = (y - \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}})(y + \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}) $$"} {:db/id 17592186212849 :question/id #uuid "11d3b3ea-12ee-5d4a-b66b-0f312638e31f" :question/math-academy-id "e-19023" :question/problem "Factor the expression $\dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36$." :question/worked-solution "The terms of our expression have a common factor of $4$. So, we simplify the expression by factoring it out: $$ \dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36 = 4\left(\dfrac{m^2}{5}-9\right) $$ Now, let's factor the expression inside parentheses using the difference of squares formula: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{m^{2}}{5} - 9 &= \left(\frac{m}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^{2} - 3^{2} \\ &= (\frac{m}{\sqrt{5}} - 3)(\frac{m}{\sqrt{5}} + 3)\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, our original expression factors as follows: $$ \dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36 = 4\left(\dfrac{m}{\sqrt5} - 3 \right)\left(\dfrac{m}{\sqrt5} + 3 \right) $$"} {:db/id 17592186212854 :question/id #uuid "a7daa55a-4856-5bc4-80ab-3eef823e1de6" :question/math-academy-id "e-19029" :question/problem "$$ \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}- {\displaystyle \frac{1}{6}} x + {\displaystyle \frac{1}{4}} y = {\displaystyle \frac{5}{12}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} x + {\displaystyle \frac{t}{12}} y = - {\displaystyle \frac{5}{6}}\end{array} \right. } $$ In the system of equations above, $t$ is a constant. To do that, we - multiply both sides of the first equation by $12$ (the least common multiple of $6$, $4$, and $12$), and - multiply both sides of the second equation by $12$ (the least common multiple of $2$, $6$, and $12$). This gives the following system: $$ {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}12 \cdot ( - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{6}} x + {\displaystyle \frac{1}{4}} y ) = 12 \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{5}{12}} \\ 12 \cdot ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} x + {\displaystyle \frac{t}{12}} y ) = 12 \cdot ( - {\displaystyle \frac{5}{6}} )\end{array} \right. } \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}- 2 x + 3 y = 5 \\ 4 x + t y = - 10\end{array} \right. } $$ A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. The two equations represent the same line if one equation is a non-zero constant multiple of the other. Now, if one equation is a constant multiple of the other, all the corresponding coefficients and constants must be proportional: $$ \dfrac{-2}{4} = \dfrac{3}{t} = \dfrac{5}{-10} $$ Notice that $$ \dfrac{-2}{4} = \dfrac{5}{-10} = -\dfrac{1}{2} $$ So, to find the value of $t$, we focus on the proportion $$ -\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{t} $$ Solving for $t$, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned} -\frac{1}{2} &= \frac{3}{t} \\ (-1) \cdot t &= 2 \cdot 3 \\ - t &= 6 \\ t &= -6 \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186212858 :question/id #uuid "00eb2c5e-e622-53e9-8c6f-9f95afd19a8c" :question/math-academy-id "e-19033" :question/problem "$$ \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}{\displaystyle \frac{5}{6}} x - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} y = {\displaystyle \frac{7}{2}} \\ r x - 6 y = s\end{array} \right. } $$ In the system of equations above, $r$ and $s$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $\dfrac{r}{s}$?" :question/worked-solution "We start by eliminating fractions from both equations to make the comparison easier. To do that, we multiply both sides of the first equation by $6$ (the least common multiple of $2$, $3$, and $6$). This gives the following system: $$ {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}6 \cdot ( {\displaystyle \frac{5}{6}} x - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} y ) = 6 \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{7}{2}} \\ r x - 6 y = s\end{array} \right. } \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}5 x - 2 y = 21 \\ r x - 6 y = s\end{array} \right. } $$ A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. The two equations represent the same line if one equation is a non-zero constant multiple of the other. Now, if one equation is a constant multiple of the other, all the corresponding coefficients and constants must be proportional: $$ \dfrac{5}{r} = \dfrac{-2}{-6} = \dfrac{21}{s} $$ So, to find the value of $$ \dfrac{r}{s} $$ we focus on the proportion $$ \dfrac{5}{r} = \dfrac{21}{s} $$ To find the value of $$ \dfrac{r}{s} $$ we start by cross-multiplying, which gives $$ \begin{aligned} 5s &= 21r \end{aligned} $$ Dividing both sides of the equation by $s$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{5s}{s} &= \frac{21r}{s} \\ 5 &= \frac{21r}{s} \end{aligned} $$ Finally, dividing both sides of the equation by $21$ yields the desired quantity: $$ \begin{aligned} 5 &= \frac{21r}{s} \\ \frac{5}{21} &= \frac{21r}{21s} \\ \frac{5}{21} &= \frac{r}{s} \\ \frac{r}{s} &= \frac{5}{21} \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186212859 :question/id #uuid "9707f903-49f4-592f-a266-a7837f7f5542" :question/math-academy-id "e-19035" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $\dfrac{7}{8}\left(2^{-s}\right) - \left(2^{-s}\right)$." :question/worked-solution "We need to write the expression $$ \dfrac{7}{8}\left(2^{-s}\right) - \left(2^{-s}\right) $$ in the form $$ k\left(2^{-s}\right) $$ Factoring out the common factor of $$ \left(2^{-s}\right) $$ in the expression, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{7}{8}(2^{-s}) - (2^{-s}) &= \frac{7}{8} \cdot (2^{-s}) - 1 \cdot (2^{-s}) \\ &= (\frac{7}{8} - 1) \cdot (2^{-s}) \\ &= (\frac{7}{8} - \frac{8}{8}) \cdot (2^{-s}) \\ &= \left(-\frac{1}{8}\right) \cdot (2^{-s}) \\ &=-\frac{1}{8}(2^{-s}) \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186212861 :question/id #uuid "e267bdeb-c900-591b-acfb-673ed2e3c454" :question/math-academy-id "e-19037" :question/problem "Given that $15(3^{x-1}) - 4(3^x) = k(3^x)$, find the value of $k$." :question/worked-solution "Let's recall the rules of exponents: - Negative exponents: $x^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{x^n}$ - Radicals as fractional exponents: $\sqrt[n]{x} = x^{1/n}$ - The product rule: $a^n \cdot a^m = a^{n+m}$ - The quotient rule: $\dfrac{a^n}{a^m} = a^{n-m}$ - The power rule: $\left(a^m \right)^n = a^{mn}$ - The power of product rule: $(ab)^n = a^nb^n$ - The power of quotient rule: $$ \displaystyle \left(\dfrac a b \right)^n = \dfrac{a^n}{b^n} $$ We need to write the expression $15(3^{x-1}) - 4(3^x)$ in the form $k(3^x)$. First, we rewrite the first term using the product rule and negative exponents: $$ \begin{aligned} 15(3^{x - 1}) - 4(3^{x}) &= 15 \cdot (3^{x} \cdot 3^{-1}) - 4(3^{x}) \\ &= 15 \cdot (3^{x} \cdot \frac{1}{3}) - 4(3^{x}) \\ &= 15 \cdot (\frac{1}{3} \cdot 3^{x}) - 4(3^{x}) \\ &= 5(3^{x}) - 4(3^{x}) \end{aligned} $$ Finally, combining the two negative terms, we have $$ \begin{aligned} 5(3^{x}) - 4(3^{x}) &= (5 - 4)3^{x} \\ &= 1 \cdot 3^{x} \\ &= 3^{k} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $k=1$."} {:db/id 17592186212875 :question/id #uuid "cb100771-08ec-5284-bbda-3a7f09c3b496" :question/math-academy-id "e-19057" :question/problem "$$ \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}5 x - {\displaystyle \frac{7}{11}} = \sqrt{3} \\ y = - 2 {( {\displaystyle \frac{7}{11}} - 5 x )}^{2}\end{array} \right. } $$ The solution to the given system of equations is the ordered pair $(x,y)$. What is the value of $y$?" :question/worked-solution "From the first equation, we have $$ 5x-\dfrac{7}{11}=\sqrt{3} $$ Notice that if we multiply this equation by $-1$, we get $$ \dfrac{7}{11} - 5x = -\sqrt{3} $$ and the expression on the left-hand side features in the second equation. So next, we substitute $-\sqrt{3}$ for $$ \left(\dfrac{7}{11}-5x\right) $$ in the second equation: $$ \begin{aligned} y &= -2(\frac{7}{11} - 5x)^{2} \\ &=-2(-\sqrt{3})^{2} \\ &=-2 \cdot 3 \\ y &= -6 \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the value of $y$ is $-6$."} {:db/id 17592186212885 :question/id #uuid "c5d5bdf0-e898-500f-9205-c98bf56a4d98" :question/math-academy-id "e-19072" :question/problem "If $\dfrac{5}{8}y - \dfrac{2}{8}y = 6$, what is the value of $y$?" :question/worked-solution "We are given the equation $$ \dfrac{5}{8}y - \dfrac{2}{8}y = 6 $$ and are asked to solve for $y$. To find $12y + 1$ from the given expression, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2$ and solve for $12y{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned} 2(6y + \frac{2}{3}) &= 2 \cdot 4 \\ 12y + \frac{4}{3} &= 8 \\ 12y &= 8 - \frac{4}{3} \\ 12y &= \frac{20}{3} \end{aligned} $$ Now, to obtain $12y + 1$, we add $1$ to both sides and simplify: $$ \begin{aligned} 12y &= \frac{20}{3} \\ 12y + 1 &= \frac{20}{3} + 1 \\ 12y + 1 &= \frac{23}{3} \end{aligned} $$ So, the value of $12y + 1$ is $$ \dfrac{23}{3} $$"} {:db/id 17592186212912 :question/id #uuid "16fe85c3-d01d-5f61-9ccd-0e9c1c22d72d" :question/math-academy-id "e-19114" :question/problem "$$ \displaystyle \dfrac{5}{6}(9w - 1) - \dfrac{1}{3}(9w - 1) = 9 $$ What value of $w$ is the solution to the given equation?" :question/worked-solution "We are given $$ \dfrac{5}{6}(9w - 1) - \dfrac{1}{3}(9w - 1) = 9 $$ Notice that both terms on the left-hand side involve the same binomial expression $(9w - 1)$. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are $\dfrac{1}{1,609}$ miles per meter. What is the value of $y$?"} {:db/id 17592186214249 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we saw how to create and apply a conversion formula to convert quantities with mixed units, such as converting from "kilometers per hour" to "meters per second." In a separate lesson, we saw how to convert between different units of area, such as converting from "square meters" to "square centimeters" and vice versa. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to create and apply conversion formulas for mixed units that contain units of area. For example, suppose a drone maps an area at a rate of $$ 0.9\,\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}} $$ What is this rate in square meters per second? We're given the rate in $$ \dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}} $$ and want to convert it into $$ \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ This means we'll need two conversion factors: one for the area units (from $\textrm{km}^2$ to $\textrm{m}^2$) and one for the time units (from $\textrm{h}$ to $\textrm{s}$): $$ \dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ One of the conversion factors should change $\textrm{km}^2$ to $\textrm{m}^2$. $$ \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}}{\textrm{h}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ The other conversion factor should change $\textrm{h}$ to $\textrm{s}$. $$ \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}}{\cancel{\textrm{h}}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{h}}}{\textrm{s}} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ So, the complete conversion formula is $$ \dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{km}^2} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{h}}{\textrm{s}} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$ Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them. - We are given that the drone maps at a rate of $0.9\,\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}}$. - There are $1,000$ meters in one kilometer. We can write this as follows: $1,000\,\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{km}}$ To determine the number of square meters in one square kilometer, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{(1,000\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{m}}{\text{km}})}^{2} & =1,{000}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{km}}^{2}} \\ & =1,000,000\hspace{0.167em}\frac{{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{km}}^{2}}\end{aligned} $$ - There are $60\cdot60=3,600$ seconds per hour, or $\dfrac{1}{3,600}$ hours per second. We can write this as follows: $$ \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{3,600}\,\dfrac{\textrm{h}}{\textrm{s}} $$ Now, applying the conversion formula, we have $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 0.9 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{km}}^{2}}{\text{h}}} & \displaystyle = 0.9 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{km}}^{2}}{\text{h}}} \cdot 1 , 000 , 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{ {\text{km}}^{2}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3 , 600}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{h}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = ( 0.9 \cdot 1 , 000 , 000 \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3 , 600}} ) {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{ {\text{km}}^{2}}}{\cancel{\text{h}}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\cancel{ {\text{km}}^{2}}}} \cdot {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{\text{h}}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{900 , 000}{3 , 600}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle & \displaystyle = 250 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{m}}^{2}}{\text{s}}} .\end{array}} $$ Therefore, the drone maps the area at a rate of $$ 250\,\dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a7b5cfa1-b4ca-53f4-8040-8b31d0671753" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13534 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186214266 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll discuss strategies for combining exponential expressions. Find the point of intersection." :question/worked-solution "The line $y=4x - k$ intersects the parabola $$ y=-5x^2 + 10x - 1 $$ where $$ -5x^2 + 10x - 1 = 4x - k $$ We need to determine the value of $k$ such that this equation has one real solution. A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero: $$ \mathcal{D} = 0 $$ First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form: $$ \begin{aligned} -5x^{2} + 10x - 1 &= 4x - k \\ - 5x^{2} + 10x - 1 - 4x + k &= 0 \\ - 5x^{2} + 6x + (k - 1) &= 0 \end{aligned} $$ The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following: $$ a = -5, \qquad b = 6, \qquad c = k-1 $$ So, computing the discriminant, we get $$ \begin{aligned} D &= b^{2} - 4ac \\ &= 6^{2} - 4(-5)(k - 1) \\ &= 36 + 20(k - 1) \\ &= 36 + 20k - 20 \\ &= 16 + 20k \end{aligned} $$ To have exactly one real solution, we need $$ \mathcal{D} = 0{:} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} 16 + 20k &= 0 \\ 20k &= -16 \\ k &= -\frac{16}{20} \\ k &= -\frac{4}{5} \end{aligned} $$ Thus, the equation of the line is $$ y=4x-\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)=4x+\dfrac{4}{5} $$ To find the $x$-coordinate, we solve the original quadratic equation, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} -5x^{2} + 6x + (-\frac{4}{5} - 1) &= 0 \\ - 5x^{2} + 6x - \frac{9}{5} &= 0 \\ - 25x^{2} + 30x - 9 &= 0 \\ - (25x^{2} - 30x + 9) &= 0 \\ - (5x - 3)^{2} &= 0 \\ 5x - 3 &= 0 \\ x &= \frac{3}{5} \end{aligned} $$ Finally, we find the $y$-coordinate by substituting $$ x=\dfrac{3}{5} $$ into one of the two equations and solving: $$ \begin{aligned} y &= 4\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) + \frac{4}{5} \\ &= \frac{12}{5} + \frac{4}{5} \\ &= \frac{16}{5} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the point of intersection is $$ \Big(\dfrac{3}{5},\dfrac{16}{5}\Big) $$"} {:db/id 17592186216844 :question/id #uuid "7fcda409-30c3-5280-970e-d22be9f314b8" :question/math-academy-id "e-19662" :question/problem "The equation $k = \sqrt{\dfrac{q\ell}{r}}$ relates the positive numbers $k$, $q$, $\ell$, and $r$. First, we multiply both sides by $r$ to remove the fraction: $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {k}^{2} & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{q ℓ}{r}} \\ \displaystyle {k}^{2} \cdot r & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{q ℓ}{r}} \cdot r \\ \displaystyle {k}^{2} \cdot r & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{q ℓ}{\cancel{r}}} \cdot \cancel{r} \\ \displaystyle r {k}^{2} & \displaystyle = q ℓ\end{array}} $$ Finally, we divide both sides by $\ell$ to isolate $q{:}$ $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{r {k}^{2}}{ℓ}} & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{q ℓ}{ℓ}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{r {k}^{2}}{ℓ}} & \displaystyle = {\displaystyle \frac{q \cancel{ℓ}}{\cancel{ℓ}}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{r {k}^{2}}{ℓ}} & \displaystyle = q\end{array}} $$ Therefore, the correct answer is $$ q = \dfrac{rk^2}{\ell} $$"} {:db/id 17592186216861 :question/id #uuid "8e5c9864-c92c-53a9-b2ff-1e62e801e3ef" :question/math-academy-id "e-19690" :question/problem "Cube $M$ has a side length of $m$ inches. Cube $N$ has a surface area that is $18$ square inches greater than one-half of the surface area of cube $M$. What is the function $V$ that represents the volume of a cube $N$, in cubic inches?" :question/worked-solution "Let - $m$ be the side length of cube $M$, and - $n$ be the side length of cube $N$. Then, - the surface area of cube $M$ is $6m^2$, and - the surface area of cube $N$ is $6n^2$. We are told that the surface area of cube $N$ is $18$ square inches greater than one half of the surface area of cube $M$. In symbols, this means that $$ 6n^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 6m^2 + 18 $$ Now, we solve the obtained equation for $n{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned} 6n^{2} &= 3m^{2} + 18 \\ \frac{6n^{2}}{6} &= \frac{3m^{2} + 18}{6} \\ n^{2} &= \frac{m^{2}}{2} + 3 \\ n &= \sqrt{\frac{m^{2}}{2} + 3} \end{aligned} $$ We disregard the negative solutions since the side length must be positive. Therefore, the function $V$ that represents the volume of cube $N$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned} V(m) &= n^{3} \\ &= (\sqrt{\frac{m^{2}}{2} + 3})^{3} \\ &= ((\frac{m^{2}}{2} + 3)^{1/2})^{3} \\ &= ((\frac{m^{2}}{2} + 3)^{3})^{1/2} \\ &= \sqrt{(\frac{m^{2}}{2} + 3)^{3}} \end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186216868 :question/id #uuid "529282d5-a876-5c84-8d0d-01a28e91d92e" :question/math-academy-id "e-19697" :question/problem "

Therefore, $I(x)=\dfrac{1}{xy^3}$ $\text{is}$ an integrating factor for the initial differential equation."} {:db/id 17592186216980 :question/id #uuid "106cd4dd-2f3f-541e-899a-e2776a39e382" :question/math-academy-id "e-20898" :question/problem "Consider the inexact differential equation $$ \left(x + y^2\right)\,\textrm{d}x + \left(xy + \frac{2}{x}\right)\,\textrm{d}y = 0. $$ It is known that $$ \dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x} $$ where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by $$ P(x,y)=x+y^2,\qquad Q(x,y)=xy+\frac{2}{x}. $$ Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(x)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation." :question/worked-solution "For a differential equation of the form $$ P(x,y)\,\textrm{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0, $$ we have that if $$ \dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=g(x) $$ where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is $$ I(x)=\exp\left(\int g(x)\,\textrm{d}x\right) $$ where $\exp(x)$ denotes the exponential function $e^x.$ We are given that $$ \dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}. $$ Since $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is $$ \begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int {x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x} \\ & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\ & =x.\end{aligned} $$ Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation: $$ \begin{aligned}x[(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+(xy+\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{({x}^{2}y+2)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0.\end{aligned} $$ For this exact equation, we have $$ \widetilde{P}(x,y)=x^2+xy^2,\qquad \widetilde{Q}(x,y)=x^2y+2. $$ To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\widetilde{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$ The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\ & =\int ({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\ & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+F(y).\end{aligned} $$ Next, let's integrate $\widetilde{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$ The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\ & =\int ({x}^{2}y+2)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\ & =\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+2y+G(x).\end{aligned} $$ Comparing the two solutions, we must have $$ F(y)=2y,\qquad G(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}. $$ Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is $$ \frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^2y^2}{2}+2y=c. $$"} {:db/id 17592186216981 :question/id #uuid "b69fa09b-2661-5edc-8fcb-c29120e56325" :question/math-academy-id "e-20935" :question/problem "Find an integrating factor for the following equation in differential form. $$ x\,y' = 4y - 3x $$" :question/worked-solution "For a differential equation of the form $$ P(x,y) \,\textrm{d} x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0, $$ we have that if $$ \dfrac{1}{Q} \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right) = g(x) $$ where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is $$ I(x) = \exp\left({\int g(x)\,\textrm d x}\right) $$ where ${y}_{0}(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation $$ {y}^{′}={y}^{2}-\frac{4}{x}y+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} $$ find the general solution of the equation." :question/worked-solution "The equation $$ {y}^{′}={y}^{2}-\frac{4}{x}y+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}, $$ is a Riccati differential equation of the form $$ {y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x), $$ where $$ a(x)=1,\,b(x)=-\frac{4}{x},\,c(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}. $$ To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution $$ y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x), $$ where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution. Differentiating gives $$ {y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x). $$ In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\frac{2}{x}.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}$, we have $$ y=z+\frac{2}{x}\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}. $$ Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation: $$ {z}^{′}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}=(z+\frac{2}{x})^{2}-\frac{4}{x}(z+\frac{2}{x})+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} $$ Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify: $$ \begin{aligned}{z}^{′}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} & =({z}^{2}+\frac{4z}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})-(\frac{4z}{x}+\frac{8}{{x}^{2}})+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} \\ {z}^{′}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} & ={z}^{2}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned} $$ We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =x+C \\ z & =-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned} $$ where $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Finally, let's substitute $z=y-\frac{2}{x}$ to recover the initial variable $y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y-\frac{2}{x} & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x+C}+\frac{2}{x} \\ & =\frac{2}{x}-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186217792 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a5aa962c-7d0e-52df-8d52-ef49cea07bf7" :answer/type {:db/id inexact differential equation $$ (\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y=0. $$ It is known that $$ \frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{x} $$ where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by $$ P(x,y)=\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)=4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}. $$ Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(x)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation. $\,$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant." :question/worked-solution "For a differential equation of the form $$ P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0, $$ we have that if $$ \frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=g(x) $$ where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is $$ I(x)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int g(x)\,\text{d}x) $$ where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(x)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{x}.$ We are given that $$ \frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{x}. $$ Since $\frac{3}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is $$ \begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{-1}\text{ }\text{d}x} \\ & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\ & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{3}[(\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{(6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned} $$ For this exact equation, we have $$ \overset{~}{P}(x,y)=6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)=4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1. $$ To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\overset{~}{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$ The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$ $$ \begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\ & =\int (6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\ & =2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+F(y).\end{aligned} $$ Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$ The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$ $$ \begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\ & =\int (4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\ & =2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+y+G(x).\end{aligned} $$ Comparing the two solutions, we must have $$ F(y)=y,\,G(x)=0. $$ Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is $$ 2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+y=c. $$"} {:db/id 17592186217793 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "82fd609a-7d57-5e8f-ba67-820976003caf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186216612}] :question/id #uuid "21520ba3-80e3-5455-9216-9ff33775a80b" :question/math-academy-id "q-337099" :question/problem "Consider the inexact differential equation $$ {x}^{2}y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x-({x}^{3}+2{y}^{4})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y=0. $$ It is known that $$ \frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{4}{y} $$ where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by $$ P(x,y)={x}^{2}y,\hspace{2em}Q(x,y)=-{x}^{3}-2{y}^{4}. $$ Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(y)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation. $\hspace{2em}$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(y)=$ {{field-1}}. $\hspace{2em}$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant. Use the displayed quotient only where it is defined, and use the integrating-factor method on regions with $y\ne0$." :question/worked-solution "For an integrating factor depending only on $y$, use $$ I(y)=\exp\left(-\int\frac{P_y-Q_x}{P}\,\mathrm dy\right). $$ The displayed quotient is evaluated where $P\ne0$. Since it simplifies to $4/y$, we can choose $$ I(y)=e^{-4\ln|y|}=\frac1{y^4},\qquad y\ne0. $$ Multiplication gives $$ \frac{x^2}{y^3}\,\mathrm dx+ \left(-\frac{x^3}{y^4}-2\right)\,\mathrm dy=0. $$ This equation is exact, because $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{x^2}{y^3}\right) =-\frac{3x^2}{y^4} =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(-\frac{x^3}{y^4}-2\right). $$ To find a potential $F(x,y)$, integrate its $x$-derivative while holding $y$ fixed: $$ F_x=\frac{x^2}{y^3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(x,y)=\frac{x^3}{3y^3}+G(y). $$ Differentiate with respect to $y$ and match the other coefficient: $$ -\frac{x^3}{y^4}+G'(y)=-\frac{x^3}{y^4}-2, \qquad G'(y)=-2. $$ Therefore the requested implicit general solution is $$ \boxed{\frac{x^3}{3y^3}-2y=c},\qquad y\ne0. $$ Indeed, $\mathrm dF=y^{-4}(P\,\mathrm dx+Q\,\mathrm dy)$, so the level curves give the original differential equation on the stated regions. Although the quotient formula initially requires $P\ne0$, the resulting integrating factor and exact equation extend to $x=0$ whenever $y\ne0$. The original equation also admits $y=0$. That solution lies outside the question's explicit $y\ne0$ region, where the integrating factor is undefined. The factor $1/3$ in the potential is necessary: omitting it changes $F_x$ and does not merely rename the arbitrary constant."} {:db/id 17592186217811 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a8dbb76d-8427-52ed-aba3-9a213f0ea7db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5x - 4y = 12" :db/id 17592186216722} {:answer/id #uuid "bfa13469-2842-5d4e-a19a-988bfc74a16a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9x - 12y = 1" :db/id 17592186216723} {:answer/id #uuid "d54bf9f7-6a3b-5003-950d-e6ee96f33991" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "22x - 12y =-15" :db/id 17592186216724} {:answer/id #uuid "1373d079-fb69-5911-afee-e39baeccea78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x - 12y = 7" :db/id 17592186216725} {:answer/id #uuid "6ced5865-0913-5006-99eb-7d03b478b9f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "26x - 12y =-25" :db/id 17592186216726}] :answer-field/id #uuid "b16282b1-4a13-5f6d-a5c9-ef5ecaf27d7a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186216721}] :question/id #uuid "db651854-8afe-5663-907b-d13cb2687eb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-45729" :question/problem "A circle has its center at $(-\frac{7}{2},-\frac{11}{2})$. If the line $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of $JK^(―)$, what is the equation of $l$?"} {:db/id 17592186218348 :tutorial/content "Now that we have practiced identifying Clairaut equations, let’s see how to solve them. The key feature of Clairaut’s equation is its special form, which leads to a family of **straight-line** solutions and one **singular solution**. Recall that a Clairaut equation has the form $$ y = x\,y' + g(y'), $$ where $g$ is a differentiable function. To simplify the notation, we introduce the substitution: $$ p = y' $$ With this substitution, the equation becomes $$ y = xp + g(p). $$ Next, we differentiate both sides of the substituted equation with respect to $x$. Remember, $p$ is a function of $x$, so we must use the product rule on the $xp$ term and the chain rule on $g(p)$: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xp)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(g(p)) \\ p & =(1\cdot p+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}x})+{g}^{'}(p)\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned} $$ Using $p' = \dfrac{\textrm{d}p}{\textrm{d}x}$, the expression simplifies to $$ p = p + x p' + g'(p)\,p'. $$ Now, if we simply subtract $p$ from both sides and factor out the common term $p'$, we arrive at the pivotal equation for finding our solutions: $$ 0 = p'(x + g'(p)) $$ Since this expression is a product that equals zero, the equation can be satisfied in two different ways. Each way provides us with one type of solution. - **Case I: The General Solution.** The first possibility is that the derivative of $p$ is zero. If $p' = 0$, then $p$ must be a constant. Let's denote this constant as $c$: $$ p = c $$ Substituting $p = c$ back into the original Clairaut equation ($y = xp + g(p)$), we directly obtain the **general solution** $$ y = cx + g(c). $$ This gives a family of straight-line solutions. Each value of $c$ produces a different line, where $c$ is the slope and $g(c)$ gives the $y$-intercept. - **Case II: The Singular Solution.** If instead $x + g'(p) = 0$, then we obtain a singular solution. Let's first solve for $x$ in terms of $p$: $$ x = -g'(p). $$ Then, let's substitute this $x$ back into the original Clairaut equation: $$ \begin{aligned}y & =(-{g}^{'}(p))p+g(p) \\ & =g(p)-p{g}^{'}(p)\end{aligned} $$ This gives us the **singular solution** defined parametrically by the equations: $$ \begin{aligned}x & =-{g}^{'}(p), \\ y & =g(p)-p{g}^{'}(p)\end{aligned} $$ Now, let’s take a look at a concrete example of how to find the general solution to a Clairaut equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "1a89bff4-f460-5475-8f45-3e9a5b8b9ca0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14169 :tutorial/title "Solving a Clairaut Differential Equation"} {:db/id 17592186218363 :tutorial/content "Now, let's find the singular solution of the Clairaut differential equation $$ y = xy' + (y')^2. $$ **Step 1**: Differentiate the equation to find the conditions for the solution. To begin, we introduce a parameter by setting $p = y'.$ Substituting this into the equation gives $$ y = x p + p^2. $$ Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xp+{p}^{2}) \\ {y}^{'} & =(1\cdot p+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}x})+2p\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}x} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{'}+2p{p}^{'} \\ 0 & =x{p}^{'}+2p{p}^{'} \\ 0 & ={p}^{'}(x+2p)\end{aligned} $$ This equation tells us that either $p' = 0$ or $x + 2p = 0.$ - The condition $p' = 0$ leads to the *general solution* of the Clairaut equation. We've already seen how to deal with this case. - The condition $x + 2p = 0$ leads to the *singular solution*, which is the envelope of the general solution's family of curves. On the next slide, we will use the second condition to find the singular solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "daa98f4a-8066-5c1a-a454-a7912394aee6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14859 :tutorial/title "The Singular Solution"} {:answer/id #uuid "a48d3a96-c864-58b6-bf0a-f9b9b5c13ff6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t, \frac{3}{7}t + 1)" :db/id 17592186219871} {:answer/id #uuid "05c98b74-6e6f-55ba-a3df-e5a03d63ddaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t, \frac{2}{7}t + 1)" :db/id 17592186219872} {:answer/id #uuid "1ada8d11-71a1-5d0a-bf83-db61e98fa2a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t, \frac{3}{7}t - Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-1$, then we will get a $+3y$ term that can cancel with the $-3y$ term in the first equation: $$ {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{8}{5}} x - 3 y = 6 & \\ {\displaystyle \frac{2}{5}} x - 3 y = - 6 & | \hspace{0.222em} \times ( - 1 )\end{array} \right. } \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad {\left\{ \begin{array}{l}{\displaystyle \frac{8}{5}} x - 3 y = 6 \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{2}{5}} x + 3 y = 6\end{array} \right. } $$ When we add the two equations, we obtain $$ {\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{8}{5}} x \cancel{- 3 y} & \displaystyle = 6 \\ \displaystyle - {\displaystyle \frac{2}{5}} x \cancel{+ 3 y} & \displaystyle = 6 \\ \hline \displaystyle ( {\displaystyle \frac{8}{5}} x - {\displaystyle \frac{2}{5}} x ) & \displaystyle = 12 \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{6}{5}} x & \displaystyle = 12 \\ \displaystyle x & \displaystyle = 10\end{array}} $$ Now, substitute $x = 10$ into one of the original equations to solve for $y$. We'll use the second equation: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{2}{5}x - 3y &= -6 \\ \frac{2}{5}(10) - 3y &= -6 \\ 4 - 3y &= -6 \\ - 3y &= -10 \\ y &= \frac{10}{3} \end{aligned} $$ Finally, we compute $$ \dfrac{3}{5}x - y{:} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{3}{5}x - y &= \frac{3}{5}(10) - \frac{10}{3} \\ &= 6 - \frac{10}{3} \\ &= \frac{18 - 10}{3} \\ &= \frac{8}{3} \end{aligned} $$ Hence, the value of $$ \dfrac{3}{5}x - y $$ is $$ \dfrac{8}{3} $$"} {:db/id 17592186221042 :question/id #uuid "397c3c58-b56f-5655-8444-a285f0e17e96" :question/math-academy-id "e-20751" :question/problem "The functions $u$ and $v$ are defined as $$ \displaystyle u(x) = \dfrac{4}{5}x - 8 \quad \text{and} \quad v(x) = \dfrac{2}{5}x + 6. $$ If the function $w$ is defined as $w(x) = u(x) + v(x)$, what is the $x$-coordinate of the $x$-intercept of the graph of $y = w(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?" :question/worked-solution "First, we find $w(x)$ by adding $u(x)$ and $v(x){:}$ $$ \begin{aligned} w(x) &= u(x) + v(x) \\ &= (\frac{4}{5}x - 8) + (\frac{2}{5}x + 6) \\ &= (\frac{4}{5}x + \frac{2}{5}x) + (-8 + 6) \\ &= \frac{6}{5}x - 2 \end{aligned} $$ To find the $x$-intercept of $w(x)$, we set $w(x) = 0$ and solve for $x{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned} w(x) &= \frac{6}{5}x - 2 \\ 0 &= \frac{6}{5}x - 2 \\ \frac{6}{5}x &= 2 \\ x &= \frac{5}{6} \cdot 2 \\ &= \frac{10}{6} \\ &= \frac{5}{3} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the $x$-coordinate of the $x$-intercept of $w(x)$ is $$ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{5}{3}} $$"} {:db/id 17592186221150 :question/id #uuid "35a158c3-37b6-5123-ba90-1fd05218ce43" :question/math-academy-id "e-21271" :question/problem "Find $e^{At}$ for $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ - 3 & 4\end{array} \right]}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $4.$*" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\ & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined. Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are $$ \lambda_1=t, \qquad \lambda_2=4t, $$ both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(4t) &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$ - Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get $$ 3t\alpha_1 = e^{4t} - e^{t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{3t}\bigl(e^{4t}-e^{t}\bigr). $$ - Multiplying the first equation by $4$ and subtracting the second one, we get $$ 3\alpha_0 = 4e^{t} - e^{4t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{3}\bigl(4e^{t}-e^{4t}\bigr). $$ Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following: $$ \begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}))t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\ & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}+4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\ & ={e}^{t} \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}))t \\ & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{4t} \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}))t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\ & =\frac{1}{3}((4{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{t})+(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t})) \\ & ={e}^{4t}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ e^{At} = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ {e}^{t} - {e}^{4 t} & {e}^{4 t}\end{array} \right]}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186221151 :question/id #uuid "18064c11-63d3-599a-b504-7b589f46c3dc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21272" :question/problem "Find $e^{At}$ for $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}7 & 4 \\ - 5 & - 1\end{array} \right]}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $3 \pm 2\textrm{i}.$*" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\ & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 4 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined. Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are $$ \lambda_1= (3+2\textrm{i}) t, \qquad \lambda_2= (3-2\textrm{i}) t, $$ which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}r((3+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(3+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(3+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned} $$ Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned} $$ Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following: $$ \begin{aligned}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ & =\frac{7}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)), \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\ & =2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\ & =-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ e^{At} = e^{3t} {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}\cos ( 2 t ) + 2 \sin ( 2 t ) & 2 \sin ( 2 t ) \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{5}{2}} \sin ( 2 t ) & \cos ( 2 t ) - 2 \sin ( 2 t )\end{array} \right]}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186221154 :question/id #uuid "503c762b-0313-598a-a80c-c53d14ec250a" :question/math-academy-id "e-21318" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem: $$ y' = x^2y + e^x, \qquad y(0)=-1 $$ Use the **implicit** Euler method with one step to approximate $y\left(\dfrac12\right).$" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem $$ y' = f(x,y), \qquad y_0 = y(x_0), $$ the implicit Euler method with step size $\Delta x$ is given by $$ \Delta y = y'_\text{new} \cdot \Delta x, $$ with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. First, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=\dfrac12,$ we will use a step size of $$ \Delta x = \dfrac12 - 0 = \dfrac12. $$ Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In our case, $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\ & =({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}{y}_{\text{new}}+{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}{y}_{\text{new}}+{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}}).\end{aligned} $$ We substitute this into $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and solve for the general formula for $y_\text{new}{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}{y}_{\text{new}}+{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}})\end{aligned} $$ which gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}} \\ (1-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}){y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{y+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}}}{1-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is $$ \displaystyle x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x = 0 + \dfrac12 = \dfrac12. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{y+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{x}_{\text{new}}}}{1-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{-1+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{1/2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{4(\sqrt{e}-2)}{7}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ \displaystyle y\left(\dfrac12\right) = \dfrac{4}{7} \left(\sqrt{e} - 2\right). $$"} {:db/id 17592186221156 :question/id #uuid "41b1a655-6092-57b6-8f95-396c566e7a83" :question/math-academy-id "e-21445" :question/problem "Given that $\mathcal{L} \big\{t^n\big\}=\dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find $\mathcal{L}\left\{ u(t-2)\big(t^2+3t+2\big) \right\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "The second shifting theorem states that if $a \ge 0$ and $\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\}$ exists for $s > s_0,$ then $$ \mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\} = e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+a)\big\}, \qquad \text{for} \; s > s_0, $$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function. In our case, we wish to find $$ \mathcal{L}\left\{ u(t-2)\big(t^2+3t+2\big) \right\}. $$ Therefore, $a=2,$ and we have $$ \mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-2)\,g(t)\big\} = e^{-2s}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+2)\big\}, $$ where $g(t)=t^2+3t+2.$ Notice that $$ \begin{aligned}g(t+2) & =(t+2)^{2}+3(t+2)+2 \\ & ={t}^{2}+4t+4\,+\,3t+6\,+\,2 \\ & ={t}^{2}+7t+12.\end{aligned} $$ Since $\mathcal{L} \big\{t^n\big\}=\dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ and $\mathcal{L} \{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}L\{g(t+2)\} & =L\{{t}^{2}+7t+12\} \\ & =L\{{t}^{2}\}+7L\{t\}+12L\{1\} \\ & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+7\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+12\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\ & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{7}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{12}{s}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get $$ \begin{aligned}L\{u(t-2)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-2s}\,L\{g(t+2)\} \\ & ={e}^{-2s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{7}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{12}{s}).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186221160 :question/id #uuid "14669099-db40-5dd2-b4d5-4db016374643" :question/math-academy-id "e-21538" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem: $$ y' = -x - y, \qquad y\left(-1\right) = 0 $$ We wish to approximate the solution using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method. First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(1).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be $$ \Delta x = \dfrac{1-0}2 = \dfrac12. $$ Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $\Delta y$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\ & =(4({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ & =2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned} $$ We substitute this into $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and solve for the general formula for $y_\text{new}{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ \frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2(y+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2})}{3}\end{aligned} $$ We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y\left(\dfrac12\right)$ and $y(1).$ **Step 1**. From the initial conditions, we have $$ x = 0,\qquad y = 0. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x = 0 + \dfrac12 = \dfrac12. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2(y+2({x}_{\text{new}})^{2})}{3} \\ & =\frac{2(0+2{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2})}{3} \\ & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**. }_{0}={e}^{-4t}+4{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-4t}+4{e}^{t}). $$ Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find $L\{u(t-1)({t}^{2}+1)\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then $$ L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0}, $$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function. In our case, we wish to find $$ L\{u(t-1)({t}^{2}+1)\}. $$ Therefore, $a=1,$ and we have $$ L\{u(t-1)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-s}\,L\{g(t+1)\}, $$ where $g(t)={t}^{2}+1.$ Notice that $$ \begin{aligned}g(t+1) & =(t+1)^{2}+1 \\ & ={t}^{2}+2t+2.\end{aligned} $$ Since $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}L\{g(t+1)\} & =L\{{t}^{2}+2t+2\} \\ & =L\{{t}^{2}\}+2L\{t\}+2L\{1\} \\ & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+2\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+2\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\ & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{2}{s}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get $$ \begin{aligned}L\{u(t-1)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-s}\,L\{g(t+1)\} \\ & ={e}^{-s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{2}{s}).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186221934 :question/worked-solution "The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then $$ L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}={e}^{-as}\,L{g(t+a)},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0}, $$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function. In our case, we wish to find $$ L{u(t-5)({t}^{2}+4t+1)}. $$ Therefore, $a=5,$ and we have $$ L{u(t-5)\,g(t)}={e}^{-5s}\,L{g(t+5)}, $$ where $g(t)={t}^{2}+4t+1.$ Notice that $$ \begin{aligned}g(t+5) & =(t+5)^{2}+4(t+5)+1 \\ & ={t}^{2}+10t+25\,+\,4t+20\,+\,1 \\ & ={t}^{2}+14t+46.\end{aligned} $$ Since $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L{1}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}L{g(t+5)} & =L{{t}^{2}+14t+46} \\ & =L{{t}^{2}}+14L{t}+46L{1} \\ & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+14\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+46\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\ & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{46}{s}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get $$ \begin{aligned}L{u(t-5)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-5s}\,L{g(t+5)} \\ & ={e}^{-5s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{46}{s}).\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186221944 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-333532" :question/problem "$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x(t))+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=1-{x}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }0]^{T}?$ $\,$ The equilibrium is an {{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $$ \displaystyle \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y \\ 1-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & 1 \\ -2x & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & 1 \\ -2(1) & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$ To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ -\lambda \cdot (-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned} $$ Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $$ \displaystyle {\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}. $$ Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$"} {:db/id 17592186221979 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem $$ {y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}), $$ the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by $$ Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx, $$ with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(1).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be $$ Δx=\frac{1-0}{2}=\frac{1}{2}. $$ Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $Δy$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\ & =(2{x}_{\text{new}}-3{y}_{\text{new}})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ & ={x}_{\text{new}}-\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned} $$ We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+{x}_{\text{new}}-\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ \frac{5}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+{x}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2(y+{x}_{\text{new}})}{5}.\end{aligned} $$ We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ and $y(1).$ **Step 1**. From the initial conditions, we have $$ x=0,\,y=1. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ {x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2(y+{x}_{\text{new}})}{5} \\ & =\frac{2(1+\frac{1}{2})}{5} \\ & =0.6.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**. From the previous step, we have $$ x=\frac{1}{2},\,y=0.6. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ {x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{2(y+{x}_{\text{new}})}{5} \\ & =\frac{2(0.6+1)}{5} \\ & =0.64.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)≈0.60,\,y(1)≈0.64. $$"} Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx, $$ with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. First, note that we are given $y(-1)$ and asked to find $y(1).$ The distance from $x=-1$ to $x=1$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be $$ Δx=\frac{1-(-1)}{2}=1. $$ Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\ & =\frac{1}{2}((3x+4y)+(3{x}_{\text{new}}+4{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\ & =\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+4y)+2{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned} $$ We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+4y)+2{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+6y)+2{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned} $$ Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+6y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =-\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+6y)\end{aligned} $$ We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y(0)$ and $y(1).$ **Step 1**. From the initial conditions, we have $$ x=-1,\,y=-\frac{1}{2}. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ {x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=-1+1=0. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =-\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+6y) \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 0+6\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)) \\ & =3.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**. From the previous step, we have $$ x=0,\,y=3. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ {x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =-\frac{1}{2}(3x+3{x}_{\text{new}}+6y) \\ & =-\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+6\cdot 3) \\ & =-\frac{21}{2} \\ & =-10.50.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ y(0)≈3.00,\,y(1)≈-10.50. $$"}
