Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′} &=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=2\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =2{\cos }^{2}⁡2x+2{\sin }^{2}⁡2x \\  & =2\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+(B-\frac{1}{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|\end{aligned}
$$

If we redefine the arbitrary constant $B$ as

$$
B:=(B-\frac{1}{2})
$$

our general solution becomes

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\underbrace{-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|}_{g(x)}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|.
$$

Let $Q$ be the amount of pollutant in the basin at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which pollutant enters the basin minus the rate at which pollutant leaves the basin.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which additives enter the basin.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.03\,\text{kg/L}$ of the pollutant enters the basin at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *pollutant* enters the basin is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.9\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which additives exit the basin.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the basin remains $750\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of pollutant in the basin, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{750}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min},$ *pollutant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{30Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{25}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.9-\frac{Q}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}Q=0.9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/25},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{25}\alpha =0.9\,⟹\,\alpha =22.5.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=22.5.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/25}+22.5.
$$

We're told that the basin initially contains $6\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved pollutant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=6,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =6 \\ A{e}^{-0/25}+22.5 & =6 \\ A & =-16.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=22.5-16.5{e}^{-t/25}.
$$

Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

If the associated homogeneous BVP has nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous BVP has either no solution or infinitely many solutions. 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution ${y}_{h}(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

However, in this particular case, we can integrate the equation directly. By doing so, we get the general solution

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax+B.
$$

 

Note that the derivative ${y}^{′}$ is

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}+A.
$$

Applying the condition $y(0)=0$ gives

$$
B=0.
$$

So, we have 

$$
y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax.
$$

 

Applying the condition $y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{3}+A)-(1+A) & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}+A-1-A & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ A-A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the boundary value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+Ax.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3},\,g(x)=x.
$$

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
{y}^{″}=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)-{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has either infinitely many solutions or no solution. Since we have found a solution that contains an arbitrary constant and satisfies both boundary conditions, the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

- $$
\displaystyle {y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}
$$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- ${a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1})$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda ={\lambda }_{1}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $3{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda =0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (3\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{2}{3}.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2/3}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

With $\lambda =\frac{2}{3},$ the recurrence relation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{4}{(\frac{2}{3}+n)(3(\frac{2}{3}+n)-2)}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3n(n+\frac{2}{3})}\,{a}_{n-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{n(3n+2)}\,{a}_{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, with ${a}_{0}\ne 0$ arbitrary, we evaluate the first three coefficients using the given recurrence relation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & \ne 0, \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{4}{1(3\cdot 1+2)}\,{a}_{0}=\frac{4}{5}{a}_{0}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{4}{2(3\cdot 2+2)}\,{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{4}{5}{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{0},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first Frobenius solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & ={x}^{2/3}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} \\  & ={x}^{2/3}({a}_{0}+\frac{4}{5}{a}_{0}x+\frac{1}{5}{a}_{0}{x}^{2}+⋯) \\  & ={a}_{0}({x}^{2/3}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{5/3}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{8/3}+⋯).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y = x\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}-2\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2 - 3\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right).
$$

Suppose we apply the substitution $y'(x) = t.$ Using the techniques shown earlier in the lesson (differentiating with respect to $x$), we can reduce this to the following first-order linear equation:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} - \dfrac12 x = 2t-\dfrac32.
$$

Using the method of integrating factors, we compute $I(t)$ based on the coefficient $P(t) = -\dfrac12{:}$

$$
I(t) = e^{\int -1/2\,\textrm dt} = e^{-t/2}.
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ converts the left-hand side into an exact derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{-t/2} & =(2t-\frac{3}{2}){e}^{-t/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{-t/2}) & =(2t-\frac{3}{2}){e}^{-t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{-t/2} & =\int (2t-\frac{3}{2}){e}^{-t/2}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{-t/2} & =2\int t{e}^{-t/2}\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{-t/2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts for the first integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{-t/2} & =2(-2t-4){e}^{-t/2}-\frac{3}{2}(-2){e}^{-t/2}+C \\ x{e}^{-t/2} & =(-4t-8){e}^{-t/2}+3{e}^{-t/2}+C \\ x{e}^{-t/2} & =(-4t-5){e}^{-t/2}+C \\ x(t) & =-4t-5+C{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to construct the function $y,$ we simply substitute $y' = t$ and $x = x(t)$ into our original equation. Note that the solution $y(t)$ is dependent on the parameter $t.$

Suppose a body of mass $125\,\textrm{kg}$ is released from rest and falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the body's velocity, in meters per second, $t \geq 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction. The air resistance on the body is proportional to the square of its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=49\,\textrm{kg/m}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Assuming the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag, let's find the equation for the velocity $v(t).$

First, note that only two forces act on the body: the force due to gravity, given by the weight $$w = mg = 125g,$$ and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity squared (and negative since it acts in the negative direction): $$D = -kv^2 = -49v^2$$ Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is $$F = w + D = 125g - 49v^2.$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain a separable first-order differential equation:

$$\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 125g-49{v}^{2} & =125\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt} & =g-0.392{v}^{2} \\ & =g-0.04g{v}^{2}\end{aligned}$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get $$\begin{aligned}\frac{dv}{dt} & =g(1-0.04{v}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{1-0.04{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} & =g \\ \int \frac{1}{1-0.04{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt & =g\int dt \\ \int \frac{1}{1-(0.2v)^{2}}\,dv & =g\int dt \\ \frac{1}{0.2}\text{artanh}(0.2v) & =gt+{C}_{1} \\ \text{artanh}(0.2v) & =\frac{1}{5}gt+C \\ 0.2v & =\operatorname{tanh}(\frac{1}{5}gt+C) \\ v(t) & =5\operatorname{tanh}(\frac{1}{5}gt+C),\end{aligned}$$

where $C = 0.2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the body is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0) = 0,$ and solve for $C{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}v(0) & =5\operatorname{tanh}(\frac{1}{5}g\cdot 0+C) \\ 0 & =5\operatorname{tanh}(C) \\ \operatorname{tanh}(C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t){:}$

$$v(t) = 5\tanh\left(\dfrac1{5} g t\right)$$

Assuming the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag, let's find the equation for the velocity $v(t).$

First, note that only two forces act on the body: the force due to gravity, given by the weight $$w = mg = 125g,$$ and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity squared (and negative since it acts in the negative direction): $$D = -kv^2 = -49v^2$$ Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is $$F = w + D = 125g - 49v^2.$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain a separable first-order differential equation:

$$\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 125g-49{v}^{2} & =125\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt} & =g-0.392{v}^{2} \\ & =g-0.04g{v}^{2}\end{aligned}$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get $$\begin{aligned}\frac{dv}{dt} & =g(1-0.04{v}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{1-0.04{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} & =g \\ \int \frac{1}{1-0.04{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt & =g\int dt \\ \int \frac{1}{1-(0.2v)^{2}}\,dv & =g\int dt \\ \frac{1}{0.2}\text{artanh}(0.2v) & =gt+{C}_{1} \\ \text{artanh}(0.2v) & =\frac{1}{5}gt+C \\ 0.2v & =\operatorname{tanh}\left(\frac{1}{5}gt+C\right) \\ v(t) & =5\operatorname{tanh}\left(\frac{1}{5}gt+C\right),\end{aligned}$$

where $C = 0.2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the body is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0) = 0,$ and solve for $C{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}v(0) & =5\operatorname{tanh}\left(\frac{1}{5}g\cdot 0+C\right) \\ 0 & =5\operatorname{tanh}(C) \\ \operatorname{tanh}(C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t){:}$

$$v(t) = 5\tanh\left(\dfrac1{5} g t\right)$$

In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.

In many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,

- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and

- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.

For example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\,\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\,300\,\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.

- A solution containing $20\,\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

To construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative 
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}$
describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}}
$$

We compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.

The rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =100\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.

Since the volume remains constant at $650\,\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{Q}{650}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{L}}.
$$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{Q}{130}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The net rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\text{in} - Q'_\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \dfrac{1}{130}Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \quad Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g}}
$$

A differential operator $D$ is **linear** if the following linearity condition is satisfied.

$$
D(ay_1(x) + by_2(x)) = aD(y_1(x)) + bD(y_2(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's consider some examples:

- First, let's consider the following differential operator:

$$
D_1(y) = x\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} +x^2y
$$

This operator is indeed linear. To see this, we need to check that the linearity condition above holds. So we start by applying our operator to the function $y = a y_1(x) + b y_2(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+{x}^{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Since derivatives distribute over sums, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1})+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(b{y}_{2})+{x}^{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =ax\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}_{1})+bx\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}_{2})+a{x}^{2}{y}_{1}+b{x}^{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =a\underbrace{(x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}{y}_{1})}_{{D}_{1}({y}_{1})}+b\underbrace{(x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}{y}_{2})}_{{D}_{1}({y}_{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, since $D_1(ay_1 + by_2) = aD_1(y_1) + bD_1(y_2),$ the operator $D_1$ is linear.

- Now, let's consider the following differential operator:

$$
D_2(y) = y\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}
$$

This operator is *not* linear. To see this, we need to check that the linearity condition above does not hold. So we start by applying our operator to the function $y = a y_1(x) + b y_2(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}) \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+ab{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to $aD_2(y_1) + bD_2(y_2),$ we see that they are *not* the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2}) & =a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}\ne {D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the operator $D_2$ is *not* linear.

If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form

$$
y = x^\lambda \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n,
$$

where $\lambda$ and $a_n$ for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain:

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary $a_0,$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n \geq 1$ terms.

We are given the three terms of the ODE as power series with the $\color{blue}n=0$ term isolated in each.

$$
\begin{aligned}10{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =10({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }10((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 7x{y}^{′} & =7\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }7(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ (3x-1)y & =-{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(3{a}_{n-1}-{a}_{n}){x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we continue from this point.

**Step 4**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

Collecting the terms for ${\color{blue}n=0},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}10({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+7\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } &= (10{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +7\lambda -1){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } \\ &= (10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\geq 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[10((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}+7(\lambda +n){a}_{n}+(3{a}_{n-1}-{a}_{n})]{x}^{\lambda +n} &= {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[10(\lambda +n)^{2}{a}_{n}-3(\lambda +n){a}_{n}-{a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1}]{x}^{\lambda +n} \\ &= {x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[(10(\lambda +n)^{2}-3(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1}]{x}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[(10(\lambda +n)^{2}-3(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1}]{x}^{n} & =0 \\ (10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1){a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[(10(\lambda +n)^{2}-3(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1}]{x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**:  Set the coefficients of the series equal to $0.$

Setting the coefficients of the $n=0$ term equal to $0$ with arbitrary $a_0\neq0,$ we obtain the indicial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1){a}_{0} & =0 \\ 10{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(5\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-\frac{1}{5},\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we're interested in $\lambda\in(0,1),$ we take $\lambda=\dfrac12.$

Similarly, setting the coefficients of $x^n$ for $n \geq 1$ equal to $0,$ we obtain the following recurrence relation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(10(\lambda +n)^{2}-3(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1} & =0 \\ (2(\lambda +n)-1)(5(\lambda +n)+1){a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $\lambda=\dfrac12$ into the above and solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2(\frac{1}{2}+n)-1)(5(\frac{1}{2}+n)+1){a}_{n} & =-3{a}_{n-1} \\ 2n(5n+\frac{7}{2}){a}_{n} & =-3{a}_{n-1} \\ n(10n+7){a}_{n} & =-3{a}_{n-1} \\ {a}_{n} & =-\frac{3{a}_{n-1}}{n(10n+7)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(n)=n(10n+7).$

The circuit is a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\cos(4t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $30\,\Omega,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.002\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\textrm{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\cos(4t)=30I+500q+5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(30I+500q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -24\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =30\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+6\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+100I=-\dfrac{24}{5}\sin(4t).

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\cos(4t)=30I+500q+5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(30I+500q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}\right) \\ -24\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =30\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ gives

$$

You may have seen already that for the parabola

$$
y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

with

$$
a\neq 0
$$

the **axis of symmetry** of this parabola is given by the following formula:

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We're now in a position to derive this formula.

Since

$$
a \neq 0
$$

we can take out a factor of $a$ from the right-hand side in the parabola formula:

$$
y = a\left(x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + \dfrac{c}{a} \right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract*

$$
\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2{:}
$$

$$
\underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2}_{\textrm{perfect square}} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2+ {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Simplifying the last two terms, we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \dfrac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2} = \left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 + \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}
$$

Next, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a((x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}}) &= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + a \cdot \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}} \\
&= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a} \\
&= a(x - \underbrace{\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right)}_{h})^{2} + \underbrace{\frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a}}_{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

By denoting

$$

$$

$$

where the vertex is given by

$$
(h,k) = \left(-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a} \right)
$$

Finally, since the parabola's axis of symmetry is the vertical line passing through the vertex, the equation of the axis must be

$$

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by
$\textrm{LCM}\big(x-9, x-3 \big) = (x-9)(x-3)$.
- The values $x=3$ and $x=9$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{1}{x - 9}} + 2 & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{5}{x - 3}} \\ \displaystyle ( x - 9 ) ( x - 3 ) \cdot  ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{x - 9}} + 2 ) & \displaystyle  = ( x - 9 ) ( x - 3 ) \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{5}{x - 3}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{( x - 9 ) ( x - 3 )}{x - 9}} + 2 ( x - 9 ) ( x - 3 ) & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{5 ( x - 9 ) ( x - 3 )}{x - 3}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{( x - 9 )} ( x - 3 )}{\cancel{x - 9}}} + 2 ( x - 9 ) ( x - 3 ) & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{5 ( x - 9 ) \cancel{( x - 3 )}}{\cancel{x - 3}}}\end{array}}
$$

After canceling, we're left with the equation

$$
x - 3 + 2(x - 9)(x - 3) = 5(x - 9)
$$

This is a quadratic equation. Solving this equation for $x$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 3 + 2(x - 9)(x - 3) &= 5(x - 9) \\
x - 3 + 2(x - 12x + 27) &= 5x - 45 \\
x - 3 + 2x^{2} - 24x + 54 &= 5x - 45 \\
2x^{2} - 28x + 96 &= 0 \\
x^{2} - 14x + 48 &= 0 \\
(x - 6)(x - 8) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives two *potential* solutions, $x=6$ and $x=8$. We now need to compare these solutions against the prohibited solutions mentioned previously.

- Since $6\neq 3$ and $6\neq 9$, we conclude that $x=6$ is a valid solution $\:{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- Since $8\neq 3$ and $8\neq 9$, we conclude that $x=8$ is a valid solution $\:{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=6$ and $x=8$."] [:db/cas 17592186175790 :question/worked-solution "We make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by
$\textrm{LCM}\big(t+1,\: t-3,\: t-1 \big) = (t+1)(t-1)(t-3)$.
- The values $t = \pm1$, and $t=3$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{3}{t + 1}} + {\displaystyle \frac{5}{t - 3}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{12}{t - 1}} \\ \displaystyle ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 ) \cdot  ( {\displaystyle \frac{3}{t + 1}} + {\displaystyle \frac{5}{t - 3}} ) & \displaystyle  = ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 ) \cdot  ( {\displaystyle \frac{12}{t - 1}} ) \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{3 ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 )}{t + 1}} + {\displaystyle \frac{5 ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 )}{t - 3}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{12 ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 )}{t - 1}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{3 \cancel{( t + 1 )} ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 )}{\cancel{t + 1}}} + {\displaystyle \frac{5 ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) \cancel{( t - 3 )}}{\cancel{t - 3}}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{12 ( t + 1 ) \cancel{( t - 1 )} ( t - 3 )}{\cancel{t - 1}}} \\ \displaystyle 3 ( t - 1 ) ( t - 3 ) + 5 ( t + 1 ) ( t - 1 ) & \displaystyle  = 12 ( t + 1 ) ( t - 3 )\end{array}}
$$

Solving this equation for $t$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3(t - 1)(t - 3) + 5(t + 1)(t - 1) &= 12(t + 1)(t - 3) \\
3(t^{2} - 4t + 3) + 5(t^{2} - 1) &= 12(t^{2} - 2t - 3) \\
3t^{2} - 12t + 9 + 5t^{2} - 5 &= 12t^{2} - 24t - 36 \\
8t^{2} - 12t + 4 &= 12t^{2} - 24t - 36 \\

- 4t^{2} + 12t + 40 &= 0 \\
t^{2} - 3t - 10 &= 0 \\
(t + 2)(t - 5) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

- Since $5 \neq \pm 1$ and $5 \neq 3$, $t = 5$ is a valid solution $\:{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

$$
(-2) + 5 = 3

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2} = (x-2) + \dfrac{(x-2)^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{(x-2)^3}{3^2} + \cdots
$$

How do we determine the radius and interval of convergence for this series?

First, note that the terms of the series are all powers of $(x-2).$ For this reason, we say that the series is **centered** at $x=2.$

To compute the radius of convergence, we use the ratio test for convergence. We define 

$$
a_n = \dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n^2},
$$

and we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{2}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{2}}{(x-2)^{n}}| \\  & =|x-2|\lim_{n\to \infty }\left(\frac{{n}^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}}\right) \\  & =|x-2|\lim_{n\to \infty }\left(\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}+2n+1}\right) \\  & =|x-2|\lim_{n\to \infty }\left(\frac{1}{(1+\frac{2}{n}+\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}\right) \\  & =|x-2|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x-2|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if 

$$
L < {\color{blue}1}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\left| x-{\color{red}2} \right| < {\color{blue}1}.
$$

Therefore, 

- the radius of convergence is ${\color{blue}1},$ and

- the interval of convergence is centered at the point $x={\color{red}2}.$

To find the interval of convergence, we solve the inequality $\left| x-2 \right| < 1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|x-2| & <1 \\ -1<x-2 & <1 \\ 1<x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the series converges for any $x$ in the open interval $(1,3).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series at the endpoints of this interval. So, we need to investigate the endpoints $x=1$ and $x=3$ separately using another test for convergence.

- We start with the left endpoint. When $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(1-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{16}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.

- We then look at the right endpoint. When $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(3-2)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{1}^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{16}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the $p$-series test.

We can use these results to evaluate more complex limits. For example, suppose we wish to evaluate the following limit:

$$

$$

$$

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n = e

In the given limit, we let

$$
\dfrac{2}{x+3}=\dfrac{1}{n}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{x + 3} &= \frac{1}{n} \\
x + 3 &= 2n
\end{aligned}

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives $y'(\theta)$ and $x'(\theta).$ 

Doing this using the usual methods, we get

$$
x'(\theta)=-\sin\theta(2\cos\theta+1), \qquad 
y'(\theta)=2\cos^2\theta +\cos\theta - 1.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta$ where $y'(\theta)=0.$

Writing down the equation $y'(\theta) = 0$ and factoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1 & =0 \\ (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
2\cos\theta-1 = 0, \qquad \cos\theta + 1= 0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve the equation

$$
2\cos\theta-1 = 0,  \qquad 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

The solutions to this equation are 

$$
\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3}.
$$

- Then, we solve the equation

$$
\cos\theta + 1=0, \qquad 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

The solution to this equation is 

$$
\theta = \pi.
$$

Therefore, we have three candidate solutions:

$$
\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \qquad \theta_2 = \pi, \qquad \theta_3 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have $x'(\theta) = 0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solutions into the expression for $x'(\theta).$ If $x'(\theta) = 0,$ further investigation is necessary.  

- Substituting $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+1) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(1+1) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\sqrt{3} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting $\theta_2 = \pi,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+1) \\  & =-0\cdot (-1) \\  & =0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we draw *no conclusion* regarding $\theta_2 = \pi.$

- Substituting $\theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{3}\right)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{3}\right)+1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\sqrt{3} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is a valid solution.

We now make the following conclusions:

- $\nabla \times (k \mathbf F) = k \nabla \times \mathbf F$

- $\nabla \times (\mathbf F + \mathbf G) = \nabla \times \mathbf F + \nabla \times \mathbf G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (3F+G) & =∇\times (3F)+∇\times G \\  & =3∇\times F+∇\times G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $\nabla \times \mathbf{F}.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 3x & {y}^{2}z & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(2)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}z)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(2)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(3x)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}z)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x)]k \\  & =(0-{y}^{2})i-(0-0)j+(0-0)k \\  & =-{y}^{2}\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (3F+G) & =3∇\times F+∇\times G \\  & =3[-{y}^{2}\,i]+[3{y}^{2}\,i+4z\,j+k] \\  & =-3{y}^{2}\,i+3{y}^{2}\,i+4z\,j+k \\  & =(3{y}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+4z\,j+k \\  & =4z\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(-1,1,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F-G))(-1,1,0) & =4(0)\,j+k=k.\end{aligned}

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(1-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

$$

$$
\lim_{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1
$$

We can use this special limit to evaluate other limits, such as

$$
\lim_{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin 2x}{x}
$$

For this limit, notice that as $x\to0$, both the numerator and denominator approach $0$. So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\dfrac00,
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x \to  0}\frac{\sin 2x}{x} &= \lim_{x \to  0}(2 \cdot \frac{\sin 2x}{2x}) \\
&= 2 \cdot lim_(x → 0)\frac{\sin 2x}{2x}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, this limit looks very similar to our special limit for sine. So, if we make the substitution

$$
\theta = 2x
$$

then, since $\theta \to 0$ as $x \to 0$, we have

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} \: \dfrac{\sin {\color{blue}2x}}{\color{blue}2x} = \lim_{\theta \to 0} \: \dfrac{\sin {\color{blue}\theta}}{\color{blue}\theta} = 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x \to  0}\frac{\sin 2x}{x} &= 2 \cdot lim_(x → 0)\frac{\sin 2x}{2x} \\
&= 2 \cdot 1 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

One series that occurs regularly for this purpose is the geometric series

$$
\dfrac{1}{1-r} = 1+r+r^2+r^3+\cdots\,
$$

For example, let's determine the general term $a_n$ for

$$
n\geq 0
$$

of the sequence with generating function

$$
\dfrac{3}{5+2x}
$$

First, we rewrite the generating function by factoring out the term of the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{1-r}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{5 + 2x} &= \frac{3}{5} \cdot (1)/((1 + \frac{2}{5}x)) \\
&= \frac{3}{5} \cdot (1)/([1 - (-\frac{2}{5}x)])
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we expand the right-hand side using the geometric series formula:

$$
\frac{3}{5}[1 + (-\frac{2}{5}x) + (-\frac{2}{5}x)^{2} + (-\frac{2}{5}x)^{3} + ⋯]
$$

This simplifies to

$$
\frac{3}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)x + \frac{3}{5}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^{2}x^{2} + \frac{3}{5}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^{3}x^{3} + ⋯
$$

Finally, we identify that the general term $a_n$ of our sequence is

$$
a_n = \dfrac{3}{5}\left(-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^n

$$

Then, we express the function as a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)} = \dfrac{2}{1-2x} + \dfrac{2}{2+3x}
$$

Next, we expand each of the partial fractions as a geometric series:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{1 - 2x} &= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 2x} \\
&= 2 \cdot (1 + (2x) + (2x)^{2} + (2x)^{3}) \\

\end{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = -\dfrac{\cos\theta  + 2\cos(2\theta)}{\sin\theta + 2\sin(2\theta)}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P.$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )} \\  & =-\frac{0+2(-1)}{1+2(0)} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =(1+2\cdot 0)\cdot 0 \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =(1+2\cdot 0)\cdot 1 \\  & =1\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,1).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =2(x-0) \\ y & =2x+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P.$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}))}{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right))} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ))}{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right))} \\  & =\frac{0-2(-1)}{0-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{0+2}{0+1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right))\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =(1-2\cdot 0)\cdot 0 \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right))\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =(1-2\cdot 0)\cdot (-1) \\  & =1\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}

$$
ax^2+bx+c = 0,
$$

where $a\neq 0.$ We can derive a general solution to this equation by completing the square.

First, let's subtract $c$ from both sides to isolate the variable terms:

$$
ax^2+bx = -c
$$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing by $a$ gives

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x = -\dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side and move the constant terms to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{b}{2a}x=-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)}^{2} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}}-\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the terms on the right-hand side over a common factor of $4a^2,$ we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2  = \dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}.
$$

Taking the square root of both sides yields

$$
x + \dfrac{b}{2a}  = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}}
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{b}{2a} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a}\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.
$$

This formula is called the **quadratic formula**. You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons." "Consider the quadratic equation

You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons."] [:db/cas 17592186185307 :tutorial/content "Recall that our goal is to find new features that are uncorrelated — equivalently, features whose covariance matrix is diagonal. In the previous section, we found an orthogonal matrix $V$ such that $V^T\!CV$ is diagonal. This motivates defining a **transformed observation matrix** $Y = XV.$ The columns of this new matrix $Y$ are our new features.

Substituting $C = \dfrac{1}{n-1} X^T X$ into the expression $V^T\!CV$ and noting that $(XV)^T = V^T X^T{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\underbrace{{V}^{T}\,CV}_{\text{diagonal}} & ={V}^{T}(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)V \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y}_{\text{covariance of Y}}\end{aligned}
$$

The covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal, so the new features $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m$ are uncorrelated. The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues of $C,$ so $\text{Var}(y_i) = \lambda_i.$ By arranging the columns of $V$ in order of decreasing eigenvalue, the new features are also arranged in order of decreasing variance.

The columns of $V$ (the unit eigenvectors of $C$) are called the **principal components**. The $1$st *principal component* is the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue, the $2$nd corresponds to the second-largest, and so on.

This procedure is the core of **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)**. To summarize:

*We define the change-of-variables $Y = XV,$ where the columns of $V$ are the **principal components** of the data, arranged in order of decreasing eigenvalue. This ensures that:*

- *The new features $y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m$ are uncorrelated (diagonal covariance).*

- *The new features are arranged in order of decreasing variance ($\text{Var}(y_i) = \lambda_i$).*

Now let's understand what these vectors mean in terms of the original data." We wish to compute the probability $P(10\leq Y \leq 14).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$

*The **volume** of a sphere **increases** at a rate **inversely proportional** to its **radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a sphere* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- We're told that $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t}$ *increases* at a rate *inversely proportional to its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{k}{r},
$$

where $k > 0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$

The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by

$$
V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{r} \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\left(\frac{k}{r}\right)}{4\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{4\pi {r}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K = \dfrac{k}{4\pi} > 0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{K}{r^3}.
$$" "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

> *Suppose that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma$. The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n$, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as*
> $\overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$.

Moreover, if we define

$$

$$

then, by the properties of mean and variance, we have

$$

$$

and consequently,

$$
X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
$$

The expected value and the variance of a uniform random variable $X_i \sim U[a,b]$ can be found as

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$

&= \frac{a + b}{2} \\
&= \frac{1 + 5}{2} \\
&= \frac{6}{2} \\
&= 3, \\
σ^{2} &= \operatorname{Var} [X_{i}] \\
&= ((b - a)^{2})/(12) \\
&= ((5 - 1)^{2})/(12) \\
&= \frac{16}{12} \\
&= \frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of $X$, we obtain

$$
X \mid ∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N(110 \cdot 3, 110 \cdot \frac{4}{3}); ∼N(330, \frac{440}{3})

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{\frac{1}{2}+y} \\  & =\frac{2(x+y)}{1+2y},\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}.\end{aligned}

$$

\end{aligned}

$$

Suppose we have two normal populations $X$ and $Y{:}$

$X \sim N(\mu_x, \sigma^2_x), \qquad Y \sim N(\mu_y, \sigma^2_y)$
where $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means, and $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are the population variances.

In a previous lesson, we saw that the difference between the sample means is given by

$$
\overline{X} - \overline{Y} \sim N\left(\mu_x - \mu_y,\dfrac{\sigma_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{\sigma_y^2}{n_y} \right)
$$

where $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means, and $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes. By $z$-scoring this result, we can express this as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{\sigma_y^2}{n_y}}} \sim N(0,1)
$$

In most practical situations, the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are unknown and must be replaced with estimates $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$. In this situation, the random variable

$$
\begin{aligned}
T &= ((X^(―) - Y^(―)) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/(\sqrt{\frac{S_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{S_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}})
\end{aligned}
$$

follows a $t$-distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

We can approximate the number of degrees of freedom $k$ in various ways.

- *Method 1:* We can approximate the degrees of freedom using the so-called **Welch-Satterthwaite approximation:**
$$
\displaystyle k \approx \frac{\left(\dfrac{s_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{s_y^2}{n_y} \right)^2}{\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{s_x^2}{n_x} \right)^2}{n_x - 1} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{s_y^2}{n_y} \right)^2}{n_y - 1}}
$$
where the final result is rounded *down* to the nearest integer.
- *Method 2:* We can also approximate the degrees of freedom using the formula
$k = \min(n_x - 1, n_y - 1)$
where $\min(a,b)$ denotes the **minimum** of $a$ and $b$.

In this lesson, we'll use the second method. You'll get practice applying the first method in separate lessons.

Please bear in mind that this method is simpler but also more conservative:

- Under Method 2, our estimate for the degrees of freedom will be *smaller* than Method 1.
- Thus, the tails of the resulting distribution will be fatter, leading to *larger* critical values for a given significance level $\alpha$. Note that "larger critical values" here means larger in the absolute sense, i.e.,
$$
|t_{k_1}| >  |t_{k_2}|
$$
whenever $k_1 < k_2$ for critical values $t_{k_1}$ and $t_{k_2}$.
- Therefore, the probability of a Type I error (i.e., rejecting $H_0$ when it is true) *decreases.*

Remember that as $k\to\infty$, the $t$-distribution approaches $N(0,1)$. The standard normal curve has *extremely thin* tails!

![](images/5c/5c73c5fd8613e99814ab47a1a41a46a4511991d3c7eeca33eefe5913a907c10c.png)"] [:db/cas 17592186193806 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be an $n \times m$ observation matrix with standardized data, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Suppose we have the following **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $X{:}$ 

$$
X = U \Sigma V^T
$$

Note that in the SVD, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal, which implies that $U^T U = I$ (the identity matrix). 

Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of $X$ can be derived as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T})(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}\underbrace{({U}^{T}U)}_{I}Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ 

Now, notice the following:

- The matrix $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ is a diagonal $m \times m$ matrix with the eigenvalues of $C$ (in descending order) on the main diagonal.

- The matrix $V$ is an $m \times m$ matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of $C.$

To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix $X,$ the columns of the matrix $V$ in the SVD are the **principal components** of the data." $$

$$

Recall the following:

- We defined $p$ as "the probability that the coin lands on heads when tossed randomly."
- Since we want to check whether the coin is unfair, we have the following null and alternative hypotheses:
$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{0}:p & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {H}_{1}:p & \ne \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
- The significance level is $\alpha = 5\%$.

Under the conditions specified in the null hypothesis, the random variable $X$ is a binomial random variable given by

$$
X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right)
$$

The probability mass function of $X$ under the null hypothesis is shown below.

![](images/79/79306d39f30f044beb30aaa7f6356b7a226c0f3958597d2e230601d51474b801.png)

Note the following:

- When we select a significance level $\alpha$ in a two-tailed test, the convention is to allow $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ at either tail.
- So if $\alpha = 5\%$, we have $\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = 2.5\%$ at either tail.

Now, suppose we conduct our experiment and get $2$ heads out of $10$ tosses.

If the result $X=2$ is statistically significant, it will lie in the critical region in the *left* tail of the probability distribution of $f(x)$.

We can compute the probability of getting

$$
X\leq 2
$$

We are told that the populations are normally distributed, but we do not know the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$.

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{S_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{S_y^2}{n_y}}}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, where

- $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means,
- $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes, and
- $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$ are the sample variances.

- $H_0: \mu_x = \mu_y$ is the null hypothesis

$$

"Consider two samples of size $n_x = 14$ and $n_y = 18$ from independent normal populations $X$ and $Y$ with unequal population variances, where the unbiased estimates of $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ from these samples are

$$
\overline{x}=47
$$

and

$$
\overline{y}=40
$$

and unbiased estimates of the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are $s_x^2=7^2$ and $s_y^2=8^2$.

We wish to carry out a hypothesis test at the $10\%$ significance level to determine whether there is sufficient evidence that the population mean $\mu_x$ of $X$ is larger than the population mean $\mu_y$ of $Y$.

To solve a problem like this, we proceed as follows.

We are told that the populations are normally distributed, but we do not know the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$.

In cases like this, the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{S_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{S_y^2}{n_y}}}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, where

- $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means,
- $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means,
- $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes, and
- $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$ are the sample variances.

In our example, the null and alternative hypotheses are the following:

- $H_0: \mu_x = \mu_y$ is the null hypothesis
- $H_1: \mu_x > \mu_y$ is the alternative (one-tailed) hypothesis

We can estimate the number of degrees of freedom $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \min (n_{x} - 1, n_{y} - 1) \\
&= \min (14 - 1, 18 - 1) \\
&= \min (13, 17) \\
&= 13
\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e.

$$
\mu_x - \mu_y = 0
$$

we compute the test statistic:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= (x^(―) - y^(―) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/\left(\sqrt{\frac{s_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{s_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}}\right) \\
&= (47 - 40 - (0))/\left(\sqrt{\frac{7^{2}}{14} + \frac{8^{2}}{18}}\right) \\
&\approx 2.635
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: -3u+2v \right\rangle
$$

over the domain 

$$
D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 2, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z+2y,\,3y+z,\,x-z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=-3u+2v} \\  & =⟨(-3u+2v)+2v,\,3v+(-3u+2v),\,u-(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(-3u+4v)\cdot (3)+(-3u+5v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+12v+6u-10v+4u-2v \\  & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+2y,\,3y+z,\,x-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}u\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is ${\color{blue}u}.$" "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

So, the missing expression is ${\color{blue}u}.$"] [:db/cas 17592186198032 :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $\mathbf F =  \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1+xyz\rangle$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/97/977d93ad65c9f3690def4242f98f4de5e5c89faf02fe47d06f5ed251d8a4a292.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $\mathbf F$ through these two sides.

- Let $S_1$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z = 1$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_1$ is

$$
\mathbf n_1 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z = 1$ on $S_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =1+xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}1+xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}1+xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}1+xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+\frac{1}{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let $S_2$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_2$ is

$$
\mathbf n_2 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z = 0$ on $S_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =-\text{Area}(D) \\  & =-(1-0)(1-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+(-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v \\ w\end{array} \right]} 
\longrightarrow 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v , w ) \\ y ( u , v , w ) \\ z ( u , v , w )\end{array} \right]}
$$

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \ \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v,w), y(u,v,w), z(u,v,w)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right|  \: \textrm{d}u \textrm{d}v \textrm{d}w
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u = x+y^2, \qquad
v=  y+z, \qquad
w = 2z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y \\ z\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y , z ) \\ v ( x , y , z ) \\ w ( x , y , z )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 4,\,0\le w\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2y & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$

$$

$$

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $$
\displaystyle \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}
$$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

First, notice that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,
$$

where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/2a/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png)

Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\left(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5}\right)-\left(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}\right) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}.
$$" "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

$$

$$

$$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and

- $$
\displaystyle M_y = \iint\limits_D x \, \lambda (x,y) \: \textrm{d}A
$$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.

$$

and $\lambda(x,y) = x+y.$ 

Since we require the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass, we need to compute the moment about the $x$-axis: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\cdot (x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}xy+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{6}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{5}{6}(\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{5}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
f(x,y,z) = \cos{x}+\cos{y}+\cos{z},
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\pi.
$$

Since the angles are acute, we also have the constraints $0 \lt x,y,z \lt \dfrac\pi 2.$ 

Let $g(x,y,z) = x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y,z), \qquad g(x,y,z) = \pi
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,-\operatorname{sin}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡y &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sine function is one-to-one on the interval $\left( 0, \dfrac \pi 2\right),$ we can conclude that $x = y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y =x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi  \\ x+x+x & =\pi  \\ 3x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $$
\displaystyle \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),
$$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186198594 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x-1,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(2(1)-1,1+0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2(2)-1,2+(-1)) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,2) & =(2(2)-1,2+2) \\  & =(3,4) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2(1)-1,1+3) \\  & =(1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/1d/1d5943d2cf79e7c77f6db3e939242d7e31068f46506fa618abd24b6ac813d32a.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{v}^{2}\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 21\cdot 4\,\text{d}v \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
