$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/c7/c7b22b03b9952bfe068e9252f7336568aa8d761c32a1bc31c444ebb97ee925ba.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,0\cdot ({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\pi +0 \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186198612 :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-y)=1-1=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/e2/e22757cf7c4e2be17cb71e63c550aa39a10ee1dc5895c63acd5a45f0baa94623.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(1-2t)\,i+(-1+2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=1-2t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1-y=1-(2t-1)=2-2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-2t)\cdot (2)-(2-2t)\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-2t)+(2-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}3-4t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot {[3t-2{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\cdot (3-2) \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

$$

$$

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is 

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le \frac{1}{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =0 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 2,\,0\le x-y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u={x}^{2}+y,\,v=x+z,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le 2,\,-1\le w\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2x & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$

$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x\le 5,\,0\le x+2y\le 1,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x+2y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 5,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x+2y){e}^{(x+2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}[{\int }_{0}^{1}v{e}^{{v}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{5}{[\frac{{e}^{{v}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}(e-1)\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(e-1)[u]_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(e-1)(5-1) \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}

$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=2\lambda x \\ 1 &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y &=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right),\,\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$ | $$
\displaystyle \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)
$$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $$
\displaystyle \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right),
$$ and its minimum value is $10-\sqrt{2}.$"] [:db/cas 17592186199457 :tutorial/content "Recall that the moments of inertia $I_x$ and $I_y$ of a thin plate $D$ about the $x$- and $y$- axes are given by

For example, suppose we have the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{F} = \langle x, \,0, \, -y^2 \rangle
$$

and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the conical solid shown below. 

![](images/0b/0be83ceada68d0b56be4872f21652a7d18932ff059ea704576ca3cce892fa87b.png)

 

Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$ 

First, since $S$ is a closed surface, we have that

- the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = 2 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ is oriented *upward*, and

- the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = 0$ is oriented *downward*.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- First, we consider the upper cone $S_1.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then

$$
P = x, \qquad
Q = 0, \qquad
R = -y^2.
$$

 
As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\cdot \left(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\right)-0\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\right)+(-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane.

- Next, we consider the lower plane $S_2.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,-1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨x,0,-{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across the entire surface is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" "Remember that when we measure the flux of a vector field through a *closed* surface, we always calculate with respect to an outward-pointing unit normal vector.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'} & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'} & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{vmatrix}=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" "Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*"] [:db/cas 17592186199471 :tutorial/content "Repeated integrals can feature three or more variables. In this lesson, we'll learn how to evaluate repeated integrals containing three variables.

For example, let's consider the repeated integral below:

$$
\int_{1}^2 \int_0^2 \int_0^1 x(y+z)^2 \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
$$

To evaluate this integral, we first integrate with respect to the inner variable $(z),$ then with respect to the middle variable $(y),$ and finally with respect to the outer variable $(x).$ 

We can write the first step more explicitly as

$$
%\int_{1}^2 \int_0^2 \int_0^1 x(y+z)^2 \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x=
\int_{1}^2 \int_0^2 \left[ \int_0^1 x(y+z)^2 \:\textrm{d}z\right] \textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
%= \int_{1}^2 \left[ \int_0^2 \left[ \int_0^1 x(y+z)^2 \:\textrm{d}z \right] \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x.
$$

We now carry out the integration.
First, we integrate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $z,$ *treating $x$ and $y$ as constants:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}x(y+z)^{2}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{[\frac{(y+z)^{3}}{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(\frac{(y+1)^{3}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3})\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}x((y+1)^{3}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x((y+1)^{3}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

The next step is to integrate with respect to $y,$ which we can write more explicitly as

$$
\dfrac13 \int_{1}^2 \left[ \int_0^2x \left( (y+1)^3 - y^3 \right) \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ *treating $x$ as a constant,* we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}x((y+1)^{3}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y]\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}x{[(\frac{(y+1)^{4}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{4})]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}x[(\frac{81}{4}-\frac{16}{4})-(\frac{1}{4}-0)]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \left(\frac{64}{4}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}16x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}16x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{[8{x}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(32-8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 24 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

By restricting $\mathbf x$ to a line through $\mathbf{a},$ we can consider $f$ as a function of one variable. Then, we'll use the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function to derive the formula.

Let $\mathbf{x}_0$ be a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then, the line through $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}_0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),

where $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}(1) = \mathbf{x}_0.$

Now, we define a function $F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by restricting the domain of $f$ to this line:

$$
F(t)
= f(\mathbf{x}(t))
%= f(\mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}))
$$

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of this single-variable function about $t=0$ is given by

$$
F(t) \approx F(0) + F'(0)t + \dfrac12F''(0)t^2.
$$

We can find the first derivative of $F$ using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a+t({x}_{0}-a)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{x}}$ is a row vector and $(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a})$ is a column vector, this is a scalar quantity and, hence, equal to its transpose:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a) \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a))}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\end{aligned}
$$

With this, we can find the second derivative of $F{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}F}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}) \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}f}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Evaluating the function and its derivatives at $t=0$ and using the fact that $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a},$ we have

$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}F ( 0 ) = f ( \mathbf{x} ( 0 ) ) \\ {F}^{\prime } ( 0 ) = {𝒇}^{\prime } ( \mathbf{x} ( 0 ) ) ( {\mathbf{x}}_{0} - \mathbf{a} ) \\ {F}^{\prime\prime } ( 0 ) = ( {\mathbf{x}}_{0} - \mathbf{a} {)}^{T} {𝒇}^{\prime\prime } ( \mathbf{x} ( 0 ) ) ( {\mathbf{x}}_{0} - \mathbf{a} )\end{array} \right. }

Putting these values into the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function about $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & ≈F(0)+{F}^{′}(0)t+\frac{1}{2}{F}^{″}(0){t}^{2} \\  & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)t+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a){t}^{2}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot 1+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot {1}^{2} \\ f({x}_{0}) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186199558 :tutorial/content "Recall that any rational number can be written as

$$
\dfrac{m}{n}
$$

where $m,n \in \mathbb{Z}$. This means that any rational number can be defined using a pair of integers:

$$
(m, n) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}
$$

This, in turn, means that $\mathbb{Q}$ can be injectively embedded into the Cartesian product $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$, and we already know that $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ is countably infinite.

Therefore, we have the following theorem:

> *The set of rational numbers is countably infinite, i.e.,*
> $\mid \mathbb{Q} \mid = \aleph_0$.

Let's describe how we can "count" all the elements of the set $\mathbb{Q}^+$, the set of all positive rationals. We'll then use this to construct a bijection from $\mathbb N$ to $\mathbb Q$.

First, we write down the elements of $\mathbb Q^+$ in an infinite array that extends forever to the right and bottom, as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0ec1463b9b71ed6050c1d58b0911b3ca42b425dbdd36d83bc51f0679fef4fac.png)

We skip any equivalent fraction representations if the corresponding number appears somewhere in the previous rows. For example, notice that

$$
\dfrac{2}{2}=\dfrac11 = 1
$$

so we can skip this in the second row of the table.

Now, we can traverse the array in the manner shown below.

![](images/d9/d9b12de7f732fdec24d234a26be3888c37a220e2c12052215fa9609640040999.png)

By assigning each natural number $n$ to the $n$-th distinct fraction encountered in this path, we define a bijection $f: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q^+$ between $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Q}^+$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= \frac{1}{1} = 1 \\
f(2) &= \frac{2}{1} = 2 \\
f(3) &= \frac{1}{2} \\
f(4) &= \frac{1}{3} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can use this to construct a bijection $g: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(1) &= 0 \\
g(2) &= f(1) = 1 \\
g(3) &= -f(1) =-1 \\
g(4) &= f(2) = 2 \\
g(5) &= -f(2) =-2 \\
g(6) &= f(3) = \frac{1}{2} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

Or, more compactly:

$$
g(n) = 
{\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}0 , \hspace{1em} & n = 1 \\ f ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} n ) , \hspace{1em} & n \text{ even} \\ - f ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} ( n - 1 ) ) , \hspace{1em} & n > 1 \text{ and odd}\end{array} \right. }

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186199596 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we saw how to define the limit of a null sequence (i.e., a sequence whose limit equals zero) and how to construct a formal proof that a given sequence is null.

In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include sequences that converge a finite (not necessarily zero) limit. If such a limit exists, it's usually denoted as $L$.

Consider the following sequence:

$$
a_n = \dfrac{n+1}{n}, \qquad n \geq 1
$$

It's easy to see that the limit of this sequence is

$$
{\color{red}{L}}={\color{red}{1}}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n \to  \infty}a_{n} &= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{n + 1}{n}\right) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{n}{n} + \frac{1}{n}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(1 + \frac{1}{n}) \\
&= 1 + 0 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

This means that for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a natural number $N(\varepsilon)$ such that the distance between $a_n$ and

$$
{\color{red}{L}} = {\color{red}{1}}
$$

is *smaller than* $\varepsilon$ for all

$$
n\geq N
$$

In other words,

$$
\forall n\geq N,\qquad \mid a_n - {\color{red}{1}} \mid < \varepsilon
$$

Let's draw a few sketches to illustrate this idea.

- If we select $\varepsilon = 0.5$, then $\mid a_n-{\color{red}{1}} \mid < \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq 3$.

Since $n_1=62$, $n_2=70$,

$$
\widehat{\,p}_1=\dfrac{48}{62}=\dfrac{24}{31}
$$

and

$$
\widehat{\,p}_2=\dfrac{35}{70} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

we have that

- $n_1 \widehat{\,p}_1 = 48> 5$,
- $n_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1) = 62 - 48 = 14> 5$,
- $n_2 \widehat{\,p}_2 = 35> 5$,
- $n_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2) = 70- 35 = 35> 5$.

As a result, we may use a normal approximation:

$$
\dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{\mid}} \sim N(0,1)
$$

where

- $\!\widehat{\,p}_1, \widehat{\,p}_2$ are the sample proportions,
- $p_1, p_2$ are the population proportions,
- $n_1, n_2$ are the sample sizes.

Then, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population difference of proportions $p_1-p_2$ can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,p}_1-\widehat{\,p}_2 \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}
$$

where

$$
P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}
$$

and $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

We are interested in finding a $98\%$ confidence interval. So, we have

$$
\alpha=1-0.98=0.02 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.01
$$

We are given that that

$$
P(Z > 2.326) = 0.01
$$

As a result,

$$
z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.01} = 2.326
$$

Therefore, a $98\%$ confidence interval for the difference of the population proportions $p_1-p_2$ is the following:

$$
(\frac{24}{31} - \frac{1}{2}) ± 2.326 \cdot \sqrt{(\frac{48}{62}(1 - \frac{48}{62}))/(62) + (\frac{35}{70}(1 - \frac{35}{70}))/(70)}
$$

which simplifies as
$0.274 ± 0.186$.

Let's now examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The end-points of our confidence interval are $0.274 \pm 0.186$.
- Statement II is false. All values within the confidence interval are positive:
$(0.274 - 0.186, \, 0.274 + 0.186) = (0.088, \, 0.460)$
- Statement III is true. Since all values within the confidence interval are positive, this suggests that the proportion of eighth-grade students who vote in student elections is greater than that of ninth-graders. In other words, $p_1 > p_2$.

In other words, we want to test the following null and alternative hypotheses:

- $H_0{:}\: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_K$
- $H_1{:}$ There is at least one population mean that differs from the others,

where $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_K$ are the population means of each group.

We've already introduced the $F$-ratio test statistic for this problem:

$$
W = \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}}
$$

Now, we will discuss the distribution of $W$.

Let's assume that the data points are independent and follow a normal distribution with equal mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2{:}$

$$
X_{jk} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad j=1, 2, \ldots, n_k, \quad k=1, 2, \ldots, K
$$

where $n_k$ is the size of the $k$th group.

Also, recall that

$$
\textrm{SST} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X})^2, \qquad \text{SSW} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2, \qquad \text{SSB} = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k (\overline{X}_k - \overline{X})^2
$$

Given a sample of $n$ independent normal random variables with variance $\sigma^2$, for the sample variance $S^2$, we have

$$
\dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim\chi^2(n-1)
$$

We can use this result to find the distribution of $\text{SST}/\sigma^2$. Since

$$
\textrm{SST} = (n-1)S^2
$$

it follows that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{SST}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2(n-1)
$$

We can also apply this result to *each* group mean:

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n_k-1), \quad k = 1, \ldots, K
$$

This approach breaks down the computation into simpler intermediate steps and allows us to clearly see the dependencies.

Consider a *scalar* function $L(\mathbf A),$ defined as

$$
L(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)^T \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2.$

Suppose we want to compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$, which is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$. The entry in the $i$th row and $j$th column of the gradient matrix is given by 

$$
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}.
$$

To simplify the differentiation, we define $\mathbf y \in\mathbb R^{2\times 1}$ as 
$$
\mathbf{y} 
= 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{array} \right]}
=\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}.
$$

Then, we can write $L$ in terms of $\mathbf y$ as 

$$
L = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

To compute $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}$, we apply the multivariable chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^2 \frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} \cdot \frac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}}
$$

Note that the summation is from $k=1$ to $k=2$ because $\mathbf y$ has two components, and we're differentiating with respect to each of them.

Now, let's analyze the two factors of the product that appear in this summation.

- We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{y}L & ={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2y \\  & =y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} = y_k.
$$

- Writing $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$ in component form

$$
y_i = \sum_{j=1}^3 a_{ij} x_j - b_i,
$$

we have
$$
\frac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}} =
{\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{x}_{j} , & i = k , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. }
$$
Only the $k$th row of $\mathbf{A}$ affects $y_k$.

Putting our two results together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j},\end{aligned}
$$

because all terms vanish except the one where $k=i$.

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

In the next example, we will use this formula to compute the gradient for specific vectors." $$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\text{E}[X∣Y]]
$$

$$
\text{E}[X∣Y=n]=\frac{n+1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\frac{1+Y}{2}].
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \text{E}[1+Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+\text{E}[Y])\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,…,301\},$ we use the formula for the mean of the first $n$ integers:

$$
\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1+301}{2}=151.
$$

$$

To do this, we need to apply the chain rule. The chain rule for total derivatives tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{1 \times n}
= 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{1 \times q}
\cdot 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Now, recall that the gradient of a scalar function is the transpose of the total derivative:

$$
\underbrace{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f}_{n \times 1} = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
$$

To derive the chain rule in terms of gradients, we apply the identity $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & =\underbrace{{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}}_{n\times q}\cdot \underbrace{{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T}}_{q\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient chain rule is

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
\cdot 
\nabla_{\mathbf{y}} f.
$$

In a separate lesson, we saw how to convert between different units of area, such as converting from "square meters" to "square centimeters" and vice versa.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to create and apply conversion formulas for mixed units that contain units of area.

For example, suppose a drone maps an area at a rate of

$$
0.9\,\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}}
$$

What is this rate in square meters per second?

We're given the rate in

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}}
$$

and want to convert it into

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}}
$$

This means we'll need two conversion factors: one for the area units (from $\textrm{km}^2$ to $\textrm{m}^2$) and one for the time units (from $\textrm{h}$ to $\textrm{s}$):

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}}
$$

One of the conversion factors should change $\textrm{km}^2$ to $\textrm{m}^2$.

$$
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}}{\textrm{h}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}}
$$

The other conversion factor should change $\textrm{h}$ to $\textrm{s}$.

$$
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}}{\cancel{\textrm{h}}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\cancel{\textrm{km}^2}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{h}}}{\textrm{s}} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}}
$$

So, the complete conversion formula is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{km}^2} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{h}}{\textrm{s}} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}}
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

- We are given that the drone maps at a rate of $0.9\,\dfrac{\textrm{km}^2}{\textrm{h}}$.
- There are $1,000$ meters in one kilometer. We can write this as follows:
$1,000\,\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{km}}$
To determine the number of square meters in one square kilometer, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows:
$$
\begin{aligned}{(1,000\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{m}}{\text{km}})}^{2} & =1,{000}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{km}}^{2}} \\  & =1,000,000\hspace{0.167em}\frac{{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{km}}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
- There are $60\cdot60=3,600$ seconds per hour, or $\dfrac{1}{3,600}$ hours per second. We can write this as follows:
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{1}{3,600}\,\dfrac{\textrm{h}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the drone maps the area at a rate of

$$
250\,\dfrac{\textrm{m}^2}{\textrm{s}}

$$

\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\int h(y)\,\text{d}y)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(y)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{y}.$

Let's denote

$$
P(x,y)={y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)=xy.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3})=3{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}-y) \\  & =3{y}^{-1}-{y}^{-2},\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(y) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -(3{y}^{-1}-{y}^{-2})\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-(3\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1/y)) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{y}^{-3})\cdot \operatorname{exp}⁡(-1/y) \\  & ={y}^{-3}\,{e}^{-1/y}.\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(y)\cdot ({y}^{3}\,\text{d}x+xy\,\text{d}y)=I(y)\cdot 0
$$

which simplifies as

$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$

$$

Since $\frac{3}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{-1}\text{ }\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}[(\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{(6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$

$$

$$
F(y)=y,\,G(x)=0.

If the line $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of $JK^(―)$, what is the equation of $l$?"] [:db/cas 17592186218348 :tutorial/content "Now that we have practiced identifying Clairaut equations, let’s see how to solve them.

The key feature of Clairaut’s equation is its special form, which leads to a family of **straight-line** solutions and one **singular solution**.

Recall that a Clairaut equation has the form

$$
y = x\,y' + g(y'),
$$

where $g$ is a differentiable function.

To simplify the notation, we introduce the substitution:

$$
p = y'
$$

With this substitution, the equation becomes

$$
y = xp + g(p).
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides of the substituted equation with respect to $x$. Remember, $p$ is a function of $x$, so we must use the product rule on the $xp$ term and the chain rule on $g(p)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xp)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(g(p)) \\ p & =(1\cdot p+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}x})+{g}^{'}(p)\cdot \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Using $p' = \dfrac{\textrm{d}p}{\textrm{d}x}$, the expression simplifies to

$$
p = p + x p' + g'(p)\,p'.
$$

Now, if we simply subtract $p$ from both sides and factor out the common term $p'$, we arrive at the pivotal equation for finding our solutions:

$$
0 = p'(x + g'(p))
$$

Since this expression is a product that equals zero, the equation can be satisfied in two different ways. Each way provides us with one type of solution.

- **Case I: The General Solution.**
The first possibility is that the derivative of $p$ is zero. If $p' = 0$, then $p$ must be a constant. Let's denote this constant as $c$:

$$
p = c
$$

Substituting $p = c$ back into the original Clairaut equation ($y = xp + g(p)$), we directly obtain the **general solution**

$$
y = cx + g(c).
$$

This gives a family of straight-line solutions. Each value of $c$ produces a different line, where $c$ is the slope and $g(c)$ gives the $y$-intercept.

- **Case II: The Singular Solution.**
If instead $x + g'(p) = 0$, then we obtain a singular solution. 
Let's first solve for $x$ in terms of $p$:

$$
x = -g'(p).
$$

Then, let's substitute this $x$ back into the original Clairaut equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(-{g}^{'}(p))p+g(p) \\  & =g(p)-p{g}^{'}(p)\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the **singular solution** defined parametrically by the equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-{g}^{'}(p), \\ y & =g(p)-p{g}^{'}(p)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

$$
y(0)≈\frac{8}{3}.
$$

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3+x-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =3+0-2\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{3} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $\frac{5}{3}$ |
| $0$ | $\frac{8}{3}$ | $3$ |  |  |  |  |

$$

$$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |

| $0$ | $\frac{8}{3}$ | $3$ | $\frac{9}{2}$ |  |  |  |

$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

\displaystyle {\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
g(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau/2}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad s > \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

We apply the **Integration in Time Property**: if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\!\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=e^{t/2}$. Thus, for $s>\dfrac{1}{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L\{f(t)\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{t/2}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-\frac{1}{2})}.\end{aligned}

The method consists of two parts: the **Adams-Bashforth** (**AB2**) **predictor**, and **Adams-Moulton** (**AM2**) **corrector**.
We'll begin by deriving the AB2 predictor.

Consider an initial value problem:

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a)=c
$$

Writing the differential equation in integral form, we have

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Let $\Delta x = x_\text{new} - x$ be the step size, and define the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t - x}{\Delta x}.
$$

Then, $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so the integral becomes

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x.
$$

Now, define a new function $g$ of $\theta$ as the integrand:

$$
g(\theta) = f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))
$$

The Adams formulas result from approximating $g(\theta)$ by a simple function that agrees with its known values, and then integrating that approximation from $0$ to $1.$ We now determine some known values.

- Evaluating $g$ at $\theta = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(0) & =f(x+0\cdot Δx,y(x+0\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x,y) \\  & ={y}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, evaluating $g$ at $\theta=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =f(x+(-1)\cdot Δx,y(x+(-1)\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x-Δx,y(x-Δx)) \\  & =f({x}_{-1},y({x}_{-1})) \\  & ={y}_{-1}^{'},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_{-1}$ is the previous $x$-value and $y'_{-1}$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).$

Since we have two known values, the simplest reasonable approximation to $g(\theta)$ is a *straight line* passing through these two points: $(0,y')$ and $(-1,y'_{-1}).$
This straight line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\theta ) & ={y}^{'}+\frac{{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}}{0-(-1)}(\theta -0) \\  & ={y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating this approximation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta )\,d\theta  \\  & ={({y}^{'}\theta +\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}){\theta }^{2})|}_{\theta \,=\,0}^{\theta \,=\,1} \\  & ={y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy={\int }_{0}^{1}g(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx\approx {\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx=\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

It is this approximation that we define as the AB2 predictor:

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

The Adams formulae result from approximating $g(\theta)$ by a polynomial interpolant constructed from known function values and integrating that polynomial from $0$ to $1.$

Notice that evaluating $g$ at $\theta = 0,$ we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
g(0) &= f(x + 0\cdot\Delta x, y(x + 0\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x, y) \\[5pt]
&= y'.
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, evaluating $g$ at $\theta=-1$, we get
$$
\begin{aligned}

&= f(x - \Delta x, y(x - \Delta x)) \\[5pt]

\end{aligned}
$$

So, to derive the AB2 predictor, we can approximate $g(\theta)$ by a *linear* interpolant using its values at $\theta=0$ and $\theta=-1.$

The Lagrange basis polynomials are
\[
\ell_0(\theta) = \theta + 1,\qquad
\ell_{-1}(\theta) = -\theta,
\]

so the interpolant is
$$
\begin{aligned}

&= y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating the interpolant, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}

&= \int_0^1 \big(y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta\big) \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]

\end{aligned}

we had $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,
$$

and we defined

$$
g(\theta) = f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x)).
$$

For the predictor, we considered two known values of $g(\theta){:}$ 

- For $\theta = 0,$ we have $g(0) = y'.$

- For $\theta = -1,$ we have $g(-1) = y'_{-1}.$

Then, we approximated $g$ with a linear function passing through these two points.

Now, for the corrector, we use *three* known values, and approximate $g(\theta)$ by a *quadratic* passing through these three points.

To obtain a third value, we also want the slope at the *new* $x$-value $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$ But, the true value $y_\text{new}$ is not yet known.

Instead, we evaluate the slope at the new point estimated by the AB2 predictor! This corresponds to $\theta = 1{:}$

$$
g(1) = f(x + \Delta x, y(x + \Delta x)) \approx f(x_\text{new}, y_p) = y'_p,
$$

where $y_p$ is the new $y$-value predicted by AB2, and $y'_p$ is the slope evaluated at $(x_\text{new}, y_p).$
So, our three points are

$$
(-1,y'_{-1}), \quad (0,y'), \quad (1,y'_p).
$$

Let $q(\theta)$ be the quadratic that passes through these three points. After simplifying, this quadratic can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta +1){y}_{p}^{'}-(\theta -1)(\theta +1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta -1){y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 g(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
\approx \int_0^1 q(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
= \dfrac1{12}(5y'_p + 8y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\cos \,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\sin \,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}
$$

exists for every real $s > a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. Moreover, for each integer $n\geq 0$ and every such $s,$ we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{ t^n f(t) \} = (-1)^n F^{(n)}(s).
$$

In particular, for $n=1,$ we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{ tf(t) \} = -F'(s).
$$

$$

So, we rewrite the expression as

$$
\dfrac{n^{2}}{(n + 2)(n + 3)} - \dfrac{2n}{n + 2} = -\,\dfrac{9}{n + 3}
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by
$\textrm{LCM}\big(n+2,\: n+3,\: (n+2)(n+3) \big) = (n+2)(n+3)$.
- The values $n=-2$ and $n=-3$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle ( {\displaystyle \frac{ {n}^{2}}{( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 )}} - {\displaystyle \frac{2 n}{n + 2}} ) \cdot  ( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 ) & \displaystyle  = - \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{9}{n + 3}} \cdot  ( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 ) \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{ {n}^{2}}{( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 )}} \cdot  ( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 ) \hspace{0.278em} - \hspace{0.278em} {\displaystyle \frac{2 n}{n + 2}} \cdot  ( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 ) & \displaystyle  = - \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{9}{n + 3}} \cdot  ( n + 2 ) ( n + 3 ) \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{ {n}^{2}}{\cancel{( n + 2 )} \cancel{( n + 3 )}}} \cdot  \cancel{( n + 2 )} \cancel{( n + 3 )} \hspace{0.278em} - \hspace{0.278em} {\displaystyle \frac{2 n}{\cancel{n + 2}}} \cdot  \cancel{( n + 2 )} ( n + 3 ) & \displaystyle  = - \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{9}{\cancel{n + 3}}} \cdot  ( n + 2 ) \cancel{( n + 3 )} \\ \displaystyle {n}^{2} \hspace{0.278em} - \hspace{0.278em} 2 n ( n + 3 ) & \displaystyle  = - 9 ( n + 2 ) .\end{array}}
$$

$$

$$

- A horizontal shift left by $3$ units means we replace every $x$ in the original function with $(x + 3)$.
- A vertical shift up by $2$ units means we add $2$ to the entire function.

$$
r(x) = \dfrac{a - 5}{x} + 7
$$

To shift left $3$ units, we replace $x$ with $x + 3{:}$

$$
\dfrac{a - 5}{x + 3} + 7
$$

Then, to shift up $2$ units, we add $2$ to the whole expression:

$$
\left(\dfrac{a - 5}{x + 3} + 7\right) + 2
$$

Therefore, by simplifying, we find the equation that defines $s$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
s(x) &= (\frac{a - 5}{x + 3} + 7) + 2 \\
&= \frac{a - 5}{x + 3} + 9
\end{aligned}
$$" "To apply a transformation to the graph of a function, we modify its equation according to the direction of the shift:

$$
y=-5x^2 + 10x - 1
$$

where

$$
-5x^2 + 10x - 1 = 4x - k
$$

We need to determine the value of $k$ such that this equation has one real solution.

A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero:

$$
\mathcal{D} = 0
$$

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5x^{2} + 10x - 1 &= 4x - k \\
- 5x^{2} + 10x - 1 - 4x + k &= 0 \\
- 5x^{2} + 6x + (k - 1) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

$$
a = -5, \qquad b = 6, \qquad c = k-1
$$

So, computing the discriminant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
D &= b^{2} - 4ac \\
&= 6^{2} - 4(-5)(k - 1) \\
&= 36 + 20(k - 1) \\
&= 36 + 20k - 20 \\
&= 16 + 20k
\end{aligned}
$$

To have exactly one real solution, we need

$$
\mathcal{D} = 0{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
16 + 20k &= 0 \\
20k &= -16 \\
k &= -\frac{16}{20} \\
k &= -\frac{4}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the equation of the line is

$$
y=4x-\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)=4x+\dfrac{4}{5}
$$

To find the $x$-coordinate, we solve the original quadratic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5x^{2} + 6x + (-\frac{4}{5} - 1) &= 0 \\
- 5x^{2} + 6x - \frac{9}{5} &= 0 \\
- 25x^{2} + 30x - 9 &= 0 \\
- (25x^{2} - 30x + 9) &= 0 \\
- (5x - 3)^{2} &= 0 \\
5x - 3 &= 0 \\
x &= \frac{3}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the $y$-coordinate by substituting

$$
x=\dfrac{3}{5}
$$

into one of the two equations and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 4\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) + \frac{4}{5} \\
&= \frac{12}{5} + \frac{4}{5} \\
&= \frac{16}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is

$$
\Big(\dfrac{3}{5},\dfrac{16}{5}\Big)

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}
$$

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which coagulant enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\textrm{kg/L}$ of the coagulant enters the tank at a rate of $30\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *coagulant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =1.5\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which coagulant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which coagulant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $700\,\textrm{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $30\,\textrm{L/min}$ and leaves at $20\,\textrm{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
700 + 30t - 20t = (700+10t)\,\textrm{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of coagulant in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\dfrac{Q}{700+10t}\,\textrm{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $20\,\textrm{L/min},$ *coagulant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{700+10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{700+10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{700+10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{70+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =1.5-\frac{2Q}{70+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q=1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =12 \\ 0.5(70+0)+\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =12 \\ 35+\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =12 \\ \frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-23 \\ C & =-23(70)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.5(70+t)-\frac{23(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.5(70+t)-23{\left(\frac{70}{70+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of coagulant in the tank $8$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(8) & =0.5(70+8)-23{\left(\frac{70}{70+8}\right)}^{2} \\  & =39-23{\left(\frac{70}{78}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈20.48\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which additives exit the basin.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the basin remains $750\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of pollutant in the basin, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{750}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min},$ *pollutant* leaves at a rate of

$$

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$

In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.

In many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,

- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and

- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.

For example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\,\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\,300\,\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.

- A solution containing $20\,\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

To construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative 
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}$
describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}}
$$

We compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.

The rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =100\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.

Since the volume remains constant at $650\,\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{Q}{650}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{L}}.
$$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{Q}{130}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The net rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\text{in} - Q'_\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \dfrac{1}{130}Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \quad Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g}}
$$" "In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.

$$

$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\geq 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[10((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}+7(\lambda +n){a}_{n}+(3{a}_{n-1}-{a}_{n})]{x}^{\lambda +n} &= {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[10(\lambda +n)^{2}{a}_{n}-3(\lambda +n){a}_{n}-{a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1}]{x}^{\lambda +n} \\ &= {x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }[(10(\lambda +n)^{2}-3(\lambda +n)-1){a}_{n}+3{a}_{n-1}]{x}^{n}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, we obtain

$$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\cos(4t)=30I+500q+5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.

$$

You may have seen already that for the parabola

with

the **axis of symmetry** of this parabola is given by the following formula:

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We're now in a position to derive this formula.

Since

$$
a \neq 0
$$

we can take out a factor of $a$ from the right-hand side in the parabola formula:

$$
y = a\left(x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + \dfrac{c}{a} \right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract*

$$
\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2{:}
$$

$$
\underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2}_{\textrm{perfect square}} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2+ {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

$$

$$

$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$

$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}

$$

x &= 2n - 1

$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Now, if our surface $S$ is defined as $z= f(x,y),$ then it can always be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf r(x,y)= \left\langle x,\: y,\: f(x,y)\right\rangle  \qquad (x,y)  \in D.

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂f}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle -\frac{∂f}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂f}{∂y},\,1\right\rangle ,\end{aligned}

and using the fact that $z = f(x,y),$ we can write this as

$$

The surface $S$ shown above consists of the part of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ that lies under the plane $z=9.$ Let's compute the surface area of $S.$

The plane intersects the paraboloid when $z=9.$ Thus, the curve that describes the intersection points is

$$
x^2+y^2 = 9,
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Therefore, our surface can be described by the equations

$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{(x,y): \, x^2 + y^2 \le 9\right\}.
$$

To compute the surface area of $S,$ we use the formula

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}

$$"] [17592186179597 :question/worked-solution "The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$"] [17592186179606 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$"] [17592186179607 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$"] [17592186179608 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$

$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/2b/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}\right)=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\left(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot \left(\frac{t}{2}\right)-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186179609 :question/worked-solution "First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{θ \to  0}\frac{\tan 2θ}{θ} &= \lim_{θ \to  0}\left(\left(\frac{\sin 2θ}{\cos 2θ}\right)\right)/(θ) \\
&= \lim_{θ \to  0}\left(\frac{\sin 2θ}{θ} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos 2θ}\right) \\
&= \lim_{θ \to  0}\frac{\sin 2θ}{θ} \cdot lim_(θ → 0)\frac{1}{\cos 2θ}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

- Consider the first limit. Notice that as $\theta \to 0$, both numerator and denominator approach $0$. So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get
$$
\displaystyle \lim_{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{\theta} = \dfrac{0}{0},
$$
which is an indeterminate form. Instead, let's recall the following special limit:
$$
\displaystyle \lim_{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin x}{x} =1
$$We rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:
$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to 0}\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\operatorname{sin}2\theta }{\theta } & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}\left(2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}2\theta }{2\theta }\right) \\  & =2\cdot \lim_{\theta \to 0}\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\sin {\color{blue}{2\theta }}}{{\color{blue}{2\theta }}}\end{aligned}
$$Let $x = 2\theta$. Then, since $x\to0$ as $\theta \to 0$, we have
$$

- Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get
$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$"] [17592186179909 :question/problem "Calculate $∇\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}F\right)$ for the vector field $F$ where

$$"] [17592186179911 :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

In our case, we have

$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ z{e}^{y} & 3 & -x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left[\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(3)\right]i-\left[\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(z{e}^{y})\right]j+\left[\frac{∂}{∂x}(3)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(z{e}^{y})\right]k \\  & =(0-0)i-((-1)-{e}^{y})j+(0-z{e}^{y})k \\  & =({e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-G) & =∇\times F-∇\times G \\  & =({e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k-[2x{e}^{y}\,i-2{e}^{y}\,j] \\  & =({e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k-2x{e}^{y}\,i+2{e}^{y}\,j \\  & =-2x{e}^{y}\,i+(3{e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k.\end{aligned}

Finally, evaluating at the point $(-2,0,3),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F-G))(-2,0,3) & =-2(-2){e}^{0}\,i+(3{e}^{0}+1)\,j-3{e}^{0}\,k \\  & =4\,i+4\,j-3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186179912 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,0,\operatorname{ln}⁡x⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)={e}^{2x}.$ Given that

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(1,1,-4).$"] [17592186179912 :question/worked-solution "We shall use the following identity:

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right)=-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right)\text{d}x=\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+1 \\ C & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=9-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\,m.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186179914 :question/worked-solution "![](images/4c/4c997edf5c34a22fc71eac697c161434797c938df40760ae1089fd6e62db795d.png)

\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+y=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =y-x=3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\left(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t))\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}t)-(3(\operatorname{sin}t-\operatorname{cos}t))\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t-\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =9t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9(2\pi -0) \\  & =18\pi \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180041 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

Along the curve $C,$ we have

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
