The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(1-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(1-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(1-x) & =0 \\ 1-x & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=1\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $\frac{k}{2}>0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{k}{2}<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=1\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right)=k(1-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right)\text{d}x=\int k(1-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k\left(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\right)+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k\left(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-x\right)+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k\left(0-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}\right)+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k\left(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\right)+3.
$$

Also, since $v=3\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=\frac{3}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k\left(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\right)+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(3)^{2} & =k\left(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}\right)+3 \\ \frac{9}{2} & =\frac{3}{8}k+3 \\ \frac{3}{8}k & =\frac{3}{2} \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-2{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-4{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{8x-4{x}^{2}+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{8x-4{x}^{2}+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(1)=\sqrt{8(1)-4(1)^{2}+6}=\sqrt{10}\,m/s.
$$"] [17592186180096 :question/worked-solution "![](images/0f/0f8f7773a5e55c81de553eccf684f9a6128dd6e76e06b9040d5953371e72184f.png)

$$"] [17592186180100 :question/worked-solution "The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $1.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=1.5\cdot (2x+1)=(3x+1.5)\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(3x+1.5)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\left[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x\right]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({2}^{2}+2-({1}^{2}+1)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(6-2) \\  & =6\,J.\end{aligned}

$$"] [17592186180174 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\cdot 1+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t+2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={\left[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}\right]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\left[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}\right]-[0] \\  & =2+8 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180175 :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$

$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t)) & =x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$

$$"] [17592186180176 :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\left(y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{t}^{2}\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡t-{\sin }^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{t}^{2}\,dt\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180185 :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following  linearity properties for divergence:

- $∇\cdot (kF)=k∇\cdot F$

- $∇\cdot (F+G)=∇\cdot F+∇\cdot G.$

In our case, we have

$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\cdot F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{2y}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{2}{y}.\end{aligned}

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot (F+2G) & =∇\cdot F+2∇\cdot G \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{2}{y}+2\cdot \left(-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{2}{y}-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{y}+\frac{2}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1+y)}{{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180186 :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ {x}^{2}z & 0 & {x}^{2}y\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left[\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(0)\right]i-\left[\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z)\right]j+\left[\frac{∂}{∂x}(0)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}z)\right]k \\  & =({x}^{2}-0)i-(2xy-{x}^{2})j+(0-0)k \\  & ={x}^{2}\,i+({x}^{2}-2xy)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$

$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(1,1,1),$ we get

$$
(∇\times (F+2G))(1,1,1)=3\,i-3\,j-2\,k.
$$"] [17592186180212 :question/problem "Evaluate $\lim_{x \to  π/2}\left(\sin \left(x - \frac{π}{2}\right)\right)/(2x - π)$."] [17592186180284 :question/worked-solution "The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

where $C>0$ is an integration constant. Let's now derive this formula.

Our differential equation is separable, so we start by separating variables and then integrating with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$ 

$$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot \left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\left(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is,

$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$"] [17592186180729 :tutorial/content "We can use well-known series to recover the sequence associated with a generating function.

One series that occurs regularly for this purpose is the geometric series

$$
\dfrac{1}{1-r} = 1+r+r^2+r^3+\cdots\,
$$

For example, let's determine the general term $a_n$ for

$$
n\geq 0
$$

of the sequence with generating function

$$
\dfrac{3}{5+2x}
$$

First, we rewrite the generating function by factoring out the term of the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{1-r}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{5 + 2x} &= \frac{3}{5} \cdot (1)/\left(\left(1 + \frac{2}{5}x\right)\right) \\
&= \frac{3}{5} \cdot (1)/\left(\left[1 - \left(-\frac{2}{5}x\right)\right]\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we expand the right-hand side using the geometric series formula:

$$
\frac{3}{5}\left[1 + \left(-\frac{2}{5}x\right) + \left(-\frac{2}{5}x\right)^{2} + \left(-\frac{2}{5}x\right)^{3} + ⋯\right]
$$

This simplifies to

$$
\frac{3}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)x + \frac{3}{5}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^{2}x^{2} + \frac{3}{5}\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^{3}x^{3} + ⋯
$$

Finally, we identify that the general term $a_n$ of our sequence is

$$
a_n = \dfrac{3}{5}\left(-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^n
$$"] [17592186180732 :tutorial/content "In some cases, a generating function can be written as a combination of simpler functions that, in turn, can be further reduced to geometric series.

For example, suppose we have the generating function

$$

$$

To calculate the generating series, we first factor the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{2x+6}{2-x-6x^2} = \dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)}

Then, we express the function as a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)} = \dfrac{2}{1-2x} + \dfrac{2}{2+3x}
$$

Next, we expand each of the partial fractions as a geometric series:

For the first sequence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{1 - 2x} &= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 2x} \\
&= 2 \cdot (1 + (2x) + (2x)^{2} + (2x)^{3}) \\
&= (2) + (2)^{2}x + (2)^{3}x^{2} + (2)^{4}x^{3} + ⋯
\end{aligned}

The general term of the sequence associated with this generating series is

$$
b_n=2^{n+1}

$$

$$
ax^2+bx+c = 0,
$$

where $a\neq 0.$ We can derive a general solution to this equation by completing the square.

First, let's subtract $c$ from both sides to isolate the variable terms:

$$
ax^2+bx = -c
$$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing by $a$ gives

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x = -\dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side and move the constant terms to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{b}{2a}x=-\frac{c}{a} \\ {\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)}^{2}-{\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)}^{2} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)}^{2}-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)}^{2} & =\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}}-\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the terms on the right-hand side over a common factor of $4a^2,$ we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2  = \dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}.
$$

Taking the square root of both sides yields

$$
x + \dfrac{b}{2a}  = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}}
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{b}{2a} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a}\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.
$$

This formula is called the **quadratic formula**. You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons."] [17592186185307 :tutorial/content "Recall that our goal is to find new features that are uncorrelated — equivalently, features whose covariance matrix is diagonal. In the previous section, we found an orthogonal matrix $V$ such that $V^T\!CV$ is diagonal. This motivates defining a **transformed observation matrix** $Y = XV.$ The columns of this new matrix $Y$ are our new features.

Substituting $C = \dfrac{1}{n-1} X^T X$ into the expression $V^T\!CV$ and noting that $(XV)^T = V^T X^T{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\underbrace{{V}^{T}\,CV}_{\text{diagonal}} & ={V}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X\right)V \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y}_{\text{covariance of Y}}\end{aligned}
$$

The covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal, so the new features $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m$ are uncorrelated. The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues of $C,$ so $\text{Var}(y_i) = \lambda_i.$ By arranging the columns of $V$ in order of decreasing eigenvalue, the new features are also arranged in order of decreasing variance.

The columns of $V$ (the unit eigenvectors of $C$) are called the **principal components**. The $1$st *principal component* is the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue, the $2$nd corresponds to the second-largest, and so on.

This procedure is the core of **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)**. To summarize:

*We define the change-of-variables $Y = XV,$ where the columns of $V$ are the **principal components** of the data, arranged in order of decreasing eigenvalue. This ensures that:*

- *The new features $y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m$ are uncorrelated (diagonal covariance).*

- *The new features are arranged in order of decreasing variance ($\text{Var}(y_i) = \lambda_i$).*

Now let's understand what these vectors mean in terms of the original data."] [17592186185313 :tutorial/content "When we take a power of a trigonometric function, we write the power after the function but before the argument.

$$"] [17592186185326 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a sample of size $n,$ the sample variance $S^2$ is given by

$$
S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2.
$$

We will now prove that $S^2$ is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2,$ that is,

$$
\textrm{E}\left[S^2\right] = \sigma^2.
$$

A major step towards this goal is to find the expected value of the sum of squares term:

$$
\textrm E \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 \right] \qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

First, consider the following sum of squares:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2
$$

We can rewrite this term by adding and subtracting the sample mean $\overline X,$ as follows:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \left((X_i - \overline X) + (\overline X -  \mu)\right)^2
$$

Squaring and applying the laws of summations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{(({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})+(\overset{―}{X}-\mu ))}^{2} &= {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}+2({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )+(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2}) \\ &= {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}+2{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2} \\ &= {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}+2(\overset{―}{X}-\mu ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2} \\ &= {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2} \\ &= {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}+n(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where we have used the fact that $$
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \overline X) = 0
$$ and that $(\overline X - \mu)$ does not depend on $i$. Thus, we have that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 =  \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 + n(\overline X-  \mu)^2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 -  n(\overline X-  \mu)^2  . \qquad\qquad (\ast\ast)
$$

Notice that the left-hand side is the summation term $(\ast)$ we wish to find the expectation of.

Now, we make use of the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[({X}_{i}-\mu )^{2}] & ={\sigma }^{2} \\ \text{E}[(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2}] & =\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Finding the expectation of $(\ast\ast),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}] & =\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\mu )^{2}]-n\text{E}[(\overset{―}{X}-\mu )^{2}] \\  & =n{\sigma }^{2}-n\cdot \frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n} \\  & =n{\sigma }^{2}-{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =(n-1){\sigma }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}\right] &=\frac{(n-1){\sigma }^{2}}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

This tells us that the statistic

$$
\dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2
$$

is a *biased* estimate of $\sigma^2.$ Therefore, to form an unbiased estimate of $\sigma^2,$ we must divide our summation term by $n-1,$ not $n.$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{S}^{2}] & =\text{E}\left[\frac{1}{n-1}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})^{2}\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}\cdot (n-1){\sigma }^{2} \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

as required."] [17592186185342 :tutorial/content "![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

The polar curve shown above is defined as

$$
r(\theta) = 4 - 3\cos \theta, \qquad 0\leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

We have $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ at the point $P.$ The tangent to the curve at $P$ is shown in the diagram. 

To find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at $P,$ we follow four steps.

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$

Using techniques that we've previously discussed, we can show that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P.$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\right)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{0+3}{0-4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\left(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\left(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left( 0, 4 \right).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x+4\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186185349 :tutorial/content "For a geometric sequence with the first term $a_1$ and common ratio $r,$ we have the following convergence properties:

Since $|r| > 1,$ the sequence is divergent."] [17592186185351 :tutorial/content "We can compute trigonometric ratios using the sum and difference formulas for tangent together with the Pythagorean identity.

Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v$, we have

$$
\cos u = \dfrac {3}{5}, \qquad \tan v = 3
$$

How can we find the value of $\tan(u+v)$ given that $u$ lies in the fourth quadrant?

First, we recall the sum formula for tangent:

$$
\tan(u+v) = \dfrac{\tan{u}+\tan{v}}{1-\tan{u}\tan{v}}
$$

We need to find the value of $\tan u$. To do that, we first find the value of $\sin u$ using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 u + \cos^2 u= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin^2 u = 1- \cos^2 u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin^{2} u &= 1 - \cos^{2} u \\
&= 1 - \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2} \\
&= 1 - \frac{3^{2}}{5^{2}} \\
&= 1 - \frac{9}{25} \\
&= \frac{25}{25} - \frac{9}{25} \\
&= \frac{16}{25}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin u &= ± \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\
&= ± \frac{4}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the fourth quadrant, where sine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have

$$
\sin u = -\dfrac{4}{5}
$$

We can now compute $\tan u$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan u &= \frac{\sin u}{\cos u} = \left(\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)\right)/\left(\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\right) =-\frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the sum formula for the tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan (u + v) &= \frac{\tan u + \tan v}{1 - \tan u\tan v} \\

\displaystyle \int (x+x^3)\,\textrm d x?
$$ 

According to the **sum rule**, the integral of the sum of functions is equal to the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\int (f(x) \pm g(x))\,\textrm d x = \int f(x) \,\textrm d x \pm \int g(x) \,\textrm d x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1}\right)+\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+{c}_{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+({c}_{1}+{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Let's see another example."] [17592186185384 :tutorial/content "Let's complete the square on the following expression:

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$

$$

Now, here's the trick. We *add* and *then subtract* $\left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2$, writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{4}}$ last:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x  + \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

As a result, the first three terms now form a perfect square!

We wish to compute the probability $P(10\leq Y \leq 14).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$

*The **volume** of a sphere **increases** at a rate **inversely proportional** to its **radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a sphere* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- We're told that $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t}$ *increases* at a rate *inversely proportional to its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{k}{r},
$$

where $k > 0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$

The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by

$$
V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{r} \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\left(\frac{k}{r}\right)}{4\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{4\pi {r}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K = \dfrac{k}{4\pi} > 0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{K}{r^3}.
$$"] [17592186187999 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

> *Suppose that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma$. $$

$$

The expected value and the variance of a uniform random variable $X_i \sim U[a,b]$ can be found as

$$
\textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= \frac{a + b}{2} \\

&= \frac{6}{2} \\
&= 3, \\
σ^{2} &= \operatorname{Var} [X_{i}] \\
&= ((b - a)^{2})/(12) \\
&= ((5 - 1)^{2})/(12) \\
&= \frac{16}{12} \\
&= \frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of $X$, we obtain

$$
X \mid ∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N\left(110 \cdot 3, 110 \cdot \frac{4}{3}\right); ∼N\left(330, \frac{440}{3}\right)
$$"] [17592186188000 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

$$"] [17592186188002 :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""] [17592186188003 :question/worked-solution "The marginal density function for $Y$ when $y \geq 1$ is

$$"] [17592186188004 :question/worked-solution "When a polar curve is differentiable at a point $\theta_0$, there is a horizontal tangent at $\theta_0$ if

$$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta_0)}{x'(\theta_0)}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta (1+{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{-\cancel{cot}\theta \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta (1+{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{-\cancel{cot}\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta (1+{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }\right).\end{aligned}

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned}

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2,
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\textrm{Var}[X].$
We compute $\textrm{E}[X^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\left(x+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}\right)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\left({x}^{3}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\right)\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\left[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\right]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\right)\text{d}y \\  & ={\left[\frac{1}{4}y+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}-{\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\textrm{E}[Y^2]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\left(x+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}\right)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\left(x{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{4}\right)\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\left[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x{y}^{4}\right]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{4}\right)\text{d}y \\  & ={\left[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}+\frac{3}{10}{y}^{5}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{7}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{15}-{\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{73}{960}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{17}{48}-\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{5}{8}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{96}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
\Sigma
=

=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\displaystyle \frac{11}{144}} & - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{96}} \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{96}} & {\displaystyle \frac{73}{960}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$"] [17592186188189 :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma$. where $N$ is the population size.

is called the finite population correction factor, and it is appropriate to use it when $n > 5\%\cdot N$ (the sample includes more than $5\%$ of the entire population).

$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

$$

$$"] [17592186189374 :tutorial/content "So, it seems that the curve $r = 1-\sin\theta$ has a vertical tangent at $\theta = \dfrac\pi 2.$ However, to be sure of this, we need to check that the tangent lines' slopes grow to infinity as we approach $\theta = \dfrac \pi 2.$ In other words, we need to check that

- Applying L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the left-sided limit, we get

Suppose we have two normal populations $X$ and $Y{:}$

$X \sim N(\mu_x, \sigma^2_x), \qquad Y \sim N(\mu_y, \sigma^2_y)$
where $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means, and $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are the population variances.

In a previous lesson, we saw that the difference between the sample means is given by

$$
\overline{X} - \overline{Y} \sim N\left(\mu_x - \mu_y,\dfrac{\sigma_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{\sigma_y^2}{n_y} \right)
$$

where $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means, and $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes. By $z$-scoring this result, we can express this as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{\sigma_y^2}{n_y}}} \sim N(0,1)
$$

In most practical situations, the population variances $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are unknown and must be replaced with estimates $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$. In this situation, the random variable

$$
\begin{aligned}
T &= ((X^(―) - Y^(―)) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/\left(\sqrt{\frac{S_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{S_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

follows a $t$-distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

We can approximate the number of degrees of freedom $k$ in various ways.

- *Method 1:* We can approximate the degrees of freedom using the so-called **Welch-Satterthwaite approximation:**
$$
\displaystyle k \approx \frac{\left(\dfrac{s_x^2}{n_x} + \dfrac{s_y^2}{n_y} \right)^2}{\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{s_x^2}{n_x} \right)^2}{n_x - 1} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{s_y^2}{n_y} \right)^2}{n_y - 1}}
$$
where the final result is rounded *down* to the nearest integer.
- *Method 2:* We can also approximate the degrees of freedom using the formula
$k = \min(n_x - 1, n_y - 1)$
where $\min(a,b)$ denotes the **minimum** of $a$ and $b$.

In this lesson, we'll use the second method. You'll get practice applying the first method in separate lessons.

Please bear in mind that this method is simpler but also more conservative:

- Under Method 2, our estimate for the degrees of freedom will be *smaller* than Method 1.
- Thus, the tails of the resulting distribution will be fatter, leading to *larger* critical values for a given significance level $\alpha$. Note that "larger critical values" here means larger in the absolute sense, i.e.,
$$
|t_{k_1}| >  |t_{k_2}|
$$
whenever $k_1 < k_2$ for critical values $t_{k_1}$ and $t_{k_2}$.
- Therefore, the probability of a Type I error (i.e., rejecting $H_0$ when it is true) *decreases.*

Remember that as $k\to\infty$, the $t$-distribution approaches $N(0,1)$. The standard normal curve has *extremely thin* tails!

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral.

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y-x}{x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\left[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{u}{v}\,du\right]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}[{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}{\left[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}\right]}_{0}^{1}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198016 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} 
\longrightarrow 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]}
$$

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \:  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y) =  (2x+y)y^2
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x+y,
\qquad
v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{2},0\right) & =\left(2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0,0\right) \\  & =(3,0) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{2},0\right) & =\left(2\cdot \frac{5}{2}+0,0\right) \\  & =(5,0) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2\cdot 1+3,3) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(0,3) & =(2\cdot 0+3,3) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 5, \quad 0 \leq v \leq 3 \big\}
$$

![](images/c2/c296b1ee0451686608ec4b06c29d114ff1918233886d8471d3b2c118851aa25e.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =\dfrac12
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral.

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y){y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\left[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\right]}_{0}^{3}\cdot {\left[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}\right]}_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 8 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198019 :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $\Delta$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $\Delta$ separately:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=\left(u\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=\left(u\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right)\right).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{6}.
$$ 

Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. It lies between the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=3$ and $$

$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. It lies between the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$

Therefore, the image $D$ of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that is enclosed between

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/79/79869cf64ec827934397588e25d06cba0c9d12c35ecbea5cdd6aaf6cfcf12e24.png)"] [17592186198020 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(1)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(1)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2v & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨x+y,\hspace{0.222em}x-y,\hspace{0.222em}xyz⟩{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y={v}^{2}\,z=1} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2}+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨{u}^{2}+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩ \\  & =({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\cdot 0+({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\cdot 0+{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\cdot 4uv \\  & =4{u}^{3}{v}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}4{u}^{3}{v}^{3}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198021 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-y}_{P},\,\underbrace{x}_{Q},\,\underbrace{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\left(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R\right)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2x)-(x)\cdot (2y)+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-2xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\left[{x}^{2}y+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+2y\right]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}+2\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left({x}^{2}+\frac{7}{3}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\left[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7x}{3}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198022 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}

=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂u}(1+2u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂v}(1+2u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-2,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}x,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩|}_{x=1+2u+v\,y=u+v\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}1+2u+v,\hspace{0.222em}u+v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}1+2u+v,\hspace{0.222em}u+v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)\cdot (-2)+(1+2u+v)\cdot 3+(u+v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u+2v+3+6u+3v+u+v \\  & =5u+6v+3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}x,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u+6v+3)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(5u+6v+3)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[5uv+3{v}^{2}+3v]_{v=0}^{v=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5u+6)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & ={\left[\frac{5}{2}{u}^{2}+6u\right]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =10+12 \\  & =22.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198026 :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $\Delta$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

![](images/81/81650cc0dc43537ec916f2c68af66ed5581c861812f276dda2b23baccc2fb491.png)"] [17592186198027 :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $z,$ treating $x$ and $y$ as constants:

$$"] [17592186198031 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$

over the domain

D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 2, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3u+2v)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3u+2v)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z+2y,\,3y+z,\,x-z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=-3u+2v} \\  & =⟨(-3u+2v)+2v,\,3v+(-3u+2v),\,u-(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(-3u+4v)\cdot (3)+(-3u+5v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+12v+6u-10v+4u-2v \\  & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+2y,\,3y+z,\,x-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}u\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is ${\color{blue}u}.$"] [17592186198032 :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $\mathbf F =  \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1+xyz\rangle$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/97/977d93ad65c9f3690def4242f98f4de5e5c89faf02fe47d06f5ed251d8a4a292.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $\mathbf F$ through these two sides.

- Let $S_1$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z = 1$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_1$ is

$$
\mathbf n_1 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z = 1$ on $S_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =1+xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}1+xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}1+xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}1+xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\left[x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y\right]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+\frac{1}{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\left[y+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let $S_2$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_2$ is

$$
\mathbf n_2 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z = 0$ on $S_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =-\text{Area}(D) \\  & =-(1-0)(1-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+(-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198034 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y = h(x,z),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,z) = \left\langle x, \: h(x,z),\: z \right\rangle.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =\left\langle 1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,0\right\rangle  \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =\left\langle 0,\frac{∂h}{∂z},\,1\right\rangle \end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & \frac{∂h}{∂x} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{∂h}{∂z} & 1\end{vmatrix}=\left\langle \frac{∂h}{∂x},\,-1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂z}\right\rangle .\end{aligned}
$$

However, notice that the $\mathbf j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction:

$$
\mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_x = - \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z =   \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right \rangle
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,z))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot \left\langle -\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,1,\,-\frac{∂h}{∂z}\right\rangle \,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\left(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}+Q-R\frac{∂h}{∂z}\right)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198035 :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $z$, treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}y+x{z}^{2}\,dz\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}y+x{z}^{2}\,dz]dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\left[{x}^{2}yz+\frac{x{z}^{3}}{3}\right]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y(1-0)+x\left(\frac{1}{3}-0\right)\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left[{\int }_{-1}^{2}{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x\,dx\right]dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\left[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}\right]}_{x=-1}^{x=2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{3}y({2}^{3}-(-1)^{3})+\frac{1}{6}({2}^{2}-(-1)^{2}))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}3y+\frac{1}{2}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}3y+\frac{1}{2}\,dx & ={\left[\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{y}{2}\right]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =(6+1)-\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198036 :question/worked-solution "Since the domain of integration $R = [1,2] \times \left[0,\pi/2\right] \times [1,4]$ is a rectangular box and the integrand can be expressed as $f(x)\cdot g(y)\cdot h(z),$ we can rewrite our repeated integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{x}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy{\int }_{1}^{4}dz\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating each integral separately, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}\,dx{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy\,{\int }_{1}^{4}dz & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot (4-1) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot \left(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\right)\cdot 3 \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-0)\cdot (0+1)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{1}^{4} \dfrac{\sin{y}}{x} \: \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x = 3\ln 2.
$$"] [17592186198038 :question/worked-solution "We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration $u_1(x,y),$ $u_2(x,y),$ $v_1(y),$ $v_2(y),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{z}^{2} e^{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y
=
